div.head: ELECTION OF CORONER.
div.p: ELECTION OF CORONER.

910 THE FREEHOLDERS OF THE WEST DERBY DIVISION. MY LORDS AND aHNTLEIZEN,—The death of T. W. Barber, Esquire, has caused a vacancy in the Coronership of your Divi- sion, and I most respectfully offer myself as a lis and compe- tent candidate for the appointment.. I am the •,01-u• partner in the firm of Messieurs Brighouse, Blighouse.-„,rr.l...nee, soi chores, of this town, and have practised since tio eginoing tk• year 1871 in Ormskirk and Southport, both places being in your Division (having previously served my art Mies with the well known Sim of Messrs. Lace Banner, Gill, Newton, and Busby, of Liverpool.) I have bad a varied and extensive ex- perience in all the courts where solicitors have audience, In- cluding those at Liverpool, Warrington, Wigan, St. Helms, Bedford Leigh, Ormskirk, and Soutbpirt, having appeared in upwards of 2,000 cases before coroners, magistrates, and county court, judges. 1 have frequently appeared before the late aoroner and his predecessor (0. E. D. iffield, Esq.), when they held their enquiries, and more par- ticularly on the enquiries into the disastrous railway collision at Burscough Junction, near Ormskirk, the explosion at the foundry at Ormskirk, the explosion at the Melling Powder Works, Liverpool, and several colliery explosions ; and I have acted on carious rccasions in a judicial capacity as arbitrator. I may, therefore, seasonably say that I have acquired the knowledge necessary to preside over a Coroner's Court. I hold the office of Vice-Chairman for the Board of Guardians for the Ormskirk Poor Law Union, which includes 21 townships. I am a member of every committee in the town connected with institutions for the carrying out of philanthropic objects, such as the Ormskirk Dispensary, the Working Men's Institute, and others. All the solicitors in my own town, without a single exception, honour me by their support. I now respectfully solicit your vote and interest on my behalf, and if suciessful in my candidature it shad be my constint study to discharge the trust reposed in me without fear or favour, and with a constant endeavour to retain your confi- dence. I will, in a few days, send you a list of the Noblemen and Gentlemen who have kindly promised 1119 their support. I am well acquainted with the whole of the West Derby Hun- dred ; and although-well known to 0 large number of tke Pr eehol dere, yet there will, necessarily, be some to wkom I am not known. This must be my excuse for any seeming ego- tism in my address. I beg 10 subscribe myself. My Lords and Gentlemen, Your most obedient servant, MUEL B fIIGMOUIII C. Ormskirk, 3rd January, 1884.

div.p: VottVP.

- - - OLD AND NEW YEAR. New Year met me somewhat sad; Old Year leaves me tired, Stripped of favourite things I had, Balked of much desired; ' Yet farther on my road to-day, God willing, farther on my way. New Year, coming on apace, What have you to give me? Bring you scathe or bring you grace, Face me with an honest face; You shall not deceive me; Be it good or ill, be it what you will, It needs shall help me on my road, My rugged way to heaven, please God. .--Christina G. Rossetti. POEM BY LORD DUFFERIN'S MOTHER. To My Dear San on His 21st Birtlzday. WITH A SILVER LAMP. How shall I bless thee? Haman Love Is all too poor in passionate words! The heart aches with a sense above All language that the lip affords! Therefore, a symbol shall express My love ;—a thing nor rare nor strange, But yet—eternal—measureless— Knowing no shadow and no change! Light! which of all the lovely shows To our poor world of shadows given, The fervent Prophet-voices chose attr.bute of Heaven! At a most solemn pause we stand! From this day forth, for evermore, The weak, but loving, human hand Must cease to guide thee as of yore! Then as through life thy footsteps stray And earthly beaons dimly shine, " Let there be Light" upon thy way, And holier guidance far than mine. "Let there be Light" in thy clear soul, When Passion tempts, or Doubts assail, When Grief's dark tempests o'er thee roll "Let there be Light" that shall not fail! So—angel guarded—ruay'st thou tread The narrow path, which few may find; And at the end look back, nor dread To count the vanished years behind! And pray, that she whose hand doth trace This heart-warm prayer, when life is past, May see and know thy blessed face In God's own glorious Light at last! Julie 2194 1847. Good Wards.

- "That's what beats me," soliloquised the small boy, as he gazed at his ma's slipper. WHERE INDEED? "No, sir," said a practical Yankee— "no bric-a-brac on the mantel for me. It's a nuisance. Where's a man to put his feet ?" An old ex-cannibal out in the Sandwich Islands, now that be is converted to Christianity, has erected a tombstone to the memory of his father, with the following inscription:— "He was a tender husband, and a most nutritious father." The son of a hatcher had great difficulty in fractions, although his teacher did his very best. "Now let us sup- pose," said the teacher' "that a customer came to your father to buy five pounds of meat, and he had only four to sell—what would he do?" "Keep his hand on the meat while he was weighing it," was the candid answer. HOW TO BE CRARMING.—Here is a bit of sensible advice for the girls as given by the Youth's Crntpanion:—The popu- lar belief among young girls is that it is only a pretty face which will bring to them the admiration and love which they naturally crave. No books, it is said, have a larger sale than those writterf that give rules for beauty, recipes to des- troy fat or freckles, and to improye the skin or figure. Now, no recipe will change the shape of the nose, or the colour of an eye. But any girl, by daily baths and whole- some food, and by breathing pure air, can render her com- plexion clear and soft. Her hair, nails, and teeth can be daintily kept. Her clothes, however cheap, can be fresh and becoming in colour. She can train her mind, even of ordin- ary capacity, to be alert and earnest; and if she adds to these a sincere, kindly, sunny temper, she will win friends anllove as surely SS if all the fairies had brought her gifts atiltr birth. But it is of no use for a woman whose person is soiled and untidy, and whose temper is selfish and irritable at home to hope to cheat anybody by putting on fine clothes' a smile for company. The thick,muddy skin andsoured and expression will betray her. "John," said an artist the _ other day to a Chinaman who was unwillingly acting as a model, " ssaile. If you don't look pleasant, I'll not pay you." "No use," grumbled the washerrnan. "If Chinaman' feelee ugly all the time, he lookee ugly," which is true of every other man and woman in the world as well as of John. Chinaman. Jane Wehh Carlyle could so charm men that a stranger, meeting her in a stage-coach, followed her for miles post-haste to return a parasol which she had dropped. The charm lay not in beauty, but in her bright vivacity of manner, and the keen sympathy which shone through her features. ADVICE TO A YOUNG MAN.—My son, don't be in too great a hurry to accept "advanced opinions." It is "the thing" to be "advanced " in this progressive day and generation, but there's a heap of shallowness in it. Did you never notice, my son, that the man who tells you he cannot believe the Bible is usually able to believe almost anything else? You will find men, my son, who turn with horror and utter disbelief of the Bible, and joyfully em- brace the teachings of Buddha. It is quite the thing just now, my son, for a civilised, enlightened man, brought up In a Christian country and an age of wisdom, to be a Buddhist. And if you ask six men who profess Buddhism who Buddha was', one of them will tell you he was an Egyptian soothsayer, who lived two hundred years before Moses. Another will tell you that he brought letters from Phcenicia and introduced them in Greece; a third will tell you that she was a beautiful woman of Farther India, bound by her vows to perpetual chastity; a fourth will, with little hesitation, say he was a Bramha of the ninth degree and a holy disciple of Confucius; and of the other two, one will frankly admit that,he doesn't know, and the other will say, with Some indecision, that he was either a dervish of the Nile (whatever that is) or a felo de se, he I can't be positive which. Before you propose to know more than anybody and everybody else, my son, be very certain that you are abreast, at least, of two-thirds of your fellow- men. I don't want to suppress any inclination you may have toward genuine free thought and careful, honest in- vestigation, my son. I only want you to avoid the great fault of atheism in this day and generation; I don't want to see you try to build a six-store 7. house on a one-storey foundation. Before you criticise, condemn, and finally revise the work of creation, my son, be pretty confident that you know something about it as it is, and don't, as a man who is older in years and experience than yourself, don%, let me implore you, don't turn this world upside down and sit on it, and flatten it entirely out, until you have made or secured another one for the rest of as to live in while you demolish the old one. If ever you should deve- lop into an " advanced " atheist, my sort, just do that mach for the rest of mi.—Burlington Ilatokseye. HOUSES WITH SECRET CHAMBERS. Apirt from the romance and legendary lore associated with many of our old country houses, one of their most interesting features is the secret chamber, which is not only curious as a relic of architectural ingenuity, bat has been in most cases so skil- fully contrived as to escape detection from even the most experienced eye. These secret chambers were not uncom- mon in old Lancashire houses. Thus, at Widnes, near War- rington, there is a picturesque Tudor mansion with one of these hiding places. Some years ago, too, in some fields adjoining this residence were discovered various relics, amongst them arms, coins, tobacco pipes, dm., which, it has been suggested, indicate encampments of, Roundhead, and probably afterwards of Dutch, soldiers. At Mains Hall, in the parish of Kirkham, a secret room was accidentally dis- covered by some workmen behind a stack of chimneys, and another one in an old house in Goosnargh, called Ashes, which has two small cavities in its centre wall, which is about four feet thick. Lydyate Hall also, as well as Speke Hall, both in Lancashire, had secret chambers, a fall description of which is given by Mr. Gibson in his interest- ing little volume entitled, " Lydyate Hall and its Associa- tions." To these we may also add Barwick Hall, and Stonyhurst, the seat of the Sherbournes. Amongst the houses of this class in Lincolnshire may be noticed Upton Hall, where there is a secret chamber most cleverly con- trived. It is about eight feet long, five feet broad, and just high enough to allow a person to stand upright. The open- ing was accidentally aseertaiaed by removing a beam be- hind a single step between two servants' bedrooms. Lips- comb, in his "History of Buckinghamshire," refers to Dimon Hall, near Aylesbury, the seat of Judge Mayne, one of the regicides, to whom it is reported to have given shel- ter at the time of the Restoration. Referring to instances in the north of England, may be noticed Netherhall, near Maryport, Cumberland, the eat of the old family of Henhouse. In this mansions there is reported to be a veritable secret chamber, its exact position in the house being known but to Itstv is opaerrnsed—the heir-at. law and the family solicitor. that never has the secret of this hidden room been revealedal to more than two living persons at a time. It has no window, has hitherto defied the ingenuity of every visitor staym a in nd the house, in spite of all endeavours made to discover it. g This Netherhall tradition is very similar to the celebrated one connected with Glamis, only in the latter case the secret chamber possesses a window, which, nevertheless, has not led to the identification of the room. The two secret chambers of Danby Hall in Wensleydale, Yorkshire, deserve notice. One of these was discovered between the hall fire- place and the west wall of the house, and when entered was found to contain arms and saddlery for a troop of forty or fifty horse. It is generally supposed that these weapons had been hidden away in readiness ,for the Jacobite rising if 1715 or 1745. The other chamber was situated in the upper story of the old tower, access to which was gained by a nar- row staircase in the thickness of the wall, having, ills com- monly thought, been used as a chapel. THE LARGEST FARM IN THE WORLD.—OperaliollB OR the Bell Farm, in the Canadian North-West, said to be the largest farm in the world, will be conducted on a more ex- tensive scale than ever next year. The manager states that 7,500 acres will be ready for seeding next spring, and that in all between £25,000 and £30,000 sterling will be spent upon the farm next year. Of the crop just harvested, 10,000 bushels'. of wheat were exported to Montreal, and 13,000 bashels sold all over the country as seed. Not a bushel of grain raised on the farm was damaged by frost. LIVER FLUKE —Another correspondent in the Agricul- tural Gazette writes :—I interpret Mr. lidorley's account of his experience with the liver fluke mentioned last week very differently to what he does. I do not think the char- coal saved the ewes, which did not die, but that the good , feeding enabled those ewes which had swallowed but a few fluke cysts to survive their drain upon the system until, in the course of nature, the flukes died out. The life of a fluke within the sheep is limited, although it does not seem cer- tain how long is the period. But it is certain that the num- ber of flukes within any one sheep cannot exceed the nurn- ber of cysts swallowed, and that, if only a few be taken in, the sheep can be sustained over their existence, and recover normal health. Mr. Morley's ewes must have been attacked very late in the Autumn, or the damage would have shown itself before the lambs were born. As it seems to me the salt thrown on the pasture destroyed so many cysts that only a few ewes got a full complement, and that the others had but a dozen or so—or even less. These latter, being well-fed and otherwise healthy, sustained the drain of the parasites, which do not themselves destroy life, but weaken and depress until life is extinguished, by cutting off from the system the vivifying blood. The charcoal may have benefited the sheep's system, but it did not kill the flakes. They ran their course and died out. SILOS EIALF A CENTURY SINCE.—I have read with much interest what you have printed lately concerning silos, as the subject has engaged my attention for more than fifty years. My father always put his meadow hay into a hay barn, which was more than half underground, and often the next day after it was mown the grass was put in and trodden. down, and it generally came out a dark mahogany colour, and with nothing but that and turnips the Devon cattle were fattened on. In 1828 I well remember the excitement and some of the remarks then made. My father, on open- ing the door, discovered the hay to be in flames. He care- fully closed it and collected all hands, and " Follow me and do as I do," then he took a pitchfork of hay from the sledge and dashed it on the flames, and was followed by twelve or fourteen others. Then all hands marched up and down and around, and the hay that was mown the day before by three men was also well trod in. An old Trafalgar man, who always assisted at hay and harvest, said, "Ah ! if the admiral had not faced the fire, the ship and all the cargo would have been lost." But the result was that my father said he never knew the oxen lay on beef so fast as they did that winter, although the fodder appeared too much cooked, and some of it burnt. Now that a greater pressure is put upon it, both in the press and in the manufacture, I have no doubt of its success.— Wm. Searle.

THE COMING Max.—A "Boston Journal" correspondent has the following to say of a man at Toftonboro, who paddles his own canoe and lets his neighbours *die theirs. This man has a wheelbarrow, but there la not anything peculiar about it, only he has cat seven tons of hay and put it in the barn on that wheelbarrow during the past summer, and has done his other harvesting in the same way. From less than one-half acre of ground that man cut and shocked one hundred and twenty-two shocks of corn, sixteen hills in a shock. When husked the corn filled a bushel basket seventy-three times, besides five hundred ears traced up, the ears in the trace measuring from nine to sixteen inches. On this same half acre he raised more than two bushels of "leans, two bushels of turnips, twenty-four heads of cabbage, and about a cart load of pumpkins. From one potato, which he made a speciality, he raised two bushels of assorted pota- toes, and between two and three quarts of small ones. From one and one-half bushels of seed he raised sixty-five bushels of assorted potatoes, from which may be selected one thou- sand smooth and handsome tubers that will weigh more than one thousand pounds From less than nine square rods of ground he harvested ninety-one bushels of Dewin's early turnip beets that weighed from one-half to five pounds apiece, which for beauty and quality cannot be surpassed by any lot of beets raised by one man in the county of Carroll. Such a man will succeed anywhere. Foon FOR SREEP.—The most economical and appropriate sombination of food for fattening sheep will depend upon the cost of different foods in the locality. Nearly all the _ _ . . .

grains raised are healthy for sheep unground, With the exception of millet, which is probably neither healthy nor economical when fed unground ; because of its har I husk and small size it is not masticated nor digested, but mostly passes through the animal whole. Rye, oats, barley, buck- wheat, peas, beans, Indian corn, wheat, bran, shorts or middliegs, and oil meal are each and all good food for fat- tening sheep; but sheep should not be fattened upon a single food, as they are fond of variety and will gain fast when allowed to have it. Sheep are so fond of succulent food that they will pick over large fields in open winter try- ing to find it. They suffer when kept on wholly dry food for several months, and, for this reason the last food men- tioned—oil-cake—should be provided in a small quantity for them. The feeder cannot err in giving too great a variety in the food of sheep. The best ration we have ever known fed to fattening sheep was composed of equal parts by weight,..d oats, peas, and millet, and to fifteen bushels of the mixture was added one bushel of flaxseed, and all ground fine together. Etch sheep was fed two pounds of this ground mixture with hay, and made a regular gain of three pounds each week, besides growing an unusual staple of wool. This small amount of flaxseed is peculiarly soothing to the digestive organs. It is a perfect preventa- tive of all diseases caused by dry fodder.—Prof. W. San- born.

AGRICULTURAL COLLEGE, CIRENCESTER. The winter session of this college closed last week, when the diplomas, certificate, prizes, scholarships, and medals were conferred on the successful students by Mr. Story Maskelyne, M P., a member of the governing body. The Principal, the Rev. J. B. McClellan, in his report of the work of the year, said it was the most successful year the college had experienced, for not only had the number of students in the past term been larger than the rolls of the college had ever previously contained, but the diploma had been earned by a greater number of students than in any previous year—viz., 21, the highest number gained in any former twelve months being 13. Mr. Story Maskelyne, M.P., addressed the students, and congratulated the college on the success with which it was maintaining its high reputation, remarking on the satisfactory character of the term's diploma list, including, as it did, representatives of England, Ireland, and Scotland, while among the successful students were many Indian scholars. The :college diploma was conferred on Colin Valentine, Affloch, Dun Echt, Aberdeen ; Walter Stirling, Deans's-court, St. Andrews, Scotland; Leonard Goodhart Sutton, Cintra Lodge, Whitley, Reading; Edward Mansure , Woodward, Bank View, Cheadle Heath, Stockport; Thomas Richard Cholmondeley, Hodnet Rectory, Market Drayton, Shropshire; William Arthur Sanders, Sanders Park, Charle- ' ville, county Cork, Ireland; Arthur Edward Haviland Warbleton Rectory, Hawkhurst, Kent; and Cecil Stagg Cease, Essex Lodge, London-road, Bkomley, Kent. Hay- garth Gold Medal: Colin Valentine. Scholarships: Allen, Dickson, and geese, equal. TURNIP TOPS as ENSILAGE.—Mr. W. Brougham, of Cul- duthal Haase, near Inverness, has made quite a novel en- silage expterignent. The account is given in the writer's own words. After describing the making of his silo, he says :—The cement being set, and covered with straw to keep off frost, all looked secure, and the ensilage process was fairly commenced. Sandy gravel formed the bottombf the pit, on which was placed rough boards; above this a few inches of straw. Two feet of turnip tops were then placed in silo, when three men with sharp spades quickly did the work of the proper ensilage knife, while the tramp. lug reduced the tops to an equal surface. This was now freely sprinkled with salt, and then a Oin, layer of straw spread evenly over the surface, on which 2ft. of the turnip tops were again placed, and sliced as before, and the process continued till the pit was fall. This was completed oil No- vember 2ind, 1882. I/ was estimated that twelve tons of turnip tops were introduced into the pit, and that probably there was a loss of two tons by the juices passing into the gravel. This is, however, quite conjectural. The surface was covered with good strong boards, over which 21t. of clay from a pond was placed. This, of course, excluded the air, and formed a heavy load. In addition, the turnip crop was placed as far as possible within the building, where the roots, covered with the straw, were preserved in most beau- tiful condition to the end of the season. I rather expect the experiment was looked on as "a fad" on the part of an old Indian; but, whether or no, time went on, and just when the hungry beasts were feeling the greatest want of green meat the silo was opened. To the great satisfaction of all concerned, the experiment was found to be a perfect success. Cattle and Digs ate of it' greedily, so that from April 10 to May 12 we were amply provided with succulent food. If "he who makes one blade of grass grow where none grew before deserves well of the State," what does he deserve who shows how all the turnip tops in Scotland and England can thus be utilised and preserved so as to form not only food, but an excellent substitute for green fodder? That, I consider, is my contribution to the Agricultural So- ciety of Scotland, of which I was made a member last year. FLUCTUATIONS IN Woet —The remarkable depression in the value of wool which exists at the present moment may render interesting a few facts showing the leading fluctua- tions in the value of this product during the last 100 years. Of course, it ought to be borne in mind that during this period a wonderful change has been effected. The restricted domestic system of a working master with a few appren- tices, and one or two journeymen regulated by statute, and the hours of labour and the rate Of wages determined by the justices of the peace, has given place to the factory system and the aggregation of vast numbers of men and wealthy employers. A century ago the great inventions of the mule and the power-loom were but being brought into existence to add enormously to the power of production. A century ago the value of English lustre wool of good average quality was almost exactly 145. 6d. per tod, and the value appears to have gone on increasing until 1791, when 20s. per tod was reached. Prices subsequently fluctuated very much, and a backward movement reduced prices to 16s. 6d. per tod in 1797, as against 248. per tod in 1792. Several rises and falls took place in succeeding years till 1802, when an upward bound brought values to 31s. per tod, which must at that time have seemed a very excessive price. Further variations were from 1802, after a fall, a revival till 1313, prices being 28s. to 335.; 1814, 445.; 1815, 505.; 1816 to 1832, 28s. to 325.; 1834, 465.• 1835-42, over 40s. ; 1843, 255. 6d' . • 1845, 32s' . • 1847-8, 27'5.; 1849, 225.; 1850, 26g.; 1851, 305.; 1853, 375.; 1863, 525.; 1864, 655.; 1865, 59g.; 1866, 435. 6d.; 1870, 365.; 1871, 475.; 1872, 58s. From that time up to within a few weeks ago the history of the wool market has been in the main one of gradual de- cline. There was, it is true, a rise of 7s. per tod in 1879 to 1880, namely, from 275. to 345. per tod, but in 1881 265. represented the value of fine-grown English wool. Low as this limit was, next year (1882) showed only 245. per tod, and the present year (1883) again brought the level of prices to the remarkably lour figure of 225. per tod, the lowest point recorded since 1849, and, with the exception of that single depression—which lasted only for one year—the most remarkable decline in values which has been experienced in the present century. From the highest point of 65e. in 1864 to that of 225. at the present moment, there is repre- sented a startling decline, and the difference in the value of the clip of English wool at these widely varying figures is something enormous. It may be interesting to point out that, taking the wool produce of England at 5.500,000 tods per annum, the value of this produce in the year 1864 was £17,554,166, whereas the same quantity at the present mo- ment would represent a value of 1;6,104,427—that is, taking the mean average price of wool in 1864 at 635. 10d. per )tod, and at the present moment at 225. nd per tod. The differ- ence in value between the produce of these two years is thus no less than £11,449,739—a sum which indicates how enor- mous has been tile shrinkage in the value of this portion of agricultural produce in the course of 19 years.—Times.

THE APELE.—This is termed the poor man's iron. is • favourite with all, and its price is usually wlthiln the reach of the working man that may not have any of his own growing. During this season the apple has been brought before the public in a way that it has not been before. The Royal Horticultural Society of London in the month of October organised what was designated as an "Apple Con- gress," and invitations were issued for all in the kingdom who felt an interest in the apple to forward as many varieties as they could, which was well responded to. The Channel Islands and America also contributed. The result was that 1,000 varieties were exhibited, and the number of dishes exceeded 7,000. We made no note of this in this column at the time as we expected the society to issue a report that would be of practical use; for every sender was requested to state the local position, high or low ground; nature of soil and subsoil, with other details in reference to stocks and grafting, dm., from which one might expect some useful deductions might be made. But hitherto nothing is forthcoming beyond an analysis which the Gardener's Magazine gives us, or what it terms "Audit of National Apple Congress." The 7,000 dishes were scrutinised, and a note made of how many-dishes of each sort were exhibited. Blenheim Orange was shown by 166 different persons; Dumslow Seedling, or Wellington, 132. The other varieties, represented by upwards of a hundred dishes, were Cox's Orange Pippin, Ribston Pippin, and Warner's King. The following, over 50 dishes :—Alfriston, Cockle Pippin, Court Pender Plat, Cox's Pomona, Echlinville Seedling, Emperor Alexander, Fearns' Pippin, Golden Noble, Golden Pippin, Hawthornden, Kerry Pippin, Keswick Codlin, King of the Pippins' Lord Suffield, Mank's Codlin, Sturmer Pippin, WinterHawthornden, and a few others, which proves that they are varieties universally grown, and should be a guide to intending planters. It should be understood that the exhibition was not competitive, and the society paid the carriage of the apples. The magazine says that "Lan- cashire apples did not form a striking display, for they oc- cupied but comparatively little space, and lacked the effec- tive colouring of those from the southern counties." The latter defect we should say would be visible in all produc- tions from counties north of the Trent. The names of Mr. Hathaway, Lathom House, Ormskirk, and Mr. Merles, Meythorpe Nursery, Lytham, appear as contributors, the first with about 40 dishes, and the latter about half the number. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Cnetagas Pyracantha is an elegant evergreen, and in most seasons it is clothed with bright red berries, the size of the haws on the hawthorn, Crretagus Pyracantha being only a species of hawthorn. An old straw-thatched country cottage had the lower part of its front covered with the subject of our remarks, became known as the "Coral Cottage," owing to the resemblance of the berries to that species of marine vegetation. We saw recently, thirty miles southwards of Preston, some grand specimens on the fronts of some dwelling-houses that were situated in an extra bleak position. The plant is 30 hardy that it is planted on an east or north aspect throughout the kingdom, except the most northern part of it. Clematis Vitalba (Traveller's Joy) is a veritable climber of rapid growth. We have seen its shoots scrambling in wild con- fusion on the tops of trees thirty feet high. When the plant is established, two-thirds of the previous season's growth should be cast away in February or March, or just when it is starting to grow. The flowers, which are pro- duced in August or September, are not so showy as some of the species which we shall comment upon some other time. THE,WINDOW.—TRE Farm Cass.—As a substitute for stone we have attained satiefactory results by using clinkers produced by the combustion of coals or coke in furnaces. They have a rustic appearance, as well as being extremely light compared with stone. They are also easily manipulated to any size or shape. After making a suitable selection of pieces, they should be immersed in a vessel con- taining cement and water, well stirred before each lot is dipped, and if after they are dry they are not sufficiently coloured the process should be repeated. The mixture may also be taken out with an old iron spoon and poured over them, holding them over the vessel to avoid waste. If before the cement is dry some of the fine particles or dust from the dressing of stones in masons' yards are dashed against the pieces with one hand whilst they are held by the other, the process imparts a more pleasing appearance than the bare cement does. Having thus prepared a sufficient num- ber, procure a roofing slate of the desired size, so that the glass case may rest on it. This slate will form -the bed for the rockwork, of which no more should be used than is re- quisite to enclose the soil, as well as an occasional piece I such as would imitate a natural projection here and there, ' and if a piece has to be fixed for this purpose it must be Supported with sticks and cemented by pouring some on with the spoon, and when sufficiently set the sticks can be removed. To prevent the water which will drain from watering the plants flowing on the room floor we form a raised margin of cement, tin. deep, just outside the case, or inside, for it is immaterial which, so that it confines the water, which in the summer time may remain there, but provision should be made to let it out when desired, and the most simple plan is to make a hole in the slate inside the cement margin, under which a vessel may be placed to catch the water, and when all is out a plug should be put in the hole to prevent any further dripping.

DRINKING AT CLUBS.—On the morning of Christmas day a young man died at Heywood through drinking an exces- sive quantity of rum, which, it is supposed he had obtained at the Heywood Catholic Club, of which he was a member. At the inquest some pertinent questions were put as to the constitution and working of the club, and the coroner was desired by the jury to draw the attention of the " authori- ties" to the institution. The membership fee was said to be sixpence per quarter, and the coroner remarked that the ex- penses of the place had to be met out of the profits of the drink sold LIFE AT Ant-rms-Bmws.—Aix-les.Bains is situated in a delightful valley, surrounded by well-wooded hills, beyond which rise moantatns which may almost be classified as belonging to the Higher Alps. The climate is delicious. Figs and almonds, vines and pomegranates abound in the meadows and gardens, and chestnut and oak clothe the hills. This luxurious vegetation, be it remembered, is at an eleva- tion of 850 feet above the sea, and amply attests the aMelio- rating influence of the wall of mountains which protect the valley from the cold winds of the north and east The mineral waters are various in kind, for the neighbourhood abounds in medicinal springs. If we are to believe guide- books, the ailments which can be ameliorated or cured by these various sources are almost as numerous as are the ills which flesh is heir to. The method of treatment is in some of its aspects curious. There is a large staff of licensed porters, bathers, and shampooers, under the charge of some of whom the patient is placed, and When the hour of treat- ment arrives he is carried in a kind of sedan-chair from his bedroom to the bath, and after having been put through a number of operations in which the douche and shampooing form a principal part, he is borne once more back to his bed, and left to slumber under the influence of the sweet reaction. —" Pictures from Aix-les-Bain," by H.R.H. div.p: Joan Bturems's PHILOSOPHY.—Ia these times ov dis- covery and invenshun, what the world stands most in need ov iz a moral platform scales, which would sho the exackt virtew in a man; but how menny are there who would dare to step onto one ov theze contrivances and bi wayed 7—Bravery iz the instinkt ov reason.—Thare iz no doubt a grate deal ov policy in honesty, but the virtelo that iz in it iz what makes it sakred.—The proverb tells us "there is menny a slip between cup and lip," but thare ain't half az menny az thare ought to be.—A goose iz often spilte bi being cooked too much—it iz less so with many ov our plans in life.—Thare may be stitch a thing az an impos- sibility, but it never haz been fully diskovered yet.—The man who kan make the bottom round of the ladder respek- table iz the very man to make the top one honourable.— Justiss iz the religion ov the head.—Grit iz the cayenne in a man's natar that seazons all the rest ov him.—Learning iz good, but there is a grate deal ov it that iz of no more use to a man than two handles to a jack knife.—Thare iz nothing so heavy az lazyness ; each poundpv it kontains at least twenty-two ounces.—Thare iz lots ov very good people who hang onto a thing so hard when they giv it away that they tare it in two and still keep the big end for themselves.—No man kala be a feet klass talker unless he iz a good listener—two things seldum found together. GOING TO MANE ma T9017t FIZYGLEO.—A man was stand- ing in front of a dentist's office the other day, with an anxious unhappy look in his eyes, and two yards of flannel round his lower jaw. He cast sorrowful glances upward to the dentist's sign, and in a hesitating sort of way placed his foot on the lower stair; then came out to the street again as if he had forgotten something. Colonel Solan came along at that moment, and with a thoughtful interest in the man's welfare said, "Toothache, eh? Goin' to have it pulled? Ever had a tooth pulled? No? Well, you'd better go right up afore your courage fails you. Worst thing in the world is pulling a tooth. I've been through the war, had both lungs shot away, fifteen bullets in my . head, and doctors run a probe .through a hole in my shoulder right down through my body to my toe—thought %would kill me. But, man alive, I never knew what pain was till I had a tooth pulled. Maybe you think the toothache is horrible. It is. It's awful. But wait till the dentist runs them iron tongs into your mouth, pushes the tooth right down through your jawbone, and then yanks away as if he was pulling on an old hand engine, and yer'll think the toothache ain't no more to be compared to it than a flea-bite is to a railroad accident. Yer had better go right up though, and have it out. Don't let anything I said cause yer to back out. I merely wanted to prepare yer mind for it. An' dpn't take' ether. Knew a man once, about your complexion and build, who took ether, an' be died. It's dangerous. Jest go right up and have it out. ra go up with yer, and see how yer stand it when he begins twistin' the bones round. Yer won't sleep a wink to-night if yer don't have it out; an' maybe yer won't anyhow, for some- times the tooth breaks the jaw, inflammatory rheumatism strikes the whats-its-name nerves, and the what-they-call-it sets in." Just at this moment a young man practising on a French horn in one of the upper rooms blew a long ear- piercing blast, like the yell of a man in agony, and as the last sound echoed through the hall, the colonel said, "That's it; there's some one gettin' a tooth pulled now, an' the dentist hasn't any more than just given the first twist either. Come right up an' have yours pulled. Whoop! there he goes again," as another terrible blast from the horn came down the staircase. "Hold on, hold on !" yelled the colonel—bat he wasn't quick enough to stop the man with the aching tooth, who mailed out of the doorway and down the street so fast that his two yards of flannel became un- wound and streamed behind him like signals of danger— while the old colonel sat down on the lower step and laughed till his eyes ached.

HELEN'S TOWER.—Charles Blatherwick writes in "Good Wcrds "—Halfway up Belfast Lough, on the high ground to the left, you may see a remarkable landmark. This is Helen's Tower, built by the present Earl of Dufferin as a tribute of filial affection to his mother, the late Countess of Gifford, and formally named after her on attaining his majority. Looking across from the grey old walls of Car- rickfergus, it may be seen crowning the highest hill on the Claudeboye estate. Clear cut against the sky, there it stands, lashed by the winds or touched by the sun, ever firm and enduring—a fitting memorial of one of the best and noblest of women. Lady Gifford was a Sheridan, one to whom wit and beauty came as natural gif Is, yet one who dipped deeply into the fount of human knowledge, and by pure sympathy with all that was good and beautiful in life, exerted a lasting influence on all those whose privilege it was to know her. A short drive from Bangor, or, still better, a pleasant twomffle stretch across the turf from Claudeboye House, will bring you to the foot of the hill. Here, glimmering amid ferns, sedges, birches, and firs, very calm and peaceful on a golden autumn day, with Helen's Tower reflected on its face, is a quiet lake. Then a smart climb through a fir wood, and the Tower—a veritable Scotch tower, with " corbie stairs" and jutting turrets all complete—is before you. At the basement lives the old keeper with his wife; and here, after inscribing your name in the visitors' book, you follow him up the stone steps. The sleeping chamber first. A cosy little room, remark- able for the fine specimen of French embroidery which decorates the bedstead, with. the quaint inscription on the tester—

From here you are taken to the tap. Descending again, we enter the principal chamber—octagonal, oak-panelled, with groined pointed ceiling and stained glass windows. Over the fireplace is a niche for a silver lamp, and flanking the west window are two poetical inscriptions—that on the left, printed in gold mid having reference to the lamp, is by Lord Dufferin's mother; and that on the right, printed in gold black type, is by the Poet-Laureate. On reading Lady Gifford's graceful verses, we are pathetically reminded that she was not spared to see her son's brilliant career.—Tenny- son has a poem on the same subject :

Helen's Tower, here I stand, Dominant over sea and land. Bon's love built me, and I hold Mother's love engraved in gold. Love is In and out of time, I am mortal stone and lime. Would my granite girth were strong As either love, to last as long, I should wear my crown entire To and thro' the Doomsday fire, And be found of angel eyes In earth's recurring Paradise.

WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. A STRANGE CLAIIL—A shipwright at Penketh, named William Clare, sned John Carrington, of Brarnhall-street, I Sankey Green, for the sum of £2 Os 6d.—Mr. Percy Davies, who appeared for the defendant, handed the following 'details of the claim to the judge :—"Penketh, November 12, 1881 John Carrington from William Clare. expences for being brout up under A faulce sumonens for Loss of time and expences, 128; Turney's fee, £l. is; witneas not pads, 5s ; for damage don to box and artickles, 2s 61--£2 —in answer to the judge, plaintiff said he was brought up on a charge at the Borough Court, but the case was dis- missed. The Bench granted the costs for two witnesses His Honour: Very well ; you can't come here and have the costs over again.—The Registrar: He is claiming now his own expenses and solicitor's fee, also damage done to a box. —The plaintiff, cross-examined by Mr. Davies, said Mr. Moore, solicitor, who appeared for him at the Borough Court, applied for costs for his attendance, but the order was refused. The box, which was valued at about 7s 6d, was on Carrington's premises. Defendant allowed him to keep it there for two years, and did not make any charge. The damage was done to the box on the 22nd October—the day on which defendant was removing from his house.— Several witness corroborated the above statement, and Mr. Davies said that he thought if Clare had dared to call Mr. Moore, there would have been an end of the csse.—John Carrington and others were called to prove that the box was not broken, and his Honour gave judgment for defen- dant. DAMAGE TO GROWING CROPS BY SHREP.--Joseplen Quinn sued Wm. Gill, butcher, Bridge-street, Warrington, for the sum of £1 10s, damage alleged to have been done to grow- ing creps by defendant's sheep.—Mr. P. Davies defended. —Plaintiff said he bought some mangolds, potatoes, savoys, leeks, &c., which were growing in a field adjoining land kept by Mr. Gill. Defendant's sheep had got through the I hedge on to the land and destroyed part of the crop.—Mr. Davies endeavoured to show that the fence belonged to the occupier of the land on which the crops were growing, and ought to have been put in repair by him.—His Honour said the law was as plain as possible. An occupier of a field, whether he was occupier or owner, must fence his stock in either by means of shepherds or by a fence.—Judgment was given for XI.

THE SUSPICIOUS DEATH AT BURTON WOOD. THE ADJOURNED INQUEST. The adjourned inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of Ned Tiavers, nine years of age, residing in Chapel-lane, Burtonwood, who it was alleged died through a severe beating administered by Mr. Jones, schoolmaster of Burtonwood National Schools, was resumed at the Chapel House Inn, Burtonwood, yesterday (Thursday), before Mr. L. Rowbottom, deputy coroner. It will be remembered that the deceased died on the 23rd December—a few days after - the alleged beating is said to have been administered. The inquest was formally opened on Wednesday week, when it was decided that a post-mortem examination of the body should he made by Dr. Gorton, of St. Helens. At the resumed inquiry, yesterday, there were present in addition, to the Deputy-Corener (Mr. Rowbottom) and the Jury, Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. listens, representing the de— ceased's father, Mr. J. o:Swift, solicitor, St. Helens, repre— senting Mr. V. T. Jones (schoolmaster), the Rev. W. Wil— son (vicar of the parish), Dr. Garton (St. Helens), Dr. Foalson (assistant to Dr. Hanyside, Earlestewn), and Mr. Jones, (schoolmaster). The Deputy-Coroner (to Mr. Riley) : Do you propose to- calla number of witnesses ?
Mr. Riley: It will depend upon the medical testimony. I think that had better be taken first. The Deputy-Coroner : I think so. It will probably shorten. the Inquiry.

The following evidence was then taken:— William Garton, doctor of medicine and Fellow of tha, Royal College of Surgeons, said :—I practice in St. Helens,. and I made a postmortem examination of the deceased en- Thursday morning last. The outside of the stomach, was bordering on a state of decompmitiora There were some three or four marks or bresies on the Lc.t-.. tocks, but no other external marks. He appeared to be fairly well nourished. Internally I examined the chest and. abdomen. All the organs in the chest were quite healthy. On opening abdominal cavity the intestines generally were covered with pus or matter, which matter had also descended into the pelvis, or lower part of the body, to the extent of several ounces. The coils of the intestines were adhereut. On the right side of the abdomen was found a poach son— taming three pellets of hard motion, and there were also. three pouches of ulceration through the walls of this pouch. No foreign body was found outside these pouches except pus or matter. All the other organs were healthy. I was attend d by another surgeon when making the examination,. and we agreed. Tne pellets were formed of matter, and the Lei of them being in the pouch would be injurious to the boy's health and cause the ulcerations I have mentioned. l'here is no iunit to the length of time the pellets alight Lave bn h‘re, but the perforation or ulceration through- the wall of the body must have been recent. The boy ' must have been in this state for at least a couple of months, and it might have been a couple of years. During that period the boy might have appeared to be in a healthy state.

The Deputy Coroner: Was the state in which you found, the boy's intestines sufficient to cause death ? Witness: Yes. sir.—Would this he ciused by the marks on the but- tocks? Decidedly not. —How do you account for the state- of decomposition of his bowels? By the time that had elapsed since the time of his death.—Worild the state in, which y,u found him affect his appetite? Re would not be able to eat much in that condtition.—Was it calculated to- produce vomiting? It was. 4 In reply to qu, stions by Mr. Riley, witness further added/ that there was no limit to time in which the pellets might remain in the pouch to which be had alluded. The capacity of the pouch was such that there was plenty of room for them to lie dormant. Mr. Riley: Supposing the boy was placed on his abdomen at a certain angle, and he was beaten on the buttocks— Mr. Swift here said he thought the question was One which ought not to be put. The question was thereupon put in another form' and the. witness said that the perforation of the pouch was the climax of the ulcerations. Ulceration unarrested must re- salt in perforation. Mr. Riley: Do you put it so high as this, that if what I suggested did happen it would not at all hasten the death ? Witness: It would not conduce to do him an}, good. Mr. Riley: You would not say it would not hasten hie death ?
....-- . The Coroner: I will put that question. Would it hastez. the death?

Witness: Well, it might, but I won't say that it would. If ulceration was proceeding, the fact of putting him on a hard body would not be conducive to stay or remedy the " disease.—On being further questioned, the witness added that the pellets reached their position by accident, and the ease was a similar one to that of the Bishop of Peterborou3b, reported in the papers. . -

Mr. Swift: fudging from the post -mortent examination alone, and leaving out the suggestions made, you saw no- thing that would have lead you to think that this was not a natural death P—Witness: Nothing.—You still seem to- think that notwithstanding the suggestions it was a natural death P--If I had known or heard nothing I should haver put it down as a naturti death. Supposing this alleged violence did take place you think it would I._'ave bad no- thing to do with the death ?—I cannot say that. It ni!..fht have hastened his death.—Would this stick (holding a thin willow branch about half an inch in diameter) be sufficient to cause death? It depends upon the violence used. The Deputy-Coroner asked Mr. Riley if he proposod to call any witnesses after the evidence which had been given. Mr. Riley replied that he did not. Of course there was the question as to whether or not the master had assaulted the deceased, but that was another matter. The Deputy Coroner observed that it could scarcely be considered as a question of assault. It was whether exces- sive punishment bad been administered or not. Mr. Swift said he would like to refer to one or two sup, gestions that had been made. It had been suggested that the boy Wee I.4.ated ever a desk with his stomach resting thereon bet it was nothing of the sort. He was simply struck three or four times as he stood up. Mr. Riley replied that he was sorry his friend had said that. He had an array of evidence in an opposite direction. Such statements were only ex parte, and would have to be decided somewhere else he believed.

The Deputy-Coroner, observing that he did not think it necessary to call any more witnesses to speak as to the canee of death, proceeded to say that the verdict simply (*ended on the doctor's evidence, which they had heard. It ap- peared to him (the deputy-coroner) that although a report got out that the boy was badly lased, and it W.lll believed by hls parents that the flogging had caused death. The doctor's evidence proved that he was suffering from a diseae.a for a considerable time prior to the flogging taking place, and that it caused his death. Under these circum- stances, he did not think they could find any other verdict besides one to the effect that the boy died from inflamma- tion of the bowels. The doctor did not say that the treat- ment the boy received accelerated death at all, and under the circumstances the verdict they could find according to the evidence was that the boy died a natural death. The jury expressed a wish to consider the matter in pri- vate, and retired to another room. After a few minutes, absence they returned, and The Foreman said: Mr. Coroner, the jury are of opinion that this death is natural causes, but it is possible, they think, that it might have been accelerated by the treatment the lad received. The Deputy-Coroner : Think it is possible that it might be. But there is no evidence that it was. The Foreman: No, sir. The Coroner: If there was any evidence that it was caused by the treatment he is said to have received the doctor would have said so. The doctor cannot say that it was, and in your minds it is only a matter of suspicion.— The Corner then entered the verdict as "Death from na- tural causes."

div.head: CHURCH DISPUTE AT EARLES-
div.p: THE CHURCH DISPUTE AT EARLES-

TOWN. EXPECTED SETTLEMENT. There is a probability that the dispute at St. John's, Church, Earlestown, which for seme weeks past has beep the principal theme of conversation throughout the neigh- bourhood, will be settled to the satisfaction of almost every- one. It is evident that since Mrs. Matthews' death a more friendly and harmonious feeling has existed between the Vicar and his parishioners. The services in the church OD Sunday last were conducted by the Rev. H. E. Smith (carat e), who was the only clergyman present. Mr. 11. J. Dnrman presided at the organ, and the usual responses to the prayers were made by the choir and congregation, psakns and hymns were sung, and the whole service was heartily joined in by all present. In the evening the service was again eonducted by the Rev. H. E. Smith, and in addition to singing the annual psalms and hymns, the choir beautifully rendered the anthem, "0, thou that tallest." There was a crowded congregation. We have since ascertained that an interview between the Rev. Canon Whitley (who has, in a Christianlike spirit Fought to bring the dispute to a termination), the Rev. T. R. Matthews, and Mr. B. Corlett, the people's churchwarden was recently held at the Vicarage. We believe that in the course of the conversation it was remarked that the dispute could be settle as soon as Mr. Matthews chose te settle it, and that was by allowing the services to proceed same as before. The Vicar, it is stated, at last give way in so far as to say that for the present the services should be held as formerly "under protest." This means that the dis- charged choristers and organist will be allowed to take their accustomed parts in the services, and this was the course followed on Sunday last. It remains to be seen what further action, if any, the Rev. T. R. Matthews will take in the matter. There was no service in the church last evening (Thursday), but the choir had a practice, Mr. Duman presiding at the organ.

MEDICINES, ELASTIC STOCKINGS. CHEMICALS, &c., by Parcel Post. under Itt. 3d.—ay Bros., Stockport.—Advt. The new Bankruptcy Act came into force on Tuesday. RESIGNATION OP A TOWN CLERK—Mr. Hesketh Booth, who has been appointed official receiver under the Bank- ruptcy Act, has sent in his resignation as Town Clerk of Oldham.

A " MERRY' CHRISTMAS "—A weekly paper, dated De comber 30th, recerded 40 murders and manslaughters, 9 suicides, 13 mysterious deaths, GB accidental deaths, and 17 deaths from lawlessness and riot, making a total of 147. Had all the items been placed together, they would have filled about one page of the paper.

div.p: MISOELLANEOITS.

Lord Falmouth is about to quit the turf. The bellringers at Oldham Parish Church are on strike. The Board of Trade will oppose the Channel Tunnel Nile, if they are proceeded with next session. Police-sergeant Davis, of Gravesend, was stabbed on Saturday night, during a street row, by a tramp giving the tame of Elijah David. Some 1,500 workpeople at Messrs. Bolckow, Vaughan, and -Co.'s steelworks, Middlesbrough, have been locked-out as the insult of a wages' dispute. Lord Salisbury, in a letter addressed to the Secretary of the Eastern Division of the Glasgow Conservative Associa- tion, says he ccrncurs in the objection of that body" to a 'fragmentary treatment of the question of Reform." The Huddersfield Fine Art Exhibition, which was closed On Saturday, was visited during the time it was open by 329,190 persons. Financially the exhibition has been a failure the expenses having amounted to the large sum of £13,000. The dead body of John Clarke, stonemason, of 19, Vaug- han-road, Birkciale, was foand on Tuesday morning on the Liverpool. Waterloo, and Southport line of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway. It is believed that the deceased had committed suicide. An explosion of gas, resulting from a light being carried Into a room where there was a leakage, took place on Tars- tay at a steam laundry at Beigrave, near Leicester. A Woman named Elliott wasinjured, and considerable damage wais4one Mahe preinitiee- ' THR STAFFORD Bans ToltanDs.—At Stafford Police Court, en Monday, Thomas Wood, late manager of the Birming, bum, Dudley, and District Bank, was committed for trial on the charge of embezzling £2lO, belonging to the Stafford Mutual Benefit Building Society. CIIURCU BURNT DOWN.—On Sunday the old church at East bianningfi-ld, Essex, was destroyed by fire, which broke out shortly after a late Communion service. All the books and Communion plate were saved. The Rev. Mr. 4rnyth has been for many years the vicar. TEMPERANCE IN OUBRNSEY.—Tbe elates of Guernsey have given notice to the landlord of the Prince of Walee Hotel, a well-known drinking place in the States Arcade, Peterport, to quit at Christmas, 1884, as they have de- termined not to let any of their property in future to pub- licans THE FINANCIAL YEAR—The revenue returns issued on Monday night state that the total revenue for the year 1883 was £90,C35,522, showing a net increase on the revenue of the previous year of £3,690,664. Customs show an in- crease of £352,000,and property and income tax an increase of £2,838,000. FIRS AT A HOSPITAL—A fire occurred on Tuesday morn- ing in the Glasgow Public Fever Hospital at Belevere. The roof of a large washing house' attached to the main build- ing was buraed off. The fire brigade was soon in attendance, and extinguished the dames. There was great alarm, but no patients werc injured. WIFE MURDER —A shocking murder took place at Bank-% ids, Southwark, abalt four o'clock on Friday afternoon, when a waterside labourer, named It. Plumpton, aged 49, stabbed his wife ,with a pocket-knife under the left ear, Inflicting so frightful a wound that death ensued in about an hour and a half afterwards. A GENEROUS LANDLORD —Mr. Leapold de Rothschild, at his audit held at Aylesbury, bas again returned to all his tenants on his Bucks date 15 per cent, of their rent due at Michaelmas last. Po every inhabitant of four villages and to all the cottagers on his estates wherever situated, he has also given substantial presents of Ceristmas beef, and upwards of a ton has been thus distributed. The Birmingham Town Council, on Tuesday, paesed,with but two dissentients, a resolution instructing the General Purposes Committersto petition Parliament next session in 'favour of an extension of the hours of polling at parliamen- tary and municipal elections; also in favour of the imamcliate extension to municipal elections of the provisions of the Ointretpt and Illegal Practices Prevention Act. MEETING OF IRONWORHERS.—At a mass meeting of StOetihern ironworkers, on Monday, at Steckton, it was re- 'Solved not-to act up to the expressed wish of the board of arbirtationAmployers, who want restriction in the finished iron'trade abolished from January 1, by resuming Monday Rol!, the said restriction having been in force rsince last April to the extent of one-eleventh of the total output. ACcrntarrs ap THE Himmel Fittan —Viscount Throwley, Of Lees Court, near Pavel-ahem, eldest son of Earl Sondes, whilladriting on Tuesday with the Trickham fox hounds, at Ailstead, near Sittingbourne, was thrown from his horse and;eustained a fracture of collar bone. Shortly afterwards Major Knight, of Bebding Court, near Sittingbourne, was pitched head foremost from his horse, owing to the saddle ,tic,th giving way, and injured. A SHOCKING CASE —A shocking and suspicious case has been reported to the Liverpool police authorities. A fireman 4n baked the Inman steamer City of Richmond, named John Power, on returning home to his lodgings in Townsend- 'fitibee after a voysgi on Monday, discovered his wife lying ila, bed drank, and beside her the dead body of his son, 4tteen months old. The woman said the child had died on Irriday, but a medical opinion was given .that it bad, been zdead for a fortnight. -STATEMENTS BY PRISONERS. Mr. Justice Watkin Wil- liams announces that he declines to be bound by the recent decision of a meeting of Judges with regard to the admission Of statements by prisoners and their counsel. He gives an instance of a prisoner having been able to show that he was • Innocent by means of a statement made when the summing was concluded; and declares that nothing short of an Act of Parliament shad induce him to deprive a prisoner of the 'right to make a statement at any stage of the trial. MINERS' WAGES.— The Miners' Conference at Manches- ter, en Saturday, formulated a risilution to the effect that in corder he avoid any ill-feeling with the misters on the question Of a 10 per cent. increase in wages, each county Should have an interview with the proprietors on the •subject. The Conference adjourned to January 28th, at illirtninghem, and in the meantime the Association will as- Oertain the feelings of their members. In Cannock Chase Steps have already been taken with the view of enforcing the Advance of 10-per cent. • THE PORT OF Dovsn.—Dover is about to become an int= portant convict shalom Great works are to be undertaken there, and the first of them is the building of the workmen's quartere. Of all kinds of labour, convict labour is the Slowest and the least satisfactory. The work is done in the end, but the end is long deferred; arid, so, whenever Go-' vernment works are to be carried by this kind of labour, if • they are at all impertint, it means the establishment of a Convict station in the district. Dover will have its long- promised harbour of refuge. THE REV. A. H. Meow/annum—The Rs. A. H. Mac- konochie, vicar of St. Peter's, London Docks, writes :—" I have been forced by the logic of facts to see that I ought not any lengerato impoverish further a parish far too impoirer- ished already by its owe circumstances by keeping from it •the income which is due to it from the Ecclesiastical Ct.m, missioners. I have, therefore, asked the Bishop of London to allow me to withdraw from this benefice." 'The income payable by the Ecclesiastical Comniissioners to the Vicar of St Peter's, London Docks, amounts to 4.320 a year. ' POLICR RAID ON I CONSERVATIVE CLUB:A COIISSIVaI die contemporary states that the police, armed with war- rants and provided with porters and two carts, made a raid . on Saturday evening upon .a building about a mile from Exmouth, and transferred all its contents to the Police station. The building was known As a Ceaservative club, and was opened as such shortly after the refusal of the jus- tices at the late licensing 'seeskitis- to renew the license of, the house as an inn. The amount of drinking and distur- bance at the placl, especially on Sundays and after ordi- nary hours, has caused much comment, hence the action of the police. The books seized showed a. 0- membership "

two hundred. THE DYNAMITE WAN.—The London correepondent of the. Irish Times Says that in consogneece of Patrick Ford's last dynamite proclamation, it is thought likely that during next week a distribution of the police force of London will be arranged, with the view to securing the fullest and most continuous possible supervision of the public buildings; docks, Wharves, stores, shipping, and other property, which are supposed to be the special object of the dynamite party, Ile hears also that a special corps of night watchmen, com- posed exclusively of military. pensioners of English Nationality, is to be organised with a view to do away witla the necessity of employing the army to supplement the police in periods of emergency. admix HEAVY FanunaEs.—A petition for liquidation was filed on Monday, in the Bradford County Court, on behalf of John Faust Etsby, coal and lime merchant. of Bradford. The debtor's liabilities are estimated at £loo.ooo.—The failure WAS announced at the London Bankruptcy Court the Same day of Samuel King Church, colliery proprietor and commission agent, of 14, Bishopsgate•street Within, for, Melly of Great St. Helens. trading in partnership as Chureli2 Milsted, and Co. The liabilities are stated at 07,000.-Linj The failure is aunemoced of Mr. Alexander Brogden, a 4,155 colliery proprietor and irontnaster, with liabilities estimated atd£723,530. The failure. is also annoirnced of Mr. Henry Brogden (formerly' partner with Mr. A. Beogden), with liabilities estimated at 1.120 645. The Bishop of Ely has been ordered by his medical ad- viser to abstain from all active duty in his diocese. At Sway, near Lymington, on. Wednesday, two men were killed by the collapse of a gravel pit in, which they were working. THE EXECUTIONER Furgro.--Binne, the hangman, was fined 20s. at Dewsbury, on Thursday, for riding in a train without a ticket. At Durham, on Wednesday, Joseph John Moore, overseer and rate eollector, was committed for trial at the assizes, charged with embezzling union funds to the amount of £l2OO.

--,-__. THE CHURCH ASSOCIATION Aft MR. MICKONOCHIE.— The announcement which appeared in a Church newspaper that the Church Association intend to apply to Lord Penzance for a sianificavit for the imprisonment of the Rev. A. H. Mackonochie, for contempt of court, is absolutely without foundation. THE DISPUTES IN THE COAL TRADE.—A meeting of the Cannock Chase Coal Trade Conciliation Board was held on Thursday morning to consider the demand of the operatives for an increase of 2P. a day. The masters decliningato discuss the subject in the presence of the Press, a scene en- sued; and the operatives' representatives unanimously with- drew from the meeting. SAD ACCIDENT TO A LADY.—Mrs. John Lambert, of Clarendon House Nottingham, widow of the founder of the firm of Messrs. Lambert, well-known lace dressers, died late on Wednesday night from injuries received by falling down the steps leading to her residence. As she was entering the house her attention was attracted by the barking of a dog, and it is supposed that in turning to see the cause she missed her footing. It was authoritatively stated at Wednesbury, en Wednes- day, that Mr. Brogden will not resign his seat in Parliament in consequence of filing a petition in liquidation. The Liberal federation will be called in a few days to consider and decide what steps shall be taken. It is, however, con- sidered by a good number of electors that under the circum- stances Mr. Brogden should cease to represent the borough in Parliament. STRANGE DEATH.—The body of Malcolm Cameron was found, lying face downwards in a piece of vacant ground in Caithness-street, Glasgow, on Thursday morning. Cameron was spending the evening in a cousin's house on Wednesday night, and left to go home about nine o'clock. He was es- corted part Of the way home by a friend. There are some marks on Cameron's body, but it is not supposed that foal play has been used. Tux LORD RECTORSHIP OF Sr. ANDREWS.—A St. Andrews correspondent says :—Mr. J. Russell Lowell, the American Minister, has retired from the office of Lord Rector of the University of St. Andrews, to which he was recently elected by the votes of the students. In resigning, Mr. Lowell states he has had regard to the difficulties of discharging the full duties of the Rectorship in a Scottish University, arising out of his position as American Minister to this country. THE COTTON STRDIE.—There are no symptoms of giving way on either side in the strike of cotton operatives now going on in North-east Lancashire. It is reported that the operatives, despite the very meagre strike-pay which they receive, are fully determined not to yield, and as yet the, masters have not given the slightest sign of any desire to curtail the duration of the stoppage. Nearly one thousand pounds has been distributed to the weavers on strike in the Blackburn district. A DRUNKARD DROWNED.—An elderly man named Edward Woodhouse, warehouseman, walked into the Severn at New- town, .Monm outhshire, on Thursday evening, and was drowned. The only witness of the occurrence was a tele- graph boy, who said he saw Woodhouse, who was verw. drunk, walking along, grumbling to himself, that he turned down a lane leading to the river, and walked straight in, and was washed away by the current. Witness gave an alarm, but no signs of the man could be found. THE GREAT NORTHERN RAILWAY.—At an extraordinary general meeting of the Great Northern Railway Company at King's Cross, on Thursday, resolutions were adopted to create and issue £1,000,000 new stock, and authorising the issue of £330,000 debenture stock for the completion of works under construction, additional rolling stock, and the widening of Copenhagen Tunnel just outside King's Cross Station. It was decided to call up half a million on the 20th of February next and a quarter of a million on the Ist of July and the Ist of October. MURDER AT BATE —A determined murder was committed at Bath on Wednesday night. Two young unmarried labourers named Albert Miles and Chas. Kite were drinking together in the Malt and Hops publichouse, when some words occurred, and tbev went out. They returned to the house and shook hands, but it was noticed that Kite held out his left hand. He shddenly drew his right hand from his pocket and stabbed Miles in the side of the neck with a knife. Miles fell into the arms of a bystander, and died instantly. Kite went quietly to his mother's house, where he was apprehended half an hour afterwards. SCARE AT A MENAGERIE.—An exciting incident took I place at Wombwell's menagerie, at Bolton, on Wednesday. While the "lion tamer" was in the act of getting into a cage oacupied by tiger oats, one of- the animals rushed be- tween his legs, and, springing among the crowd of people who had gathered in front of the cage to watch them put through a series of performances, caused a scene of wild excitement. People rushed about in all directions in their endeavour to escape, and fortunately in the crush that took place in one corner the hoarding gave way, affording a ready means of egress from the menagerie. In the mean- time the animal was captured by the placing of a large empty barrel over it, and was safely returned to its cage. CHARGE or WIFE MIIRDER.—William Mackay, who at one time kept a public-house in the eastern district of Glas- gow, was etrly on Wednesday morning taken into custody on a charge of causing the death of his wife The couple were continually squabbling, and the accused has been re- peatedly brought up at the police court for ill-using the woman. On Tuesday they were drinking together, and at night the sound of quarrelling between husband and wife was heard by neighbours. The woman, soon after quietude was restored, was found dead in the house. A police ser- geant states that he heard Mackay threaten to take his wife's life. Mackay protests that the fatal injuries his.wite • received were the results of her tumbling about in a drunken state. ALARMING RAILWAY ,COLLISIONS. A serious railway collision took place early on Thursday morning near Shef- field. The mail train to Birmingham while running at a good speed dashed into an empty goods train. Some of the carriages were thrown off the line and several passengers in- jured. while others were severely shaken. A letter sorter living in Birmingham was much injured. The line was not cleared for some hours, and the passengers reached Birmingham at six o'clock—four hours behind time.--4. portion of a train of empty trucks from Hereford to Shrews- bury became detached the same morning, and afterwards overtook the other part. Several trucks were smashed, and others thrown off tiee line, traffic being suspended for some time. • " Tan ILBEET BILL—The Press Association claims to have good-reason for asserting that as regards the reported com- promise in the matter of the Ilbert Bill, neither the Earl of Kimberley nor the Indian Council are in any way respon- sible for the shape that the proposals recently described have taken.. Those authorities have given steady and con- tinuous support to Lord Ripon to the full extent stated by Lord Northbrook, at Bristol, some weeks ago.. Such sup- port, however, left to the Viceroy and hie advisers on the spot freedom and responsibility :for such adjustments and modifications of the measure as may seem.- to -them suitable or necessary. Though,the principle of the measure is not. aisPlace,d by the proposed compromise, it is understood that native publicists express great disappointment, so that the situation still remains under considerable strain and uncertainty. TRAGEDY IN Low:lc:lN.—The body of Mr. John B. Tower, employed as an underwriter, was found about 11 o'elock on Wednesday morning in the reservoir of the New River Company, London, under circumstances which lead to the conclusion that a murder has been committed. Round the neck of the deceased wal a handkerchief tied tightly in three or four knots at the back, and the clothes were so dis- arranged as to show that a desperate struggle had taken place. It was known that the deceased had two diamond rings-on his fingers, and the glove on one hand was found ripped up and the ring torn off. An attempt had also evi- dently been made to get the other ring off, but had failed. 'Or t the banks of the reservoir were a number of footmarks and evidences of a struggle. No arrests have yet been made. ,A postmortem examination on the body of Tower, found on Wednesday in a reservoir at Stoke Newing- ton, was held on Thursday, with the result that death was found to have been undoubtedly caused by strangulation. There were. the Press Association says, se many strange circumstances connected with the case that failure on the paraof the surgeons to establish this fact would bave left left it shrouded in mystery. TiE "K " BOOT IN CHANCERY: SOMERVELL V. Kat:T- anya} . —This was an action brought by Messrs. Somervell Brothers, of Kendal, leather merchants, and boot manufac- turers, -against Mr. Thomas Kenning, of 91, Lord-street, Listerpool, boot manufacturer, for an injunction to restrain the defendant from affixing to any boots manufactured bY him, any mark or stamp in imitation or colourable imita- tion of the plaintiff's trade mark, and from publishing any advertisements or announcements; calculated to represent or , induce the belief that the boots manufactured or sold by the defendant were boots manufactured by the plaintiffa. The fuels were shortly these :—The plaintiffs (Messrs. ' Soineriell Brothers) are 'registered proprietors of a trade mark consisting of single capital letter aK" en- abled' in" a geometrical figure, the- letter "K " dorming the' • essential' - and distinctive feature of the trade mark. The plaintiffs alleged that they had for many years manufactured and sold boots which had obtained a great reputation in the market, and which were knotin in the tradeund to the public as" K" boots, and that same of such boots were manufactured of waterproof leather, and were known in the trade and to the public as ''-waterproof 'K' boots." Aboutathe 7th instant it came to the knowledge of the plaintiffs that the defendants had been 'distributing circulars respecting boots which he called "The lwaterproof T-K boot," of which he described himself as the sole manufacturer. The motion for injunction came on for hearing in the Chancery Division of the High Court, before 'Mr. Justice Pearson, on Friday, the 21st nit. When Mr. Montague Cookson, Q.C., the leading counsel for the plain- tiffs was proceeding to state the facts to the court, counsel for the defendant rose and stated that he would on behalf of the defendant consent to a perpetual injunction with costa, if the plaintiffs would waive their claim to an account and damages. To this proposal the plaintiffs agreed, and judg- m at was given for them accordingly. • KAY'S lIC PILL'S, a specific in Neuralgia, Face-ache, Ac..
