IRELAND. The house of Mr. Lowey, near Castleblayne, caonty Monaghan, was fired into on Tuesday night, and .airs. Lowey was seriously wounded. Six MEN DROWNED.—A boat containing six nieo and some cattle, while under sale from Clare Island to Roonah Point in the mainland, was capsize and all on board were drowned. MR. HEALY ON MR. Peadma's INFLUENCE—Mr. Healy, M.P., writes that "the secret of Mr. Parnell's hold upon the Irish people is that it is to their wishes, feelings, and preju- dices his actions correspond, that it is their interests alone he considers, and that he has shown an undisguised con- tempt for every effort to compel him to attorn to British opinion." At Munster assizes, on Saturday, three young men named Patrick Driscoll, John Walahon, and Patrick Collins were indicted for having waylaid Mr. Francis Crosbie, brother of Colonel Crosbie at Ballyseedy, near Tralee, on the 14th ult., with the abject of obtaining his gun. The prisoners were convicted and sentenced, Driscoll to five years' and the two others to two years' imprisonment. NATIONALISTS OUTRAGES IN IRELAND: AN M.P. STONED. —When driving home from the Orange meeting at Dro- more, Mr. William Archdale, M.P., was stoned by a party of Nationalists at Trillick, and a number of missiles were after. wards taken out of tho carriage. The outrage has incensed the Orangemen of the district. The house of a Protestant school teacher was attacked, the windows and doors being smashed. REBUKING A CONclßEGATlON'—Preaelaing in St. Pataick's Cathedral, Dublin, which was crowded with a fashioaable congregation, the Rev. Mr. Ovenden' referring to the miser- ably small offertories, said that while thousands availed themselves of the Sunday afternoon service, a great many seemed to think more of the quality of the glove from the fingere of which they dropped with shabby penury into the collection plate than of their offering to God, DISGRACEFUL SCENES IN & CHURCHYARD.-011 Monday, according to directions, numbers of people attended Drog- heda Cemetery to point out the graves of relations for the purpose of registration. The place is piled up with human bodies, there being scarcely a yard of free earth left. The people on Monday disputed the ownership of the graves, and blows were exchanged. Relatives claimed the graves where members cf different families were interred, and the most painful and violent scenes ensued, the land- marks having been removed. The utmost confusion pre- vailed. SCENE AT AN IRISH TEACHERS' CONFERERENCE.—At their conference in Dublin, on Saturday, the National School teachers of Ireland bad an excited quarter of an hour on the presentation of a resolution censuring the president for having failed to give the toast of the Lord-Limatenant at the annual dinner. The president declared the sense of the meeting to be against the resolution being put, and the inci- dent terminated in the adoption of a resolution stating that no disrespect was intended to his excellency the Lord-Lieu- tenant. This, however, did not satisfy the Ulster teachers, several of whom left the hall. MURDER AND MANSLAUGHTER. At Cork Assizes, on Wednesday, John Biuns, a bailiff, was indicted for the wilful murder of James Macquillan at Ennis, county Clare, on the 29th September. The accused, who stabbed Macquillan during a quarrel, was found guilty of manslaugheer, and sentenced to ten years' penal servitude.—At the Munster assizes at Cork, John Murphy, Thomas Walsh, Patrick Casey, and Thomas Quinlan, who were convicted of the manslaughter of James Spence, near Croachford, were sen- tenced, Murphy and Quinlan to ten years' penal servitude each, Walsh to five years, and Casey to two years' imprison- ment with bard labour. THE IRISH PROGRAMME. —The Cemmittee on Irish Affairs, which was formed last sessions, will be directed during the forthcoming session towards circulating neces- sary information on Irish affairs, to promote discussion on practical lines, and to create means by which the public may be acquainted with the facts of contemporary Irish his- tory, the state and needs of the country, and the opinions of the people. Papers will be published on, among other sub- jects, the equalisation of the Irish with the English fran- chise, the creation of local and county goverumeut, reform of the centralised system of administration in Dublin, the labourers question, tramways and harbours, the development and improvement of Irish education. The Freeman's Journal publishes the following letter : Sir,—My attention ha e been called to a document which has appeared in your columns, signed Charles Alexander, entitled "A scheme for the better organisation of the Orange Society as a fighting force." As this document ap- pears to me to contain proposals of an illegal character, permit me to state that it has been issued without the knowledge or sanction of the recognised authorities of the Orange Institution, and consequently that the responsibility for the suggestion contained therein—of which I entirely disapprove—rests with its author.—Yeur obedient servant, ENNISKILLEN, Imperial Grand Master of the Orange 'mai. tution. Florence Court, Enniskillen, let January, 1584. ENFORCING THE POLICE Tex —A novel sale of cattle took place on Wednesday, near Killavullen, county Cork. A few days ago 15 beasts were seized from farmers who refused to pay the police tax for guarding a boycotted blacksmith, and on Wednesday were offered for sale. Mr. Harrington, M.P., was present as the representative of the National League, aud a crowd of peeple assembled. Police- sergeant Griffin, who effected the seizure, acted as auctioneer. Seven animals were offered without a bid being made, and these were driven off by some constables to Mallow. Three or four cows were afterwards bought in for their owners by Mr. Harrington for the amount of the tax, which varied from 50s to 3s, and he also purchased some other animals at very low figures, one cow going to him for the sum of Scl. Sergeant Griffin refused for some time to sell at these low figures. but ultimately agreed to take them, amid She deri- sive cheers of the crowd. At the clese of the sale Mr. Har- rington addresqed the crowd. He condemned the tax as iniquitous, and expressed admiration for the pluck and determination shown by the farmers of the district in resist- ing it. THE OPPOSITION BETWEEN NATIONALISTS AND ORA.NGE• MEN: EXCITING SCENE.—The town of Dromore, in county Tyrone, presented a remarkable spectacle on Tuesday. Nearly 700 soldiers and policemen were on duty from an early hour to prevent a conflict between the Nationalists, who had arranged to hold a demonstration, and the Orange- men, who had threatened to put down what they regarded as a rebel assembly, The Orangemen came from districts widely separated from the place of meeting, and most of them were armed with sticks, if not with something more formidable, in readiness for the expected encounter. At the head of "detachments" were Colonel Stuart RBOX. Lords Caledon and Crichton, and other well-known Orange leaders. The Nationalists also mustered in strong force and were also armed. They were headed by Mr. T. D. Sullivan, M.P., and Mr. O'Brien, M.P. The authorities had insisted that the two factions should, if they held meetings, occupy opposite ends of the town ; but in the process of assembling a party of Orangemen charged a contingent of Nationalists, and there was some disorder. Again, at the close of the meetings, at each of which characteristic resolutions were passed, the Orangemen made bold efforts to "get at" the Nationalists. In each instance the attempt to disturb the peace was met with firmness by the military and police forces, but the Orangemen were at one time so defiant that the Riot Act bad to be read, and they only finally dispersed before a charge of Hussars. Mr. Biggar attempted to hold the pro- hibited meeting at Cootehill, but he was ontmanceuvred by the authorities, and as the Orange opposition had been ap- peased by the issuing of the Government proclamation there was no disturbance.

POLITICAL. Addressing his constituents on Monday night, Captain Heron Maxwell, M.P. for Kircudbrightshire, said lie had no doubt the franchise of the burghs would be assimilated with that of the counties next session, and that the franchise would be a residential one. In his opinion the Governivent should not take up the franchise question before passing other useful legislation with which to go to the country in case of defeat, lie advocated the appointment of a Minister for Scotland. MR. GLADSTONE AND TFIE COLONIES.—The Premier writing to the editor of the Chester Chronicle, thanking him for forwarding on Saturday the carved cross thorn walkin2 stick, from Mr. William Moulton, of Swellandain, Cape Colony, says :--`' The stick is in itself, I think, beautiful, atanadcahiraegcorlelceocltlieocntiforaoi:n bmaets distant parts epalrityseoifnthtismgelsowbehei a ns a closer union as well as much free intercourse is to prevail between distant mertions of the globe. I will venture on asking you to add to your kindness already shown, by con- veying to Mr. Moulton my sincere wishes for his present welfare and all his future years." OPENING OF A LIBERAL CLVB AT CIIESTEIt.—A Liberal club was opened at Chester on Friday by Mr. Herbert Glad- stone, M.P., who expressed a hope that the Liberalism of Chester might soon be adequately represented in the House of Commons. He was sure the club would help greatly in restoriag their fallen fortunes. He thought the Liberal party had much to reassure them. After four years the Government found itself practically as strong as ever. Some political qnestions were at present causing great anxiety, as, for instance, the events taking place in China, the Soudan, , and the Transvaal ; but there was no reason to suppose that we had to face anything like such large difficulties as had been surmounted during the last four years THE PREMIER AND HIS CONSTITDENTS.—The following letter has been received by the chairman of the Midlothian Liberal Committee :—" Hawarden Castle, Chester, Dec. 29, 1883. My dear Mr. Cowan,—When the resolutions which were passed recently in various parts of the country came to my band, I did not fail to send a formal reply to each, but I wish now to add in person, and with my own hand, a few words more. I have been, I know, as scanty in demonstra- tions since the election of 1880 as I was abundant before it. This was, indeed, due to nothing else than serious physical incapability. Twelve months ago, when all the arrange- ments had been made for my rendering an account, which I am not less desirous than bounden to give, time and events have marched on, and there has not since appeared in view an opportunity for the discharge of this particular duty. But out of sight is not always out of mini; and though my daily duties keep pretty well up to the mark of my daify strength, I still contemplate with the utmost interest the time °when I may be enabled to fuldl that which is still lack- ing in my duty to my generous constituents. With regard to those resolutions, they one and all indicate that the fountain of that generosity remains uneabausted. For my own part, as well as on that of my colleagues, I venture to say we shall still seek to deserve their confidence, and that subjects which they name do not, and will not, cease to engage our thought and care.—With all good wishes for the New Year, I remain, my dear Mr. Cowan, most fsithf ully yours, W. E. GLansrolsa.',

session is indicated by the fact tam Ministers are again in town, and Thursday commenced the series of Cabinet Councils which precede the reaseimbliog of Parliament. Trle meeting was the first which has been held since November. In order to suit the convenience of some members returning from their country seats, the meet- ing was not held until two o'clock, and it lasted three hours. All the members were present except Sir Charles Mike, who was unable to return in time from his villa near Ton- lon, where he has been spending the Christmas holidays, The Press Association states that, contrary to the expecta- tion expressed in many quarters, the deliberations of the Ministry on Thursday had comparatively little reference to the details of their legislative programme for the coming session, but chiefly related to the criti- cal state of affairs in Egypt. On Saturday last and preceding days the Government received most important telegrams from Sir Evelyn Baring, and on Monday after- noon Mr. Gladstone and Earl Granville met upon the sub- ject in Downing-street, both coming from their country seats for the purpose. The information, it is stated, had especial reference to the helplessness of the Khedive in view of the condition of the Soudan. Preliminary to the meeting of the Cabinet, Earl Granville and Lord Edmond Fozmaurice had an informal conference with Mr. Gladstone as to the vigor- ous measures necessary to be taken,by this country in order to avert a serious Egyptian crisis. There is reason to be- lieve that after the discussion the Cabinet came to a sub- stantial agreement with the conclusions which the Prime Minister, the Foreign Secretary, and the Secretary for War had arrived at in their previous consultations. In deciding the course to be followed, concerning the details of which the members of the Government preserve the utmost re- ticence, full consideration was given to the fact that Tewfik Pasha, whilst strongly adverse to surrendering his claims of sovereign over the Soudan, admits his own inability to recover that territory.

BITRTONWOOD. EMU II:INWOOD WESLEYAN SCHOOL.—A large nuober persons rat down to a capital tea which was served the Bartonwood Wesleyan School on New Year's Day, when ihe annual tea party was held. The room was tastef ally be- decked for the occasion. After tea the chair was occupied by Mr. Gay, who in the course of the evening distributed a , r number of prizes to the school children for regular and punctual attendance. A programme of songs, recitations, was creditably gone through. YRODSHAM. Mr. W. Wynne Ffoutkes, Judge of the Runcorn County Court, has appointed Mr. Peter Harrop, auctioneer, Prod- sham, bailiff under the Agricultural Holdings Act, 1883. WATCH NIGHT Szuvrct.—A service was held in the Trinity Chapel, Frodsham • on- Monday night, when the Revs. G. L. Allen and F. F. Edmonds gave appropriate ad- dresses. When the New Year of 1884 had dawned, the congregation separated after the usual congratulations and good wishes.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE AT G-OLBORNE..At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, James Smith (collier) and Francis Kelly (collier) were each fined 5s for neglecting to send their children to school in accordance with the requira- ments of the Elementary Education Act. GOLBOENE WESLEYAN CHAPEL—The annual tea party in connection with the Grolborne Wesleyan Chapel was held in that place of worship on New Year's Day. About 200, persons partook of a most substantial tea, which was nicely served byte number of the lady teachers in the Sunday school. At the subsequent proceedings the chair was oc-- cupied by the Rev. (I. Smith, of St. Helens, circuit minister, and addresses were delivered by that gentleman, and Messrs. Rigby, Turton, and Entwistle. The choir, con- ducted by Mr. W. Entwistle, effectively rendered a selection of music. and Mr. W. Jones ably accompanied on the pianoforte. Recitations, Bre., were creditably given; and at the close of a most enjoyable meeting the customary votes of thanks were accorded. The members of the choir along with a few friends held their annual tea party on Wednes- day evening, when about 20 persons were present. The subsequent proceedings were of a social and enjoyable character.

SERIOUS THFIrTs AT GOLBORNE: GIYING WAY TO TENII TATION.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, Sarah Reyes, a middle-aged married woman, was charged with stealing on the 18th inst. 40 yards of window blinding, the property e Themes Turton, value 355., further with stealing on the 13th December, a hearth rug, value 7s 6d, the property of Thomas Luton; and also with stealing about seven weeks ago 22 yards of woollen shirting, value .£1 13c, the property of the said Thomas Tbrton. The prisoner pleaded guilty to all the three charges.—No witnesses were called, but the prisoner, on being asked if she had anything to say, replied : I have three little children, and we have neither food nor fire in the house. These things were out- side the shop door. It was dark, and from want and tempta- tion I took them. Please, your worships, it was the &et time.—lnspector Weir: The shirting was taken from inside I the shop.—The prisoner: I beg your pardon, it was outside. —The Clerk (to police): Do you think it is true about her being in a state of starvation 2—P.C. Ratcliffe replied that prisoner had a husband working in a cotton mill.—She was committed to prison for one calendar month. ST. THOMAS'S CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS : NEW YEAR'S GATHERINGS.—Between 400 and 500 persons sit down to a most excellent tea in Mr. Brewis's School, Golborne, on New Year's Day—the occasion being the annual tea party and entertainment in connection with St. Thomas's Church Sunday schools. In preparation for the event the school- room underwent a most elaborate deccration with coloured papers, evergreens, itc., while numerous seasonable mottoes were skilfully displayed about the room. This work had been carried out by the school teachers, and great credit was reflected upon them. At the subsequent proceedings the chair was occupied by the Rev. W. Thorpe ',curate), who was supported by Messrs. W. H. Arnott and A. Cannce. For the first time in 30 years the genial and kindly face of the respected rector (the Rev. C. T. Quirk) was missed (rota among those present his indisposition ren- dering it absolutely impossible for him to attend- The Chairman read a letter from the Rector, in which the latter said he would have been glad to be present, but his health would not permit it. He hoped they would have a pleasant and enjoyable gathering, and wished them all a happy New Year. In his opening address the rev. Chairman made a touching allusion to Mr. Quirk's absence. An ex- cellent programme was subsequently gone through in a most effective' and pleasing manner.—The annual treat to the scholars was held on the evening of the following diy (Wed- nesday). There were upwards of 300 teachers androcholars present, who partook of a capital tea. Mr. W. ft Arnett presided at the after proceedings. An excellent programme of songs, recitations, &c. was gone through, while the scholars in Miss Moon's class in the Sunday school were presented with their annual prizes of handsome books. In the un- avoidable absence of Mies Moon the prizes were presented by Miss H. Crowther. The meeting was a very enjoyable one.

Sr. JamEs'e-Caoncir. Scaoot.—The annual tea party and dance in connection with Haydock St. James's Schools was hold on Monday evening, and proved to be a very suc- cessful and enjoyable gathering. The tea was nicely served by several ladies of the congregation, and a large number of persons were present. The room was subsequently cleared for dancing, which was heartily kept up until about eleven o'clock. FOOT RAcz POD £lo.—kt the Recreation Grounds, St. Helens, on Saturday last, J. Smith and J. Stott, both of Elaydock, ran 110 yards for £5 aside. Very few spectators, however, paid for admission, and as it was rumoured that Smith had a lot in hand scarcely any betting took place, and 3to 1 went a begging oia him. That there was good grounds for Smith being so much fancied was justified by the race, as be Won rather cleverly by a good yard. Mr. J. Mercer was rejeme, and Mr. J. Kaye pistol-tirer. SINOULAR TEMPT AT HATDOCH. At the. Newton Town H.all, on Saturday last, James Molyneux, Daniel Hughes, and Joseph Bailey, young min, pleaded guilty to stealing the sum of 2Sa from the person of James Swain, at Haydock, on the 25th ult. Inspector Keir stated that the prosecutor and prisoners were In a public-house together, when the prosecutor fell asleep. He was awoke by feeling a hand in his pocket, whereupon prisoners ran away with the money. The chairman pointed out that it was a vary serious case, and but for a recent Act of Parliament the prisoners would have had to be committed for trial. Each would now be fined 20s and costs. HASDOCIC PHIIIIIIVB METHODIST CHAPEL—The annual

- tea meeting in connection with this place of worship was held in the school-room on Monday evening last. A goodly number of persons sat down to an enjoyable tea, after which a public meeting was held, when the chair was occupied by Mr. J. Livesley, sen. Addresses were given by Messrs. J. Fairhurst and C. Ba%endale. The choir under the conduc- . .

torebip of Mr. J. Livesley, jun., excellently rendered a number of selections; while a number of pieces were nicely recited by the scholars. The proceeds of the gathering were in aid of the trust fund.. On New Year's Eva a watch- night service was held in the chapel, at which there was a nice attendance. Appropriate addresses were given by Mr. J. Livesley, senior and Mr. R. Barrow. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, PARR.—On New Year's Day, the annual school tea party and entertainment were held in the above -Place, The attendance at tea was very encouraging, and the good things provided were well served by Mrs. Atherton, Mrs. Johnson, Mrs Lancaster, Mae. Sal- land, and the Misses Smith, Chgrnock, and Johnson. The entertainment after tea was presided over by the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, of Barlestown, circait minister, who after the devotional exercise, gave an address bearing upon the work el Sabbath schools. The following anthems were very effectively rendered by the cboir, under the conclactorehip of Mr. S. Smith, accompanied byMr. J. Smith .on the bar- , monium:—"New year's song" (Berthold Tours), "The ,Saviour comes," ".Seraphic choir" (Fawctte), and "Let us now go" (J. L. Hatton). Mr. .I. T. Elliott sang a solo very sweetly, " Waft her angels." (Handel); the Misses Smith sang in excellent veins and style the duet, " Sea of glass " (Glover). A pleasing duet was given on the violin and violoncello by Mr. C. Bunney and Mr. S. Smith. An address was delivered by Mr. W. Hankey, and prizes were given to eeveral scholars for good attendance and profici- ency in Scripture knowledge. The following recitations were also well given :—" Faithful unto death," Miss S. A. Charnoek; "Better contentment than covetousness." Miss H. Hill; " 'The shipwrecked sailor boy," Miss Davies ;."rve got the Bible," Miss M. Waring. The report read by Mr. C. Bonney (rt cretary) showed the number of teachers to be 11, scholars 122—an increase for the year. The income for the year was £l4 is 8i 1, and the expenditure £ls4i 214 Number of vols, in the library, 400. It was hoped the slight adverse balance would be more than swept off by the present effort After the usual votes of thanks to the ladies who provided tea, the chairman, and the singers, the singing of the Doxology and Benediction concluded a very profitable and pleasing meeting.

SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNUAL TEL PARTY AND. NNTBSTAINo MENT.—On Monday evening last the annual tea party and entertainment of the children and friends of the Holt Sun- day school took place. This small and unpretentious place of worship was crowded to its fullest extent by young and old, bent on spending the last evening of the old year in innocent enjoyment. A good substantial tea was provided, and having been disposed of to the satisfaction of all present, the room was cleared for the evening's entertain- ment'. This part of the programme is always anticipated with the liveliest interest by all, the main portion of the amusement being afforded by the children and adult mem- bers of the school. The chair was taken by Mr. W. Evans, of Ivy Cottage, Whiston, who, in his opening address ex- pressed pleasure at seeing so many present, and coneluded by wishing all a Happy New 'Year. The programme, of miseelianeims items, was then commenced with a glee, " 0h,,, who will o'er the downs so free," snag by Messrs Diamond, Highain, Hankinson, and Thomas, a quartette that of late has gained some local celebrity for the excellent manner in which it has rendered several well•known glees; the "Village chorister,," also sung by the same quartette, was deserving of the applause it received. The recitations of the youthful performers were capitally given, those call- ing for special mention being " Meddlesome Matty," by Miss M. Critchloy ; "Bruce and the spiders" by M. Parr; "A noble boy." by G. Ball; and "A walk ist a churchyard," by M. A. Welling. Mr. Thomas, of Raishill, sang the 3 ng, "Aurae is home," in aft artistic manner, and receive a hearty round of applause. The programme rivals," nd'amme al3o inclu ed • 'a two hunacrouslialognes, entitled the the Barber's conrtship." The various puts were ad- mirably sustained by Miss 0, Ball, Miss U. Ball, Min

The death is reported of the eldest Son of the Sultan of Morocco. A Denver telegram states that 27 persms have been killed by the fall of avalanches in the Colorado mountains. At Cologne, on Christmas Eve, a Watchmaker and his mother were murdered in their homes. Robbery is supposed to have been the motive of the murderers. New Year's Eve in Berlin used to be charactised by the rough behaviour and excesses of the people in the streets. Last New Year's Eve, however, thanks to the enormous number of constables on foot and on horse, who kept mov- ing about among the crowd, there were no outrages. The "disorders" reported from Bosnia and Herzegovina do not subside. A large percentage of the recruits drafted into the Imperial forces has disappeared, manommau had entered the service and received a decoration has been assassieated ; and attacks on soldiers are frequent. Something like civil war prevails in the Yazoo district' of the State of Mississippi. A few days ago some negroes fired upon a party of white men, and killed two of them. The murderers were arrested, but the process of the law— I never very expeditious in "shooting" cases in Mississippi I —was too slow for the "white chivalry," and we now learn that they have broken.into the gaol and shot or hanged four of the imprisoned negroes. SUPPOSED MURDER OF • PUBLIC EXECUTIONER.—A tele- gram from Braun (Moravia) states that Bott, the public executioner, was found dead in his bed on Saturday. His death was at first attributed to a stroke of apoplexy, but, subsequently, it was rumoured that he had fallen a victim to revenge. The judicial post-mortem examination of the body showed that two ribs were broken. Tim public prosecutor has instituted an inquiry into the affair. THE ILBERT Blue—The Daily News saw—We learn that a private telegram received from Calcutta on Saturday states that as the compromise entered into between the Indian Government and the Defence Association concedes to English subjects the right to be tried by a jury in which their countrymen'would form the majority, the leaders of the native community consider that a similar privilege I should be granted to the natives of India when tried by European magistrates. We understand that if this conces- sion is made they will be satisfied. FIGHTING IN THE SOUDAN : REPULSE OF THE REBELS. —An official despatch has been received at Cairo announc- ing that on Friday last a body of rebels attacked Gizireh, about eight miles distant from Berber. The place was gar- risoned by two companies of Bashi-Bazouks, who had erected entrenchments, and were fully prepared for attack. After six hours' severe fighting the assailants were driven back with heavy loss. The Egyptian loss was slight, but includes the commander of the Bashi-Bazouks. The Bich- aries and Ranailat tribes joined forces with the Egyptians, and assisted them in the fighting. A despatch says that the rebels intended to attack Berber, but their plan was thwarted by the resistence they encountered at Gezireh. 'THE NIHILISTS IN RUSSIA: MURDER OF THE CHIEF OF THE SEC.RET Potica.—Lieutenant-Colonel Sueleitin, chief of the secret police in the Russian capital, has been assas- sinated. Few details are given of the assassination, but that it is the work of the Nihilists is regarded as beyond doubt, and the alarm that has been caused by the event amongst those who are responsible for the sifety ,of the Czar is great. The most recent account is that Colonel Soudeikin, , about half .past five en Friday even;ng, went to a house in ' the }Taysky Prospect, at which he is suppesed to have been in the habit of meeting spies. Several members of the secret police were left to await his return in an adjoining street, and at midnight, as he had not re-appeared, they went to see what was the matter, and discovered that he had been murdered. The assumption is that hie assassins were Nihi- lists disguised' as spies or detectives, and Colonel Soudeikin is believed to have incurred their deadly hostility by dm- covering a serious Nihilist conspiracy. Much of this is, however, pure speculation, as the authorities give little in- formation, and, indeed, have little to give. BRIGANDAGE IN SICILy,—The following communication has been issued from the Foreign Office, dated December 28, 1883:—" Her Majesty's consul at Palermo in a recent despatch stated that during the last two years- it has been perfectly safe to travel about Sicily without an escort, there being no regular bands of brigands, as in former days, in existence. About a month ago, however' the capture of a Sicilian nobleman by armed men, who demanded a large slam for his release, gave good reason for doubting the assu- raece. A letter was addtessed by Her Majesty's consul to the Prefect of Palermo, inquiring whether it was safe at the preseat time, in view of this event, to travel in the island without an escort. In reply, Mr. Churchill has received a communication from the Prefecture to the effect that, although travelling is perfectly safe in Xis province, it would tie advisable to warn the authorities, 'especially in the case of wealthy travellers, in order that proper measures may he taken to protect them. 'Under these circumstances,. all persons visiting Sicily, and wishing to travel in the in- terior, are recommended to address themselves to Mr. Churchill, Her Majesty's consul at Palermo, in order that they may bepreviied with an escort in case of need. It is thought well in some parts of the island that the movements of travellers should be known to.the authorities, so that the carabinieri of the neighbourhood may be on the alert."

EXTRAORDINARY STEAM-TRAM ACCIDENT AT WIGAN. THE COUNTY CORONER KILLED. An extraordinary and fatal accident occurred on the Wigan and Pemberton. Tramway. on Saturday morning, resulting In the death of Mr. T. W. Barker, solicitor, of Southport, the coroner for the West Derby division of the county of Lancaster. Mr. Barker had been holding an in- quest at Pemberton on the body of a boy killed at a colliery in the township, and left the terminus at Pemberton for Wigan by the twelve o'clock tram. The car proceeded to the Landashire Union Railway Bridge, at Newtown, a dis- tance of a mile and a quarter from Pemberton terminus, and here bad to wait at the passing place as usual for the tram coming from Wigan. It was while stopping at that spot that the accident happened. The driver of the steam-tram, it is said, got down, to rescue a:child, and in doing so was himself knocked down, being unable to recover his place on the,engine, which ran down an incline of from 1 in 40 to 1 in Ifs at a pace which frightened the passers-by. Near the Half-way House Inn, about 1,000, yards from the terminus it Overturned a horse and cart, then dashed down the Spring Bank, and smashed, with great force, into the tram-car which was standing on the junction nearly at the bottom of the hill. In this car there were only five passengers. Mr. Parry, commission agent, who was seated with his son close to the door at the hick of the car, saw the approaching engine, but only when it was almost upon them. He cried out that something muqt be wrong, and advised his fellow-passengers to escape. All at once made for the door, and all bad jumped off except Mr. Barker, who had been seated at the farthest end of the car- , riagn, and who was censequantly the last to leave. Be was caught just as he was stepping off between the engine and the back of the car, being tightly jammed in between the body of the vehicle and the engine. Mr Rowlands, iron- monger, of -Wigan, who was in front of Mr. Barker, had a very narrow escape. He was thrown down and off the car.but how he does not blow, and he escaped with only a shaking The effect ot the collision was most singular. The stationary engine in fiont of the car was forced from the line ad literally lifted on to the footpath and into the hedge, whilst the runaway engine drove the standing tram a distance of a hundred yarde, both keeping to the track, its further course being stopped by the approaching engine and car from Wigan. The back part of the car was smashed, and the framework ot bath engines broken. Mr. Barker was found to be so. tightly jammed in by the broken framework that the help of several persons had to be obtained before he could be extricated. He was then unconscious and almost lmlseless. Both his legs and several ribs were broken, and he died a tew minutes afterwards in Mr. Graham's surgery. The driver of the stationary engine was cut about the face, but was able to proceed home. The driver of the engine which caused the accident (Joseph Thompson) was taken into custody by the police, and detained at the station pend- ing the arrival of the superintendent. Mr. Barker, who formerly acted as deputy for Mr. C. E. Driffield, Coroner for the West Derby Hundred, was appointed to the post on the resignation of that gentleman twelve months ago.— An inquest was held on Monday on the body. Mr. Edge, coroner.for Wigan, conducted the inquiry. After evidence of identification had been given, the inquest was adjourned. —Joseph Thompson, driver of the steam engine which caused the accident, was then brought up before the Wigan magistrates, charged with manslaughter, and remanded. The prisoner explained that he slipped off his engine to save a child, and could not overtake the locomotive again. The Beard of Trade have intimated that they have appointed Major-General Hutchinson to mak.% ar, icattiry into' the accident..

TRA PARTY AT TRH CROFT BOARD SCROOL.—The above annual tea Party took place on Thursday evening last, when upwards of 80 persons eat down to an excellent tea provided in the schoolroom, which ha& been very tastefully decora- ted for the occasion. The following ladies presided at the tables, namely :—Mrs. and Miss Kirkman, Mrs. Owen (of the Brewery), Miss- Ball, Miss Bate, and Miss Southern. The rector, the Rev. T. P. Kirkm in, M.A., F.R.S., was also. present. After tea, dancing anl various other games were indulged in until 12 o'clock, when the party broke up, all being highly pleased with their evening's enjoyment. Ap- ples, biscuits, figs, and oranges were distributed amongst those present during the evening. CHRIST CHORCH.—The choir of this church,"uf the num- ber of 30, were entertained at the Board School, Croft, on , Saturday evening, by the Rector, the Rey. T. P. and Mrs. Kirkman. About five o'clock the party sat down to an ex- cellent tea, provided in the schoolroom. Mrs. and Miss Kirkman presided at the tables, the Rector and Mr. Ball, the organist and choirmaster, also being present. After tea dancing and various other games were engaged in till ten o'clock, when supper was provided, and after giving hearty cheers for Mr., Mrs, and Miss Kirkman, and Miss Robin- son and Miss Owen for their kindness, the National Anthem was sung and the party broke up. Cheers were given.for Mr. Ball and Mr. Alfred Dixon for the assistance they had given to make the entertainment so succ,ssful. WINSFORD. •
IMPURE WATER.

It was reported by Dr. Fox that the water in the pump connected with Mr. Ardern's houses near the gasworks, Pepper-street, was unfit for use, being much contaminated with recent and old sewage matter. The Surveyor was in- structed to give notice to the owner to provide a proper supply.

_ WESLEYAN BAND. OF Honn.—The spirited manner in which the Juvenile Temperance cause has been taken up by Mr. Stocks and others In Winsford reflects considerable credit on its promoters. Several successful meetings, at evßich the juvenile element has preponderated. have been held already, and as no more encouraging way, as far as small folks are concerned, appears feasible, the tea meeting was held on the 31st ultimo, at which the members mustered in grhat numbers. Toe service of song which followed did not elicit such approbation and support as. was expected from the choir's rendering, and the Rev, E.. Murphy's excellent readings. WATCR-NICIEET SERVICES.—The usual services at the I close of the year tharacterised the various Methodist bodies. Each chapel had its fair representation of the congregation worshipping at it. At the Wesleyan Chapel (Hill T)p) there was a good gathering under the presiding influence of the Rev. E. Murphy, whom others assisted most efficiently. At the .Primitive Chapel, Over, the Rev. Mr. Nock urged remembrance of the way God had led the people and the confidence such called for. The High-street Primitive Chapel was wet) attended. There Messrs. R. Morgan ancl T. Minshall held forth the word of life. At the Congrega- tional Church, Over, the Rev. J. Maxwell conducted a ser- vice to which free invitation was given and fairly, responded to, but the place was not full. At the Free Methodist Chapel about 200 listened with attention to the Rev. W. T. SVIROII3. Mr. John Buckley delivered an excellent discourse abounding with lessons of encouragement for the incoming year. Mr. J. 11. Massey urged fidelity to the teaching of God s.Word. At Christ Church, Winsford, the Rev. E. Nixon held a service which was appreciated by many. ITEMS OP CHESHIRE NEWS. PRESENTATION TO MIL HORATIO LLoyD.--At Chester Castle, on Mohday morning, the Duke of Westminster, Lord Lieutenant of Cheshire, acting for the magistrates of the county, presented Mr. Horatio Lloyd. deputy-chairman of the Court of Qtrirter Sessions and Judge of the Cheshire and North Wales County Courts, with a parse containing one thousand guineas; also with a silver waiter and an illu- minated address. The presentation was. made in recogni- tion of Mr. Lloyd's services as deputy-chairman of the Court of Quarter Sessions during the past eight years. In the address the subscribers expressed a hope that Mr. Lloyd would be spared to fulfil the important duties as well of deputy chairman of the Court of Quarter Sossions as those of the other offices which be occupied with ouch distinguished ad- vantage to the.

div.p: THE CLAIM Fen COMPENSATION.

The Rev. Mr. Dickenson again wrote to the Board respect- ing his claim for compensation, and after some conversation it was decided that no compensation be paid Mr. Dickenson, as the Board considered that no clamors had been done.
BIIRFORDALANZ BUIDGE,

A deputation. consisting of the chairman, Mr. Dewhnrst, and„the clerk, was appointed to wait upon the solicitors to the Bridgewater Navigation Company to make arrangcments for the abatement of the nuisance at Burfora-:ane under- bridge.
Til'ere was no other business a public importance, and the Board rose.

PAROCHIAL .TEA,, PARTY AND • CONCERT AT FRODSHAM. The annuil parochial tea party and concert in connection with the Frodsham Parish Church took plaoe in the Town Hall on Thursday. The tea in the afternoon was largely attended, and the following ladies presided at the tables : Mesdames C. Reynolds, C. E. Linaker H. Linaker, A. Theme's, J. Ashton, J. C. Sutton, Tomlineon, Jolliffe, R. Bate, T. Rile, J. W. Rethwell, Teßate, W: H. Litiaker, H. Reynolds, Missdh Crosfirlds, LinakereDavies, and Clarke. The concert lathe evening was crowded to overthwing. It is only occasionally that we have a concert by local ama- teurs, and it must be great satisfacticn to those who take part in a concert ef this character that their efforts are fully appreciated, and on Thursday. evening the audience ex- pressed their approbation in a most demonstrative manner. The first item on the programme was a part song, "The sands of Dee" (G. A. Macfarren) which created a favourable impression. Mr. John Holland, a rising young amateur, possesses a good bassmoiee, and gave "A warrior bold" (S • Adams) witn the utmost confidence, for which he received an encore. The duet, "Underneath the leaves so green" (Montgomery), by Miss Riley and Miss K Rigby, was sung, in a pleasing manner, and Miss E R. Riley was encored for the song "Golden love" (Wellings), to which she responded with "The letter." 'lbis was given with even a better effect, and in a vivacious manner. The quartette "Spring's Delights" (Muller) by Messrs. Jones, Barrow, Hulseeand J. Holland, was well re- ceived. The "Maid of Llangollen" (Clarke), by. Mr. H. G. Linaker, was loudly applauded, and he bowed his acknowledgment: The remainder of the first part of the programme consisted of a.duet," The sailor sighs as sinks his native shore" (Balls), by Miss E. E. Riley and Mr. B. Holland, encored ;.song, "•Ehren on the Rhine" (Hutchin- son), by Mr. John Bartow, and the well-worn but welcome part song "The dawn of day" (Reay). - The second part of the programme opened with a part song, ",The cuckoo sings in the poplar tree" (G. A. ^Meet arren), by the choir, and was well sustained throughout. " The Pilgrim of Der e " Bishop), by Mr. A. Jones, and a duet, The Minute Gun at Sea" (King), by Messrs. Woods and, Barrow, were each encored. Miss K. Rigby gave "Tit for tat" (Pontet) with much naivete, and reeponcLed ta a stmn of applause. A duet by Miss Riley and Miss E. E hi:eV en- titled," Round the fire" (Pinsuti), and was given with crispness, the latter part of the duet being, followed, repeated on a rte. call. "The cruise of the Calabar," by Mr. R. J. Hulse was' a humour° peint to Northwicla in a ' us topical song, and relatedrthe eventful ex- perience of a voyage from Weston ait with one-horse power, and created much amusement. Mr.ritk.s)Haonlidanreaceteend an encore. popular song "Sailing . The Frodsham Quartette 'de their second appearance, and scored a success with "The three chafers ' (Truhn). The song "The Better Lo was feelingly rendered by Miss Riley and met wellow e r deserved encore. The glee "The Fisherman's a ight" (Bishop), and the liaticnal Anthem brought 911 excellent concert to a close. Mr. C. Riley accompanied on the piano in a very efficient,manner, and was deserving of a better instrument than the, one Provided. Mr. Thomas Riley, organist of the Parioh. Chinch, conducted the glees, which gave evidence of kia.palastaking rehearsals. Before the meeting separated a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the ladies who had presided at the tex,;and the choir, also the churchwardens—Messrs. Charles Reynolds and Charles S. Linaker—for the indefatigable manner in, which they bad laboured for the success of the parochial, tea and concert of 1884. The vote of, thanks was proposed by the Vicar,. Rev. HR. Blogg, and mended by Mr. John Ashton.

To the Financial Reform Almanack—wit which for fullnes@, accuracy, and clearness, no other production of a like character can be conlpared—we are indebted for the figures which we give below. The Almanack is this Year as instructive as ever, and it possesses several new features, all of which tend to• bring out more clearly than before—if that were.possible—the necessity for a complete revision of our fi.scal system. We may add here that the Financial Reform Association, by whom the Almanack is issued, are doing an exCellent work, and it is to be hoped that tr.:ey will meet with that increased support 'from the public which their efforts deserve and demand. Perhaps the most interesting Portion of this year's volume are the pages devoted to a detailed estimate of the amount of public money paid to dukes. marquises; and earls, and to their relatives from the corn- Mencement of the year 1850. From this we End that z 8 ducal families, with 519 relatives, have received from the public exchequer. • £9,760,090; 33 families of marquises, with 626 relatives, have drawn £8,305,950; and 200 families of earls, with 3 391 relatives, have been paid £48,181,202 total, -£66,2+7,242. In this part of the Almanack there are some curious notes, one or two of Which may be worth reproducing. Five re- latives of the Marquis CAMDEN, we are told, received £6,000 ; but "in the last generation there was a Marquis CAMDEN who made £i,000,000 from-one sinecure alone. To his credit be it spoken that this same nobleman voluntarily gave back a portion of his booty to the nation, almost the only instance of Conscience money to be found in „ the archives of the British aristocracy." On the other hand, we find the Earl of GUILFORD and. his fifteen relatives received 462,000, against whom there is this note. " This is the venerable party who for 45 years robbed the rich charity of St. Cross's Hospital and was exposed in the law courts by a dissenting minister of Southampton, being made to dis- gorge four years accumulations. Lord ROMILIN, the Master of the Rolls, said his shameless perversion of one of our noblest charities had been done under a system which not even the most unscrupulous cupidity could have carried out until hardened into a contempt 'for common decency. The Times newspaper 'of the period wrote, He Will go down to the grave with a dishonoured name and an evil fame too' well deserved Should he leave to his own offspring the property accumulated by depriving the needy of their inheritance.' The property was so left. The motto of the family is, Virtue is the only, • nobility.'" According to the -list £55,0n0i • has been received by two relatives of the present Earl of Er.noar, whose great . grandfather is said to have netted no less than £1,570,000 from the public service. The object of this list is to show how great are the vested and legislative influences brought to bear against economies in the British public service; and we confess that With facts such as these staring us in the face the difficulties in the way of a radical finan- cial reform seem almost insurmountable. We only hope that time and an incessant i Plodding will work a change. Let t not be forgotten that the £66,000,000 referred to above have been drawn by the families of dukes, marquises, and earls only; the families of viscounts and barons and their receipts have yet to be inquired into, and by these we flAre say quite £66,000,000 more have been

TEE SMALL-PDX OUTRREAK AT WinNns.—This outbreak is now almost stamped out. The last inmate of the hotpi- tal was discharged yesterday, and Mr. Higginson and the ether out patients are nearly recovered. GOOD TEMPLARISM AT Wwiens.—The "Haste to the Rescue" Lodge of the LO G.T. held a tea and entertain- silent on New Year's Day, when 60 persons were present. Mr. Samuel Lamb presided and delivered an address, as did also Bro. Morris Jones, of Liverpool. The enterte.inment was much enjoyed. THE CHURCH OP ENGLAND SELECT BIBLE CrAss,uf which Mr. F. 11. Pankhurst is president, bad tea in the National Schools on Tuesday, and an entertaining programme was gone through. The vicar, the Rev. J. Wright Williams, and Mr. Pankhurst delivered addressee. Dig WIDNES CHURCH OP ENGLAND 'TEMPERANCE SOCIETY have held a series of meetings and enlertaintnents during the festive season just past, and they have been very successful. They were brought to a conclusion on Thursday evening last, when Mr. R. W. Roalston, of Liverpool, lectured in the National Schools on "The Englishman's Castle, the home of the ancient and modern Briton." HOLY TRIRITY SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN —The teachers' association in connection with this school had their annual tea party on Tuesday. Afterwards a meeting was held under the presidency of the Rev. W. Preston, and Mr. H. Hankin- eon read an able and interesting paper on "Sunday school work." A. discussion in which the Chairman and Messrs. Yates, Goodwell, Cunningham, Fletcher, and others took part, followed. SMITH & CO.'S RUNCORN ALEIANACE.—rhie annual pub- lication has just been Issued, and is a remarkable evidence of enterprising advertising in a local firm of .chemists. It is a large, well printed volume, containing a mass of local and general information on a variety of subjects, with literary and humourous companions, which will afford many hours pleasant reading. Amongst the illustrations by which its pages are embellished is an interesting wood cut of Hewer- den Castle. NATIONAL REFORM UNION PUBLICATIONS. From time to time the National Reform Union issues pamphlets bear- ing on the political questions which agitate the public mind. Each subject is usually treated in an able, clear, and incisive style, and there is no doubt that these pam- phlets materially assist in directing and guiding public opinion in the right direction. We notice that among the latest of their publications is a reprint of Mr. Trevelyan's recent speeches on the county franchise, which have been revised by the author himself expressly for this purpose. Other pamphlets reproduce the speech of Sir Henry James at Dumfries on "The Financial Policy of Mr. Ciladstone's Government ;" Mr. Arthur Arnold's speeches in the House of Commons on Parliamentary Reform; the article on he Ilbert Bill, contributed by Mr. William Summers, Ml',, to to the North British Quarterly ; and those on Local Go- vernment and Taxation by Mr. William Rathbone, M.P., which originally appeared in the Nineteenth Century in February and March last. The most important of the re- cent issues by the Union is, however, a flysheet comprising an analysis of the new law against bribery and corruption, prepared by Mr. Arthur G. Symonds, M A., secretary of the Union. If every worker at an election would only procure c iny of this flysheet he would find it to be of immense assistance to him. This sheet should above all others have a very wide publicity amongst all who are in any way en- gaged in electioneering work.

Wakefield, who lives in Xelsong 2n-street. portance of this question. —From the evidence adduced its appeared that Mrs. Wake- field placed eight half-crowns and a two-shilling piece on - - the mantelpiece, and afterwards went to her mother's house which Wirs in the locality'. There was no person in thehouse. When she returned at the expiration of five minutes the money had disappeared. She informed her husband who went to the prisoner who was in the street in charge of a donkey and cart, and asked him if he had been in the house. The husband erdered a bye-stander to fetch a policeman, when the prisoner said he would give him the money if he would "say no more about it.' He then handed over to the prosecutor the stolen money. Sob- seguently P.S. Walley apprehended the prisoner. In answer to the charge he said "A little boy asked me to reach the money to take to his mother. I did not think of stealing it." The prosecutor's boy, whom the prisoner identified, denied this statement.—The Bench ordered the prisoner to receive six strokes with the birch rod. ROBBERY FROM a Romcossr ROOTMAKER.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Elizabeth Doyle (0), Kate Lan- caster, and John and Annie Murray, man and wife, were brought up on remand charged with stealing and receiving a pair of shoes worth 13s, the property of Henry Stone, boot and shoe maker, Church-street, Runcorn.—On the ap- plication of Superintendent Williamson, Lancaster was dis- charged, and called upon to give evidence. Mr. Stone missed the hoots on the 7th November, and a short period , subsequently Doyle entered Mrs. Lancaster's house in I Water-street, Widnes, where the prisoners Murray were then lodging. She had the shoes produced in her hand, and -stetted that her fathet had purchased them at a sale at Run- corn, but as they were too big for him he world give Mur- ray the "first chance" and eell them fer. ss. Mrs. Murray asked if they were "all right," and being answered in the affirmative Murray purchased the shoes. The same night Mrs. Lancaster, at the request of Mrs. Murray, pawned the shoes at the shop of Mr. Syred for 55.—P.5. Whalley hav- ing given evidence as to the apprehension of the prisoners, they were asked to plead. Doyle Pleaded guilty, but the two Murrays denied that they had any knowledge of the theft.—The Bench considered there was not sufficient evi- dence to convict the Murray's, but sentenced Doyle to a fortnight's imprisonment, afterwards to be an icmate of a reformatory for three years. Tern VACANT COUNTY CORGICIRSHIP.—There is every likelihood ef a spirited contest for the coronership of the West Derby Division of the county, rendered vacant by the sad death of Mr. T. W. Barker, last Saturday. The election rests with the freeholders resident in the district, and the ' voting, which is open, will take place at Ormskirk. The salary attached to the office is, it has been stated, £950 a year, in addition to minepence a mile travelling expenses. There era already, we be- lieve, five candidates in the field, these being Mr. P. Davies, 801 iSi tor, of Warrington, son of Mr. Alderman Joseph Davies, IP , Warrington ; Mr, H. L. Risley, solicitor, of St. Helens and Liverpool, who was in the field when Mr. Barker was ap- pointed; Mr. L. R. Rowbottom, coroner of Wigan, who was Mr. Barker's depicter; Mr. W. Hardy, barrister-at-law, Wigan, who for some years has acted as deputy to Mr. J. B, Edge, one of the county coroners; and Mr. Samuel Brig. house, of the firm of Meters. Brighouse, Brighomee, and Jones, solicitors, Ormskirk. The addresses of Messrs. Bow- bottom, Brighouse, Hardy, god Riley, appear in our advertising columns.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, .
OUR LONDON LETTER.

THE CABINET COUNCIL-FEASTING AND SMOK- ING-THE CONSECRATION IN THE ABBEY- THE POSTMASTER AND THE PARCELS POST- THE PRIVATE VIEW AT THE GROSVENOR- THE PEOPLE-THE DRESSES-THE PICTURES- IMPROVEMENTS IN PICCADILLY - OILED WAVES.
LONDON, THIRSDAY.

This Egypt may have had a claim of "urgency" in the deliberations of the Cabinet House measures received full attention. The questions to be settled were really less matters of inclusion than of priority. Government will meet the Haase with tie three great measures in its pro- gramme, but the franchise will be first in the list. The country has been busy during the last three weeks discussing the Household Suffrage Bill. Speakers of all shades of political opinion have had their say, and been supported, confuted, or reasoned with. The result seems pretty clear. The Irish house- holders will not be debarred of benefits that will obtain all over Great Britain. Whatever may be the hostility of the Nationalists, justice will be done to the country which they seek to sever from British rule. The Home Secretary is also very resolute about the London Government Bill. The Cabinet are pretty well agreed about their programme, and the rumours of disunion or half-heartedness on the part of two of the members are quite without foundation.

City banquets are necessarily the most Conservative feasts in London—the old plate—the old toasts—the memory of the founder—the boxes of bon-bons to be carried away for the children, according to the old usage of a hundred or a hundred and fifty years ago, and of all Lord Mayors the present one has the reputation of being the most strictly Conservatfve. But he opens the New Tear with an innova- tion. The Prince of Wales has given us smoking concerts. The Lord Mayor allows his gaests to light their cigars at the Mansion House feasts. Indeed, he does even more, for the host sets the example. lam told that in Manilla there is a usage at dinner parties after each course to band round a special brand of cigar or cheroot, which is announced to the guests by the waiter. We have not come to this yet, but reform in Mansion House matters is likely to proceed by leaps and bounds. Westminster Abbey was thronged on Tuesday last for the consecration of Bishop Barry. The day was raw, the wind east, the fog heavy, the abbey itself bleak and inde- scribably dreary; but still the crowds poured in. The Bishop elect has many friends, and his connection with King's College explained the number of men who were amorist the congregation. The music was very fine. When after Canon Westcott'a sermon was concluded, Canon Barry wars conducted by a verger to the Islip :Thapel, and re- tiring to effect in investiture by the assumption of his rochst, the choir gave Gounod's beautiful anthem, " Send out Thy light." The effect was really very fine. Church and State were curiously represented and mixed together in the ceremony. In that procession of bishops, in which London, Durham, Lincoln, Rochester, and Dover were all represented, Dr. Deane, q.c., almost seemed a little out of tlittae, and when tte two senior bishops presented Dr. tarry and the Primate the reading of the Queen's Mandate sounded singularly teenier and deilUtis. The Bisbc,p-eleet took the oath, swore nbeditace to Dr. Benson and his successors in the, primacy, gai,e the right answers to the right questions, and then again follows I the verger out to that Islip Chapel, where the mysteries of investiture were secretly and fully gone through, and thenca issuing in his robes was soon after- wards solemnly consecrated.

Mr, Fawcett '8 Circular of thaolis to the post officials will be admitted to give prais3 where it is due, The " severe strain" was well borne. Next year, perhaps, practical anew may be found of relaxing it. The tihristmas con- gratulation card has come to us from Germany as a great source both of trouble and of profit to the post office. But in Germany they manage matters otherwise. Letters in tended for delivery on Christmas mmulog a•-e posted A week or ten days in advance, but are s endorsed ion the cover. The department is able to deal with them at its Nisure, making thnely arfankiknents and thus the normal correspondence of the 25th is not retarded or interfered with. The parcels post, however, is likely to' give us the benefit of another continental arrangement. A little time ago a large post office was bpened near Euston Station. I see that this week another has been dedicated to public use at the Waterloo Station. To be sure it is only intended for pircels, bat in a short time we shall find that every large station in London will have a post office under its roof. These will be for the convenience of the department, but it will cost very little more to admit the public to its share of the benefit. It is pretty obvious that the German rule should obtain with us, and that every traveller arriving at an important station should be able to write and post a letter without leaving the building.

In the world of art, the most important thing this week was the opening of the Winter Exhibition at the Grosvenor. That private view was indeed a meeting of the worla of art and the world of fashion. Reynolds' canvases had come from the family seats of members of the aristocracy, and many of the noble owners were there ho 320 how the pictur&S looked in altered lighls and changed surroundings. The rooms were very fell, but tire day was so dark that even in the forenoon the gas had to be lit. These private views at the Grosvenor hava always been curious and interesting. The fashions are illustrated hr extreme examples. The artistic element is so strongly mpresented that the picturesque is sure to prevail. One fact was vary ebvioas from last . Saturday's gathering. Aestheticism is dead and buried. The very girls who four years ago used to get up like figures of fun and gess in scraggy attitudes mull the pet poet or critic of this unhealthy little world, wandered about the rooms decently and ratker becomingly dressed, and looking quite rational and healthy. The great Oscar was not there at all. Whistler was also absent. Browning, returned from Italy, seems to have grown stouter and ruddier. Two great stage beauties met and conversed, and knew they were being stared at. Mary Anderson affects the artistic set, and is a recognised figure at every private view. Miss Fortescue lcokesl very graceful and pretty, but did not stay long. Mrs. Tadema, with a bevy of friends, was the nearest approach to the aesthetic school in her state-coloured velve's and beef- eater bat. Ellen Terry, of course, was absent, and Marion is now in the south of Franc, but the familiar Terry face was represented by Mrs. Lewis and her sister Constance. Of the collection itself it is bard to speak in too high praise. I suppose it has never been surpassed in interest. The place of honour has been assigned to the Three Graces, three grand nieces of Horace Walpole, for which it is said the paiater received MOO. At the other end of the large gallery is the lovely Georgians, Duchess of Devonshire, playing with her child, the Georgiana whom Macauley mentions in the famous passage describing the trial of Warren Hastings, the beautiful and passionate politician who issaid, in the fervour ef a general election, once to have kissed a butcher for his vote. As you pass from one of these pictures to the other the walls are hung with portraits of the greatest men and the loveliest women of that day. Here is Mrs. Nesbit, matchless in beauty and profligate in morals, sitting as Circe, surrounded with the animals she has tamed. Was it satire that made the artist choose so fitting a character

for this the loveliest and he frailest c f all his models. And here beside her is Abington, the actress —the first Lady Teazle, who tortured poor Goldsmith by refusing to play in his comedy, and whose saucy wayward- ness .drove Garrick nearly mad ; demure and mis- chievous she looks out at as in that easy ptsition which she took from the painter nearly a hundred years ago. Not one of these pictures but has its own little story. Here is the Duke of Westminster's famous portrait of Mrs. Sid- dons, who chose her own attitude, and made the painter stop the picture when she was saddled with it. Reynolds was a courtier and never opposed a lady. The actress got different treatment frem Gainiborough. "Good gracious, madam, there MOM to be no end to the length of your nose!" Here, too, is Dr. Johnson, who must have been very ugly indeed if Reynolds has idealist(' him, and Frank Barber, his black servant, whom he taught to read and write, who stood beside him at his death-bed, and was the emeontor of his will; and here, a curious pendant one to
