ANUARY 5, 1884.

another, is the little bare-legged girl carrying.her dog across the stream (this little child was a niece of Peg Wolfing- ton's)Jull of nature an tenderness, and side by side in his Vandyke costume the late Duke of Cr'oster, so well known to the gossips of that day as Silly Billy. You pause at matisr a picture where Reynolds gave a new charm to por- traiture by inventing baby worship as a theme—the young Inether fondling the little innocent child. Row did this old h ,n'ielor, near-sighted and hard of hearing, enter so truly t the sympathies of such a subject ? But Reynolds was not only g.reat but good, and his geniality—and kindli- ness no less then his feeling for beauty—and his insight into character are impressed upon us as we walk through these galleries.

The hoarding that obscures the Green Park from opposite the month of Park-lane almost up to the entrance opposite Hyde Park corner prevents us seeing what is being done be- hind it, but when the screen flees come down there will be a surprise felt at an undoubted improvement. The iron railing along Piccadilly is shabby and inadequeo. It is of the same pattern mid the same period as that which used to fence off Hyde Park from the Bayswater-road. It is now being replaced by a much more formidable barrier. The new railings are stouter, handsomer, and higher than the old. It would be very difficult for a mob to bear then, down or a burglar to scale them. The substition will nee, s- eerily be very slow and extremely costly. It is well the work should be done, and it is being done very well ; but it affords one other illustration of the preference for solid im- provements which the authorities invariably ',show in the ornamentation of London. The Duke still remains astride his imbecile charger, propped up with crutches, in the last stage of gouty decrepitude. The pouring of oil on troubled waters has, till lately, been egarded as a kind of scientific amusement. It was done in order to convert a theory into a fact, just as a hundred years ago a big diamond was burned to prove that the gem was only a peculiar form of coal or carbon. Latterly, however. an experiment has taken a commercial aspect, has thus got to have some practical importance. The authorities at Folkestone are very keen about it. There is a quite ex- cusable rivalry between them and the good People of Dover, which is certainly not allayed by the competing railway companies. Two facts seem this week to be pretty well established. The Government is resolved that we shall have no channel tunnel, and is also determined that Dover shall have one of the finest harbours of refuge in the kingdom. And so Folkestone tries what can be done with its harbour. The last experiment suggests that it can be made absolutely safe of approach in all weathers. But the final experiment has not vet come off. Two south coast watering places are waiting for a storm, Folkestone that it may make the waters calm by pouring oil on them, and Brighton that the competition between the rival lifeboats may be fairly settled. So far as we can judge in London neither place need wait long. But the South-Eastern Co. are not yet hopeless about their tunnel. The Bo en d of Trade has given its warning, but the warning will be un- heeded.

THE PRICE OF GAS AT RUNCORN. At the Knntsford Quarter Sessions this week, the petition against the Runcorn Gas Company at the instance of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company and Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele, manufacturers, Runcorn, came on for hearirg. The object of the petition was to get an investi- gation made into the affairs of the Gas Company, with a view to a reduction in the price of gas.—Mr. Marshall ap- peared fer the petitioners, and Mr. Seger and Mr. Higgine for the Gas Company.—Mr. Marshall said that at the last sitting of the court Mr. P. B. M'Quie, accountant, was ap- pointed to make a report as to the affairs of the Company. That report had now been given in, and it showed that tb - nominal capital of the Company was £40,000, of Wbitth thire had been issued 1;809 erdit3ilry share of £5 each fully paid, and ~200 ordinary shares of £5 each upon which 105, per share had been called up and paid on 81St March, 1883, making a tote! of £25,000. The expendi- ture out of capital, Mr. M`Qtaie reported, had since 1873 been in excesS of the annant subscribed, and in addition to this expenditure they bad paid since 1878 items to the amount of £613 out of revenue which should, in his opinion, hays been charged against capital. The balance at the eredit of the revenue account on 31st March, 1883, was £2,126 15s 7d, out of which the half year's dividend to the 31st March was paid, amounting to £1,280, and the balance of £846 15s 7d was placed to the credit of the reserve fund. Until 318 t March, 1883, no attempt had been made to form a reserve fund out of the surplus profits. The Company might have commenced doing so in 1860, when they had a surplus of £47 5s 74. The pro- prietors were paid the arrears due to them in respect of statutory dividends in June, 1880, but no deduction was made from the amounts paid to there in respect of income tax from 1847 (to which year the investigation went back) to 1883, and revenue account was debited with the full income tax on the profits of those yeare, amounting in the aggtegate to the sum of £1,597 15s lid. This sum, In Mr. M'Quie's judgment, &mold be recouped from the proprietors and placed to the credit of income account for 1893, otherwise they would have paid that sum in excess of their statutory dividends. The directors did not appear to have had awarded to them the maximum remuneration fixed by their Act (£IOQ per annum) until 1878, and the benefit to the consumers arising out of this amounted to £2,183. The balance of £2,126 15s 74 which appeared on the company's statement of March, 1883, should, Mr. M'Quie thought, be increased to the amount of £3,935 8s 84. Deducting the half year's divi- dend, and transferring £994 2s id to the reserve fond to make it up to the statutory amount of £4,000, the balance of £1,661 6s 74 was a surplus ay:Rattle for a reduction in the price of gas for the current year. The company (Mr. M'Quie proceeded to say) without any surplus whatever— for they had disposed of the balance of £2,126 153 7d by payment of. the half year's divieend and a transfer of the balance of £943 15s 74 to the reserve fund—reduced the price of gas 61 per 1,000 cubic feet from Ist April I Ist. To that ext-nt they had anticipated the reduction he claimed on behalf of the consumers. The available surplus shown on this statement wouli provide for a reduction of SI per 1,000 cubic feet. The addttional 24 if exacted from the Company would make the price of gas for the current year 2s 101 in place of 3s, and there would still remain a small balance of £1.60 to the credit of the revenue account. Mr. Marshall based the case for the petitioners on this report.— Mr. Seger stated as a preliminary objection that the reserve fund instituted by the Act won not yet full, and that con- sequently no reduction could he made in the price of the gas.—Mr. Marshall maintained that the money which should have gontrto the formation of the reserve fund bad been kept in hand as a floating balance.—The Chair- man pointed out that it was in the power of the directors to render this provision of the Act altogether nugatory by keeping the reserve fund within, say, .£5 of the statutory amount—Mr. Segar, on the merits of the case, argued that the balance brought out by Mr. hitQuie was made upof minus quantities, and that the money having, rightfully or wrongfully, been paid away, was not now available. hie also pointed out that one of the peti- tioners had now ceesed to take gas front the company, and Cid this would make a difference of £5OO, which would of itself swallow up the balance of £l6O shown by Mr. M'Quie. —The Chairman said it was clear that the reduction of 61 in the price of the gas was made in consequence of the action of the petitioners, although the petition was not filed till later. Mr. M'Quie in his report had 'dealt with the Company on the footing that it should have been conducted from the beginning in absolutely Cor- rect holiness style. But the Court had to deal with the actual state of things. Dividends had bean paid without deducting income tax and this involved a sun. of £1,535. That sum was included in Mr. M'Quie's balance, but the Court did not think it was now available. Many of the persons to whom it had been paid were dead. The Court did not express any opinion as to whether it had been rightly or wrongly paid to them, but it absorbed the surplus which Mr. M'Quie brought out as available for a further' reduction in the price of gas. In the circumstances he would leave the parties to pay their own costs one ground for doing so being that the Company had failed to begin a reserve fund in 1860, when they had a surplus for the first time.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The 'monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday. Dr. Steele presided, and there were present Messrs. Riley, Lake, W. Handley, Briscoe, Brookes (secre- tary), and Jones (librarian). A. letter was read from Messrs. Howarth Brothers offaring for the acceptance of the com- mittee two large pictures, to be placed in the reading-room. —The pictures were accepted on the motion of Mr. HAND• LEY, seconded by Mr. Bniscou.—The LIBRARIAN reported thatauring the month 1,440 books had been read or selected in the reference Library, and borrowed from the lending Library, classified as follows: Theology, 22; philosophy, political economy, Ice., 21; history, travels, and biography, 191; science and art, 71; poetry, 18; fiction, 995; miscellaneous, 122.—Mr. HANDLEY spoke in high terms of the reading room, which he thought was considered a great boon. He had been in the reading room nearly every night since it had been opened. Sometimes he bad found a dozen people there, and on several occasions 24 —every chair occupied. He thought it would be a good thing to open the reading room during the day time to give people an opportunity of reading books who did not get the chance to go there in the evening.—lt was decided, on the motion of Mr. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. LAKE that the reading room should he opened on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons for three months. A short conversation took place upon the objections raised to the St. John's ,Ambulance Association using the reading room and Dr. STEELE re- marked that Mr. Linaker had since told him that neither the Commissioners nor the Library Committee had the power to allow the room to be moved.—This w4s all the buisness. Tun Comma K—.—Cautinack.—Actst.

div.head: SIONER S.
div.p: SIONER S.
RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMIS-

The monthly meeting was held in the Town Hall Waterloo-road, on Wednesday. Mr. J. Meadowcroft pre! sided, and there were present—Dr. Steele, Messrs. Shaw, Williams, Dobson, Briscoe, Fisher, Pritchard, Norman, Whittaker, Lake, P. Speakman, J. W. Lightbnrn, W. Brookes (secretary), W. H. Lin aker (law clerk), and Mr. Barker (sur.
veyor.) The CHAIRMAN, on taking his seat. wished all the mem- bers "A prosperous and a happy New Year."
THE HEALTH- OF THE TOWN.

_ Dr. Mounnz (medical officer) reported that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past mouth amounted to 27, representing a death rate of 21 per 1,000 per annum. Of these deaths eight were due to diseases of the nervous system, five to abdominal complaints, five to pulmonary affections, two to cardiac affections, and two to croup, Lc tr!atina, dropsy, exhaustion, phthisis accounted for one each. Twelve deaths occurred among children five years and under.—ln reply to Dr. Steele, the SURVEYOR said the number of deaths in the corresponding month last year aq 45, 27 in the year before, and 44 in the year before that, while in 1879 there were only 15.—Mr. DoesoN thought tho mortality was rather high when they considered that there was no epidemic in the town, while Mr. NORMAN was of opinion it was a low one.—The CHAIRMAN said there was nothing out of the ordinary way in the death rate.

div.head: COMMITTEES.
div.p: THE COMMITTEES.
The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, Canal Boats and Hospital Committee, and the General Purposes Committee contained n )thing of public interest, and they were passed without clrument.

div.head: WATERLOL) HOUSE COMMITTEE.
div.p: WATERLOL) HOUSE COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended the piyinent of accounts amounting to £95 18s 41—Mr. SHAW moved, and Mr. FISHER seconded the adoption of the recommendation.-:-Dr. STEELE inquired whether the cost of maintenance had been divided between the Board, Overseers, and Library Com- mittee.—Mr. SHAW replied that the matter was in the hands of the Finance Committee, and they would shortly submit a basis to the Board.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee's minutes stated that Vie receipts for December were :—Market rents And tolls, £24 113 s 6d ; slaughter-house rents, £1 15s 61 ; canal boat fees, £1 ss; sundries. £1 its 3d; general district rate, £930 4s 4l; total, £959 14s 7d. Accounts amounting te £344 12s 5d were recommended for payment.—The minutes were passed, on the motion of Mr. FISHER, seconded by Mr. SPEAKMAN.

div.head: INSPECTION OF LODOING-HOUSES.
div.p: INSPECTION OF LODOING-HOUSES.
On the recommendation of the Parliamentary and Legal Committee, P.S. Walley was appointed an assistant inspec- tor of lodging-houses.

div.head: MOUGHLAND•LANE FOOTPATH.
div.p: THE MOUGHLAND•LANE FOOTPATH.

In accordance with the notice he had given, Dr. STEELE moved, "That inasmuch as the Board has decided to pave the footpath in Greenway-road in front of Mr. Ditchtield's untenanted houses, that in common fairness to the inhabi- tants of the houses in Moughland's-road, who are are larger ratepayers than Mr. Ditchtleld's future tenants will be, that we pave the footpath of Monghland's-road as far as Mr. Preston's house." His object in moving that reso- lution, he said, was to protest against the Board paving in front of untenanted houses that had not:paid rates. The inhabitants of Meughland-lane had paid rates for many. years, and had asked for a pave- ment, and he thought their request ought to be granted. Three new houses in had been built in Greenway-road, only one of which was let at perhaps not more than £2O a year, and in paving these when there was a good cindered footpath he thought the Board was spending money which might have been saved. He found that the cost of paving Moughland-lane would be about £220, and as there had been no estimate in the current year's expenditure, he would,e with the permission of the Chairman, withdraw his motion, reserving to himself the right of bringing it forward at some future time.-Ir. NORMAN remarked that the cost of paving Moughland-lane would not exceed £Bo.—Dr. STEELE : At any rate we have not money to do it.-54r. SHAW observed that notwithstanding the fact that the pavement hail been made in front of the three houses in Greenway-road it would have to be taken up again, because the houses had not yet beeg This only showed that things like these should Elq he done in a hurry. It would have been a great deal bettei for gas and water to be put in the houses before the pavement was put dawn and the houses tenanted.—Mr. NORMAN stated that the water pipes had been laid to the houses more than a fortnight ago.—The matter then dropped.

div.head: A.HOTIIER MOTION WITHDRAWN.
div.p: A.HOTIIER MOTION WITHDRAWN.

Mr. P. SPEMIMAN bad given notice that he would move that Waterloo-road be widened and flagged, but he having, he said, the assurance of the chairman of the Highway and Sanitary Committee that the reconstruction of wall con- tiguous to Waterloo House would be deferred for a year he would withdraw his motion The road had already been widened at the bottom by land given by Mr. Farrell, and when the matter came befor2 them again he would go into the question of the cost of t.gging. He would also like to state that the new piece of laud adjoining that belonging to the Board would be a great acquisition to the property of the Commissioners, and he suggested that in the meantime it should be negotiated for.—The motion was then witlgrawn.

THE CONSTITUTION OF THE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. Mr. SHAAV moved "that the n2solu!ion dated January 3rd, 1882, as to the appointment of the Library Committee, be and is hereby rescinded and tha following substituted, viz.: That the Library Committee shall consist of seven gentlemen appointed by the Commissioners annually.' This resolution to take efftct after the election in Sept. next." He remarked that the committee, being formed on its present lines, bad caused at diffirent times considerable difficulty. For instance : Suppose a gentleman happened to be appointed to the Library Committee, and then was elcted a member of the' Baird of Commissioners, his con- nection with the Library Committee would cease, however much benefit the Commissioners might have received from hts services. A gentleman who ceased his connection with the Board, wou7d also cease to be a member of the committee in the same way. This seemed to him a clumsy way of ,n-iking the committee. He thought the business would be more efficiently carried on if the Library Committee was elected outside the Board of Commissioners, as he thought it would be advantageous to appoint a number of ratepayers who were as deeply interested in the discharge of public business ac they were. He thought they would find that this mode would operate in this way : that the Library Committee would select men who were willing and anxious to carry en the business of the library, and who might at. times be in a position to contribute largely to it. The re- I solution would leave the Commissioners free to appoint any , gentleman they thought fit, whether a member of the Board or not. It might naturally be asked of what use it was to have fire ratepayers and six Commissioners on the com- mittee. The ratepayers might say that they could never hope to carry anything because there was always a majority against them. It was, therefore, only right at the Board should remedy the condition of things which gave rise to such a feeling —The.Cnernmast, at this point, drew Mr. Shaw's attention to a clause in the Commissioners Clauses Act which provided that seven clear days' notice of a resolution most be given to each member oi the Poard. That notice had not been given. and Mr. Shaw could not proceed with the motion.—Mr. Shaw, in consequence of this ruling, deferred the resoltition for a month. A SUGGESTIVE REPLY.

Mr. Smith, the agent of Major Orred, waited upon the Board intimating that the transfer of a plot of land in Greenway-road was about to be made to the Ecclesiastical Commissioners. If the Board wished Major Orred was pre- pared to treat with them for a piece.—The Board went into committee to consider the matter. They decided not to purchase the piece of land mentioned, but intimated that if Major Orred would kindly make them a present of a" slice" they would be happy to become owners.—The Board then rose.

THE PLAGUE SPOTS OF RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Sarah Clarkson was charged with keeping an unregistered lodging house.— Mr. W. H. Linaker prosecuted on behalf of the Improve- ment Commissioners.—Mr. Dutton, inspector of lodging bonsai, stated that about half-past two on the morning of the 16th December be visited the, defendant's house in Wilson's-row. He was accompanied by P.S. Whalley and P.C. Noden. In the front kitchen he found a man asleep, and there was also a man sleeping on the hearth in the back kitchen. On the landing upstairs there was a sailor and a prostitute asleep, and in a room off the landing there was also a sailor and a prostitute asleep. Mrs. Clarkson and a man who was not her husband, occupied another room. The house was not registered. She had applied to him for a license of registration, but as he had heard that it was a house of bad repute he told her to get some respectable per- sons to give her a character. She brought him papers from two pawnbrokers, but he bad ascertained that they only knew her as a customer.—Mr. C. Reynolds (chairman) charac- terised the case as a bad one, and defendant was fined XI and costs £1 U.—Hannah Dickenson, of Back Penketh-lane, was summoned on a similar charge. Mr. Dutton proved that there were two lodgers in the house. The defendant said she took one man in for safety. 'He bad " not a foot to stand on," he was so helplessly drunk. As the defendant had recently been fined she was fined 30a and costs £1.— John McGavin Mersey-street. was chanted with keeping an unregistered lodging-house. Mr. Dutton said up to six, months ago the defendant's house was registered, but owing to its filthy state and the brawls which were constantly oc- curring Mae Commissioners withdrew the license. The de- fendant was properly instructed. On two occasions since that time he had found lodgers in the house, and McGavin said he must either keep lodgers or go to the workhouse.— Defendant contended that his house was registered, and produced an old license. He said there was not a better character than him in Runcorn. Supt. Williamson said so far as the police were aware the defendant was a respectable man. His wife was the master and ought to be in his place. The Bench did not consider the cam so disgraceful as the others, and fined the defendant 10a and costs lie ed —Tames Jannion, who conducted himself in a very rough manner, was convicted of keeping an, mareg 1 terad lodging- house in Back Conner-street, and he was fined Al andcosts £1 2s, or in default a month's hard labour.
A woman named Elizabeth Ryder was on Tuesday sen- tenced by the Bradford magistrates to a mOntk's imprison- ment for fortune-tellin2.. The prisoner had a very extensive " practice."

ANNUAL TEA MEETING AT THE WIDNES BAPTIST CHAPEL. On the evening of New Year's Day the annual !ea meet- ing of the Wines Baptists was held in their chapel, Nelson- street. There was an entertainment after tea, when speeches were made by the chairman (Mr. Carey) and the pastor (Mr. Yeatman), in which the progress of the chapel during the last year was comaeered. After an appropriate hymn bad been sung by tee congregation, and a prayer offered by the 19aKor, . Mr. CLEZY addressed the meeting as follows :—My dear friends, I suppose that although you have a very tempting programme you expect me to say a word or two. I seem to be a kind of standing dish, for every time you IreVe a meet- ing lam asked to come. But I did hope that on this pre- sent occasion Mr. Davies_ would have been here in my place —Mr. Davies whom you all know so well by his liberality to this church. It is not from want of desire but want of ability that Mr Davies is not here. I really thought until this morning Unit Mr. Davies was canting, and I was rather surprised to r eceive a note from Mr. Yatereen setting I was to take the cheir this evening. It is always a formidable thing for nee to say anything to a large audience, but I have very greas pleasure in congratulating you on your progress during the last year. Through the four or Eve months past you hive bad a pastor, and you can congratulate yourselves on the possession. He has worked hard, and in a financial point of view I can see renewed activity from all parts of the place you have began well by meeting together on the first even- ing of the new year. We do not know what is in store for us this year. We have gone through a few hardships and poverty in this neighbourhood, but things are looking brighter than they were, and with renewed prosperity in the district we can hens for prosperity in the religions district. And Ido really think that we will have better times than we have had Or a few years. Some prophesy that 1885 will be a disastrous year. Well, let it; but let us make hay while the sun shines, and by doing what we can in the year 1884. ( Hear, hear.) I werild not say mote, but I have a painful t leng to say. We have not had a meeting here be- fore of this kind without my mother being here She would like to have coine very much, but in her present state of health thie public meeting would have excited her so much that it would have done her more halm than good, but she has giscn me a meeen-ase of cengratuletien and best wishes for you, one of Christian love and earnest desire, that the next year may be a prosperous one. An anthem was then given by the choir, " Lord of all power and might," after which Mr. Getter again rose and said: I, as treasurer, ought to fmention to you the state of the finance. Music, and paunch!, shillings, and pence don't go very well together, but yet there is nothing like the music of a good balance, and if there had not been a balance on hand I would not have cared to bring the subject forward. We began this year with a balance of £3 15s 3d, and we cud the year, after paying all the expenses which min be fairly cen- sidered to date, with a balance of about £9. Perhaps I ought to say that our chapel-keeper's salary has not been paid for the last quarter, our has our pastor's for the last raenth. But yet, after these have been paid, we shall have a small balance in hand. There is another ca- couraging feature about the finance. I find that the first hilf of the year you collected from all sources £2l. Mr. Yateman came here in September, and now during the second half of the year you' have collected about B,44—more than double the first half; and if things go on as they are we shall be able to take courage for the future. Mr. YATENAN then addressed the meeting as follows: Dear Mr. Chairman, I am glad to see you back with us again :this evening. lam sorry Mrs. Carey is not able to be here, but for myself and on behalf of the friends present I thank her for her kind congratulations, anti wish you to kindly convey to her our sympathy, for we miss her much from our meetings, and we do not forget that she earnestly did good amongst us for the prosperity of the cause. In addres- sing you this evening, dear friends, the first thing I should do is to wish you a very happy new year; that I do with all my heart. I wish e -you one and all as individuals, and as a congregation, and as a church, all of you I wish a very happy New Year. The expresaion is on everyone's lips; and it may mean very much or very little, sincere or 'brisincere. lam sure you will believe I wish it in all sin- cerity. I want briefly to speak about the past, for in regard to it we have some cause for gratitude. And speaking first of the time when you were without a pastor, I congratulate you on your having so well kept together. Many churches under eirnilar circumstances would have been scattered. I am glad such was not your case. And now to deal more especially with the four months I have been here. Looking back we have very much cause for gratitude, I think. We may take, for instance, the improvement in the Sunday school. lain glad to be able to report great progress. Our worthy secretary, Mr. Streets, informs me that it is in a very satisfactory and healthy condition. There have been added 19 names to the roll in four months, which is a con- siderable increase considering the state the school was in before. This improvement is due to the efforts of °erste- loved friend the superintendent, Mr. Moore, ably seconded by the teachers. The congregation itself has increased;and ' I am glad to say that the Word has reet been preached in vain. Some have been brought under conviction of sin and been enabled to leave that burden at the feet of the Saviour. We can look back to some little success in that particular matter. I want ,to congratulate you on the progress in the Epnial work you have taken up—the temperance cause. Since our formation in October we have obtained about 70 members. The sum realized by the bazaar, though not as large as expected, yet has increased the sum for the new chapel. The congrega- tion, though not to large as we could wish, is still increas- ing. I have not done with the past, yet you would like me to be sincere with you, and not to put forward the good points and keep back the faulty ones. And though Ido not want to be unpleasant, yet I have to call attention to .ene thing, and that is the thinness at times of our services. The Tuesday evening services are not so well attended I want you to understand these services are very im- portant. We at thiw time gather to pray for each ether, and ter the work here. Seek to impart that greatness to the prayer meeting that you eh mid, and thus encourage your pastor by attending them. I must also call your attention to the Sunday morning service, Very few members atteud this service, and I would wiah you te take it to heart, as to Inc it is very grieving, as I arrange my sermon on Sunday mornings specially for Christians. It seems to me that you are placing a slight upon your brethren in Christ and pastor, and above all on God. Perhaps the shoe pincsSe here.' If so it is because you have a corn. So don!t, blame the butte, blame the corn. And now about the future. Some think the new chapel to be the first thing on the programme, but we have something to do to get this. The reasons are forcible for a new ' chapel, because the present chapel is dilapidated and in a poor locality. Some of our friends wile are outsiders say we 'nest first fill this chapel and then go to them. And 1 advise you to do your best to do this. If we work earnestly, faithfully, and well we shall have the chapel, and I have said unless you do this I would not take the matter up, for I have seen business like this before, and I know a lot of the worry will fall on ins. Throw away all whims and fan- cies that would retard the work and be like soldiers "ho take a pride in their regiment, in their Colette!, an'l, in their victories. If we band together like that tee Wil aceemplish it. Let us go hand in hand, hesert to heart, shoulder to shoulder to the work given us to do, and then we shalt have much to thank God for. Le' us be true to Him for His Name's sake and all times fox His goedness. ,6 Mr. CaltEv again rose P,dd said: I forgot to tell you what you will be glad to her. Mr. Gossage, our mutual friend. gene us £5 toward,, our current expenses. You knew We liberality and know how he puts his hand in his pocket. V 'ester was brought before him, without a word, and at onale, be gave me the £5. When mnd The songs, dtc., which were listened with pleasure, were given as follows :—Treble solo, Miss Sadler, 'Thy voice Is near ;" eolo, Miss Travis, " Twickenham ferry ;" solo, Miss Daintith, "Three old maids of Leigh," deservedly en- cored. and followed with " Little sister's gone to sleep ;" chorus, choir, "Behold, I bring you glad tidings :" tass solo, Mr. Jones, "Thirty years ago ;" treble solo. Miss Pairs- tithe" Silvery Rhine ;" duet, Miss Sadler and Miss Travis, " Minute gun at sea ;" tenor solo, Mr. Priestnall, " I'm thinking, John ;" chorus, chair, " Rear my grayer." Usual votes of thanks then followed. Doxology closed the pro- ceedings. . ....

BATITEDAT.—Before Aldermen Chandley and Burgess. . AN OLD OFFENDER —Joseph Corcoran, aged 24, of Stoney- yard. who is well known to the Bench, having been 17 times previously convicted, was charged on a warrant witis assault- ing Edward Bailey, on the 18th ult. According to the evidence of complainant and P.O. Williams. the former was proceeding cmletly along Buttermarket-stre'S, when prisoner hit him a violent blow on the side of the head .—Corcoran was bound over to keep the peace, at,d in default of finding sureties was ordered tote imprisoned for a month. div.head: INTERESTING ELECTORAL STATISTICS.
div.p: INTERESTING ELECTORAL STATISTICS.

A Parliamentary paper issued on Wednesday shows that the largest county division in England in point of area is the North Riding of Yorkshire, with 2,128 square' miles. The largest in respect of population is South-east Lancashire' with 534,435; the South-West Riding following with 497,333, and South-West Lancashire with 482,436. In num- ber of eltctors Middlesex is first, with 38,373; South-West Lancashire next, with 28.948; and South-East Lancashire& with 28,138. In Wales, the largest county in area is Car- marthen, with 935 square miles ; the largest in population is Glamorgan, with 235,920 inhabitants; and the largest in electorate Cllainorgan also, with 13,222 voters. The return as to out-voters is specially interesting. From this it appears that the largest number in England are in the county of Middlesex, and in Scotland North Lanark. As to lodger voters, the greatest number in any English borough is in Westminster, where there are nearly 4,000, while there are less than 700 in Manchester, Liverpool, Birmingham and Leeds combined. The most prominent English boroughs containing freemen and the possessors -of ancient electoral rights are the City of Lon- don, Coventry. York, Newcastle-upon-Tyne, and Norwich, The largest Parliamentary borough in England and Wales, it appears, is Cricklade, in Wiltshire which has an area of 248 square miles; but in point of population Liverpool is the largest, its inhabitants numbering 552,508, and its elec- tors 83,463. Glasgow, however, though its population is only 487,986—that is, 64,523 fewer than Liverpool—has 83,718 voters, or 280 more than Liverpool. The following are the local statistics:—

CHAPTER LXI.—A. DIMDFUL DAY. The fifth day after the Court Martial (no further com- munication from Major Etheredge having reached the prisoner) an early parade of Strphen's regiment was ordered, every man to be present. Of course the meaning of this quickly spread through the camp, and only did not reach the prisoner, through the kindness of those about him. The sentence of the Court Martial on Stephen was then to be read aloud. And the nature of the punishment was made but too plain by the proceedings of the Dram Major; who, as head of the drummers, had ordered "flogging exercsBe," which consists in the skilful practice of flogging bags filled with straw, with the cat o' nine tails. On the parade being formed up in due order, the com- manding officer, the Colonel, directed the prisoner, Stephen Shand, to be brought forth from the guard-room, to which he had been previously taken; and where he began to understand he was at the beginning of the end—whatever that end might be. Bracing his nerves as he best could for the impending publieity—wondering the while whether the Major might not have yet in part succeeded in his mission, but had neces- sarily acted through tilt authorities of the regiment,—with that one sole faint ray of possible light in his horizon,Stephen was marched to the Parade. _ _
And this was the spectacle that met his eyes : Soldiers— his own comrades—fermed three sides of a square, in the centre of which was planted the triangle no doubt for him to be tied to. .

Did be at that awful moment look round on the weapons held so near, and dream of the possibility of a sudden rush upon one of them, and so end defiantly a life that conld be no longer worth saving ? Or was he restrained by the thought that even yet the display of intended punishment might not necessarily in- volve its infliction? Or was he altogether too confused by the publicity, by the hopefulness of any effective action on his part at so late an hour, and by a last thought he tried to realise and take com- fort in, that the infamy was not his, but belonged to the punishment, and to the punishers, and therefore he could go through it manfully ? Ms thoughts, whatever they might be, were stopped by the Colonel's loud voice calling the regiment to "Attention !" The Adiutant then read out a formal document stating the prisoner's crime, and the finding of the court-martial that he was "guilty." The court therefore sentenced No. 1462, Corporal Stephen Shand, to be reduced to the rank and pay of a private; to eceive fifty lashes; and further, to be imprisoned with hard rabour for a period of 365 days. The severity of the sentence seemed to Stephen an answer to his own impromptu and ill-judged speech to the Court. Immediately the Sergeant Major ordered Stephen to strip, which he did by taking off his shirt, fastening his trousers about his waist, and advancing hi the triangle, where the Dram-Major began to bind him with straps. At this moment the Sergeant-Major noticed some confused talking going on near him, and angrily called for "Silence!" But he was himself a few seconds later called away by the Adjutant, who seemed greatly disturbed; and presently both went to the Colonel who was impatiently waiting to know what all this absurd behaviour meant. Carefully keeping the matter to themselves, it then tran- spired that a mistake of an extraordinary nature had been made. Is it possible to imagine the emotions of Stephen as he became partially aware that something was going on that might or might not relate to himself, but that, if not relat- ing to him, could hardly have been permitted at such a time and place? For at the very moment of the two joining the Colonel, to Impart what must plainly be disagreeable news, Stephen was immoveably strapped to the triangle; the drummers, cat in hand, were waiting the signal to begin; while the Doctor stood by, holding his watch, to observe the pri- soner's state as the punishment went on. . . . .
_ Will Stephen ever forget the break in that terriktle silence -:-,when the Colonel was heard to order him to be un- strapped, and marched back to the guard room for the pre- sent.

StKange, and yet simple enough, was the forthcoming explanadon. The crime was said in all the proceedings to have been committed on a certain day of January in the year 1866. Within the last few minutes through this public reading on the parade, a sharp listener had discovered there must be a mistake, for he knew well the prisoner had not then -entered the regiment 6,and that, in fact, the offence was committed a year late the one in which they now were.

He could not help imparting his discovery to a corporal, who told it to a sergeant, and so it reached the Sergeant- Major: When the culprit was found, it proved to be the Orderly- Room Clerk, who had been so incessantly engaged writing daily on the dozens of papers for the last twelve months, the year 1866, that when he came to 1867 he forgot what he was about, and wrote 1866 onco more. How was it the month—January--did not warn him? be was asked. And to that he answered, be had been prepar- ing matters for the Horse Guards that had dealt continually

with the dates of January, and 1866.* But the day was to be characterised by another surprise. It really seemed as if Fortune, which had borne so hardly, so mercilessly on Stephen hitherto, had suddenly made up her mind to a great change; and not content with one stroke to relieve our hero, followed it by another, which if not more impressive than the first, for that was impossible, was certainly calculated to be more permanently agreeable to rest on. A telegram reached the Colonel only a few hours later than the Parade, to say the prisoner was pardoned ; and that all necessary documents and explanations were in the hands of Major Etheredge, who was on his way to the camp. Next day he arrived, and placed in the Colonel's hands a pardon, obtained from the Queen by the Countess; who, having received from the Major all the particulars. moved Lord Harlaxton to demand an audience, went with him into the royal presence, and so moved the Queen by her nar- rative of Stephen's story, and the corroborative evidence of Major Etheredge (who waited near) that her fondest wish waa gratified. In this narrative the Countess did not—could not—under the circumstances, deal with the secret in which Stephen was so deeply concerned, though at times the temp- tation to tell all seemed irresistible. The document from the Horse Guards thus moved into action proved to be very unpleasant reading for the Colonel and the other members of the court martial. In effect it said "Recognising the esire of the members of the Court-mar- tial to support unflinchingly the idea of discipline ; approv- ing their sentence of guilty, and of a consequent punish- ment ; what the authorities fail to understand is how the court, while seeing the enormity of the act committed by the prisoner, could have ignored in the sentence the very great servivs rendered by the prisoner while only a corporal; and which is clearly proved by Major Etheredge'e original report to the .Colonel then in command, and by his testi- molly before the Court-mnrtial to which full credence most be given. Still, under the circumstances, it is not advisable to disturb the sentence. Therefore her gracious Majesty has granted Stephen Shand a free pardon, with leave to quit the service if he pleases." Thus was Stephen ISardoned, and set free to return to his home. All which h Stephen had the delight to have explained to him by the Major himself. Though the Major was not a little taken aback fo learn from Stephen he bad not actually been saved trod the Tri- angle by the Queen's goodness, but by that unlucky Orderly Clerk; who he feared would suffer for his iffstake, but who should be cared for if he needed help. That night was spent together in one of the best hotels is Dublin, where Stephen regained his portmanteau, with its treasury of letters. Early next morning the friends separated; the Major to join :his new regiment in a distant part of Ireland; Stephen to‘harry home, wondering all the way if indeed his mother's urgent message as delivered by Miss Vandeleur in the camp,really rotated to future possibilities in connection with that-yoUng lady. All past troubles forgotten, this new hope-began to rise like a bow of promise in Stephen's horizon, rich indeed in colour, and in all kinds of imaginative glory.
CUAPTER LXII.—THE CoßlNTass's.auzzir FLOWER - GAR-DEN.

The course of a novelist's story may be likened in one of its aspects to that of a river; which, beginning from a very small origin, swells by degrees, passes through all sorts of troublous, rocky, and stormy channels, then widens out, and so changes, to the great relief of the navigators, that whereas their business is to proceed, they cannot but yearn to linger, amid the genial serenity of the landscape around them; which in contrast with what they have passed through may appear invested with a beauty by no means due to its intrinsic character. - . .

The scenes the reader had passed through in connection with Stephen's military life may, we hope, similarly incline him or her to pause for a brief space, to wander mentally with us in the "Countess's garden," beforeSgain the tumult and battle of life must be resumed.

__..__ ---------. The tim i e s a few weeks later than that of Stephen's arrest; the place the Earl's Marine Vilta, on the Coast of Devon, not far from its junction with Cornwall. No mansion could have been placed in a more enjoyable Position as regards sea and land. Overlooking, from a bold promontory, the one; its grounds and gardens behind melt into most pictureeene scenery belonging to thoother. Nor is that all. One of those lovely and romantic rivers, in which Devon is so rich, flows by the base of the wall of the house, ottt into the sea. Bat it is not for the beauty of the site, or of the edifice, erected in such fine harmony with

* This incident of the story is based upon an actual fact. A. high authority in such matters, loy original informant, now tells ins that not only did a man sentenced by court-martial. jome 20 years since, escape through a flaw of this kind [though be wuuld not do so now], but that cases were not infrequent of men escaping punishment through technical errors in the ere- eedure; in f,,ct., he adds, this was almost the only chance of Fr) inexorable wore the authorities in the due inn'ction , of the sentences even.

all the surrounding, that the place is so distinguishei among gie.,diielltszs of the magnates of the neighbourhood. eitherrisitt for the artistic wealth within the walls, thongh that is considerable for its high original quality if net for its extent,: that persons are drawn here from distant parts,/ and beg for admittance. Notwithstanding the splendour of the multitudinous beds on the lawn, the attractions of the orchid houses, and' the , wealth of tropical life and blossom in the conservatory, it is the fame of Lady Harlaxton's lower border, that has eclipsed all the rest, and has spread so far and wide. The visitors, if coming specially- to see the pictures, or the glass houses, are sure to pass more quickly than usual through them, in order to reach the new border of hardy plants. Many of these persons arrive in no spirit of sym- pathy or admiration, but rather to criticise the whole scheme as an absurdity. It is only another of the new ideas that spring up from time to time merely through our weariness of the old ones, however precious, and all sufficing for sen- sible people these old ones are. They have all along culti- vated hardy fir wers, so has everybody else, and what have they made of them? Why, a muddle, consisting of a great deal of weedy foliage, with a very small amount of flower? At odd times, with a few lucky plants, there may be a fair show of bloom, but leaving the ground for the most part a dreary mass of hap-hazard forms, and unlucky combinations of colour. .

And then they will tarn to the rich glow, and mathe- matically precise forms of Use flower beds, and ask how any sensible person could even bring the two inro any possible comparison? The Countess thought differently, when first she began to think at all of the matter; knowing as she did how rich our own country was in native plants of beauty, while their number and quality were so marvellously increased by con- tributions from every quarter of the world, not absolutely tropical. She owned that no effect had been yet produced worthy of them, so far as she had seen; but she had, nevertheless, strong faith that the very finest effects possible in garden- ing would be obtained frosn them in the open air, when they were cultivated with the attention always bestowed on tender and rarer p'ants ; when they were arranged with lov- ing hand in an orderly manner, each one to the most suit- able horns that could be found for it; and so their whole capacities for giving us enjoyment be brought out, by see- ing them in full prosperity to begin with. The border, entered through an arched gateway, is shut off front the rest of the garden by walls, covered with the finest hardy creepers, evergreen, and deciduous in alternate succession. A wide and long stretch of grassy lawn fills the whole middle space; bearing here and there low flowering shrubs or trees, chosen for their beauty or picturesque grace, as well as for their blossoming qualities. On each side of the lawn runs a gravel walk, and then the border, some ten feet wide. Then another gravel walk, and so to the second, and narrower border for the wall trees, which form the background. The first thing one notices on entering is the harmonious effect of the border. There is not only definite and beauti- ful form visible throughout it taken as a whole; but as we advance we find that the general form is composed of con- stantly varying minor forms, that delight and engross the eye. But even while we realise this first effect, and wonder how it has been obtained, a +wend grows upon us; namely, the espial but by no means formal distribution over the whole border of the plants in dower; which speedily leads to the further discovery that the flowers are connected and con- trasted in lovely seqeences of colour. A pink or scarlet mass of bloom is followed by 0110 of white or cream colour; then a lilac, violet or blue, if succeeded by primrose, yellow o. orange. That reached, the series begins again, but nver with the same plants, and consequently never with the same precise hues of colour. But even these contrasts are modified wherever they would otherwise be harsh, by some intermediate tint or shade that brings the whole into softness and harmony. "All this for the present season Only? " the visitor may well ask, seeing borders from end to end so rich in blossom. , And then he finds that let the visit be paid at any other period of the year (some four months of the winter only I excepted) the same kind of effect will ba found; while a great part of the means, the particular plants, may, and at certain seasons must, be entirely different. "What then," he perhaps asks in wonder, "are the plants in pots, and brought from other places of reserve, as they come into flower?"

"Nothing of the kind. Consider the growth, health, and perfection of all you see, and the very possibility of pot growth becomes out of the question." "It is a great puzzle!" But one worthy of explanation. When the Countess be- gan her experiment, for she was too modest to call it any more, she took her head gardener into hes counsel, and said to him—

-17ify ideas are very general—very vague—wanting to attain to certain results, but as yet only seeing dimly how they are to be obtained, if at all. Let me Indicate how far I have gone:— "Suppose, then, we culled the very finest, hardy, flower- ing shrubs and perennials at present to be found in this country ; that we divide them into evergreens and deci- dams, for many dwarf, herbaceous plants ke,p their leaves in winter; "That we obtain accurate memorandt for every shrub, and every perennitl, of the time, colour, and duration of its flower; also of its height, and character of growth, and colour of leaf, if at all remarkable; "Then, how shall we so use them, that from spring to autumn there may be a constant and equul floral procession passing before our eyes, without a single gap, and yet with constant change 2" "It's a knotty problem, your ladyship," said the head gardener with a smile; "but you have so thoroughly shown what to do, and the means of doing it, that I don't think it can be Very bard to find the way to do it !" "I am glad to hear you say so Of course lam aware it -would be, or at least might be, an endless task, if every yard or two of ground had to be the subject of deliberation, involving all the aims I have dwelt on!" "Quite so. We must build on the mechanical. Start with a routine, and improve afterwards in what we may call the graces." "That is exactly what I seem to want. Find me a rough, and as you say, mgchanical plan that may dispose of all the means at our disposal to some such end as I have sketched Out; and you will please me, and perhaps make yourself famous. For to say nothing of what persons in my own position might do if so started, there is not a villa or cottage garden in the three kingdoms that might not, under such guidance, become a Beene of beauty and delight, how- ever limited in its scale; and so be a powerful influence in making people care to spend more of their time, money, and thought on one of the sweetest, most useful, and most re- fining of all earthly pleasures." Week after week passed without any report of-progress, and the Countess, who did not like to appear impatient, and therefore asked no questions of the bead gardener, wondered Iwhether he was failing altogether, and therefore remained silent, and as she fancied .uncomfortable, when they did meet. But at last he came to meet her, his face beaming with the light of his thoughts, and he lost not a moment in say- ing— " I hope your ladyship will forgive my being so late in bringing you news of the success or failure of my efforts to work out your design • but in truth I coulcrnot please my- self at all, till I bethought me of an aged neighbour of mine who has a small but beautiful garden. A poet he calls himself, but he has not been lucky enough to get the 'world to call him so too. In disgust he came here, lives upon a trifling sum, and earns it chiefly by his garden. "Well, I went te him, told him all you had said, and he went to work at onee. I shrewdly suspect as much for his own sake as for mine, or for your ladyship; for he listened with great interest, and. when I had done said,' Come to me this day week, and I'll provide you!" "And he has kept his word, at lease I think so.' It would take too much time to describe his plan in the full detail he has given it, bit by bit to me; and besides, T fancy he means to work it thoroughly. out On paper, and send it to some garden publication, But thefts are the heads— (l) Arrangement with regard to permanent and picture - equal effect; (2) with regard to the seasons and their successions; aid (3) with regard to the seccessien and harmonious con- trast or combination of the towers. Any permanently picturesque effect with perennials alone is imposeible, even if winter be left out of the question, for they are-always changing; now lost in the earth, now grow- ing to their full beauty, then decaying, and at last once mere disappearing." "And how does your poet meet that difficulty ?" "By planting shrub ,and perennial alternately ; choosing only low growing and for the most part slender habited shrubs ;but distinguished for gracefulness or picturesqueness of forma and beauty as well as duration of flower.' "Can they be found in sufficient number ?" "Undoubtedly I" "An excellent beginning! Of course the shrubs would have no dead level, but vary constantly in height." "Certainly. The planting," he says, "may be from both the aides to the COMMOR centre in the middle, as otherwise the general effect would be from one side only: Toe front row, of dwarfs, must be exclusively evergreens; from the firstlings of spring to the full tide of summer,or the declin- ing but rich flowers and foliage of autumn. Between every twa such plants of the front row would appear one of the second row; and so on through all the rows, however nu- merous; though I de not propose more than fire (two on each side of the tall central one), for easiness of access and culture, and for being throughout near to the eye. Lastly, " the shrubs in the second row should be all deciduous, those tin the third, the central row, all evergreen; so that, seen bora the frost, a deciduous shrub would always appear be- tween two evergreens in front of it; and each ever- green beyond would appear between two of its deciduous brethren." . "I see! All the space well filled, and at intervals the shrubs giving consistency and a permanent character to the whole." "It is very good," said the gardener. "But now I reach what was my difficulty, how to zombine the succession of the seasons, and the successior of the flowers as regards colours, into one harmonious whole under a mechanical plan, that any person could understand and work." "But your friend, the poet, I see, already has got you out of that difficulty also, which was mine, when I tried to put things in shape by the aid of my pen, pencil, and water- colours.' i " After many trials, on as many plans, each upsetting

div.head: AtE
div.p: AtE

long rows of the border worked out com i pletely n no ...a- lance 17,4. it, and At for no other plan, we found the natural lorder the best,—Spring, Summer, and Autumn, then *Spring again. To these we eventually attached a starting point. All varieties of red lowers for Spring, white flowers for Summer, and blue flowers for Autumn. Of course your ladyship will anticipate that as there are only three seasons and four colours to deal with, they all change their alliances when the floral year ends, and Spring returns, to which the fixed succession of Red, White, Blue, and Yellow attaches tho last-named colour.

"Se that anyone possessing this very simple key knows I that if they have planted in a row a red fhwer for spring, the next mast be a white flower for summer, and se en till the entire set of changes is worked out at the twelfth plant." "When you have nothing left but to repeat yourself?" said the Countess.
"Not exactly. We must repeat the materials; but there is a fresh and happy change, the thirteenth plant is always a winter one."

"Ab, I am glad you do not propose to leave winter out, with nothing but its own icy cold to comfort it?" "We provide (but just as if we couldn't help ourselves) a very decant winter garden. That thirteenth plant is to be always either an evergreen shrub—berry beating—or of variegated foliage; or a flowering deciduous shrub, such as that most precious plants, the naked flowered jasmine. Then, too we have plants like the Christmas rose, that never fails us. if we only take the trouble to put a hand- .

light, or even a pane of ilium on bricks over it, simply to protect the flowers when blossoming." "But what was the change you spoke of by that wonder- working thirteenth plant?" asked the Countess. "Simply this. It breaks the succession et the flower colours by taking one to itself, either in fact or in theory. So the spring, following that winter plant, now comes forth in modest and virgin beauty of snowy white, instead of beginning as before with a red flower." "Another objection occurs to me," said the Countess. "There must be gaps between, interrupting the local dis- play • you can't have the spring group, the summer group, and the autumn group all blossoming at once." "That is true, my lady. But the plants of one season do, if well shosen for their lengthened period of blossoming, melt into the next; and the succession of colours is arranged primarily for that very connection. A spring red flower is immediately followed by a summer white one; and when spring comes again, by a yellow; thus giving a contrast in both cases. "But the thing chiefly to be relied on is to fill up space that might be otherwise vacant of bloom, with bulbs, and . . . . _
annuals, of differing heights, for the different lins. These can be so planted as to supply all possible deficiencies, and without serious interference with the legithuite occupants of the soil."

"A most happy arrangement altogether. I like it ex- tremely. And this susm up the method for future work in the border ?" "My friend, the poet, is one of those men who, when they have got hold of a good idea, are almost sure to show their pleasure by immediately leaving it behind, in the search for what they believe something more precious still. So was it now. "Whilst I was enthusiastic about what he had achieved, he was enthusiastic about what he had not only not achieved, but not even condescended to explain; be- yond the rather alarming announcement that he had something in his brain which would quite displace the other !"

" Really," said the Countess, smiling. "It came out at last—as an alternative only, or an ap- pendage—a valuable one for those who have the artistic eye and instinct to do it justice. "It was to make a border of plants, shrubs, and peren- nials arranged as before, not singly, but planted in threes, in a triangle, each three combining three colours of one and the same season, perhaps varieties of the same nlant, a white or a yellow, between two blues or reds, for instance, or the reverse. This again might change, so that three, of one predominant colour only, and one season might be cm trasted with the next three in the row, also of one colour, of the succeeding season; and also contrasted, and still more effectively because for a longer period, when the :same sea- son recurred farther on." "It would be magnificent if the colours were finely cho- sen." _

"And that, my paet friend was sure, no lady in tbe land could do so well e.g the countess of liarlaxton." And now the border exists, and grows yearly in beauty: as faults are removed, or new charms suggested by the very success of all that is already done. (To be continued.)

div.head: NEW YEAR FESTIYITIES. WARRINGTON.
div.p: NEW YEAR FESTIYITIES. WARRINGTON.

The advent of the new year was marked in Warrington I by the usual merry peals from the church bells, by the holding of watch night services at several places of worship in the town, end a hearty exelange of compliments between friends. The day was not generally observed a holiday but ' several meetings of a social character were held, and we also noticed that many of the shops and offices were closed. The weather was much more seasonable than last week and there was a slight fall of snow in the evening. Many took advantage of a brisk walk, whilst a large number visited Manchester and Liverpool for the purpose of witnessing the pantomimes, which, as in former years, are being prc.- duce 3 on a scale of much grandeur,
Ntutir SERVICE AT BOLD•STREET
WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

The Rev. J. Eglitlton preached to a large. congregation in the Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, Warrington, on the morn. jog of Christmas Day, taking as his text the 2nd Chapter of Luke, and the 11th verse. A. collection was made at the close for the benefit of the poor, and realized £9.—There was a large congregation at the watch-night service on New Year's Eve, when theeltev. J. McTurk, who conducted the first part of the service, preaehed an excellent sermon from the words of the Bth and 11th verses of the 3rd Philippians --;" Yea doubtless, and I count all things but lost for the excellency of the know- ledge of Christ Jestre, my Lord." The preacher said: The hand of Time is upon us to-night. We hear his rapid breathing; we feel the beating of his great heart: The dying year solemnises us all. We tread carefully and fear- fully the narrow platform of the sacred moments, right under the full undimned blaze of the piercing eye of Goi, and each irretrievable step brings us consciously nearer te the dread realities of the eternity awaiting us. Wild with an awful tempest mutt he be *leo is not sobered by the weird music of the midnight hour! Doll and untutored most be the ear that does not recognise in it an articulate ''God-message. Looking behind us we cower before our life- history—so often is the record against us, so blurred and blotted is it by failure and sin; looking before us we cower in the presence of the mysterious unknown—the unveiled hours of joy or sorrow, of shame or honour. The past and future alike afflict us. We tremble as the one retreats and as we set our feet on the threshold of the other. Now with the responsibilities-of life upon us, with a crushing sense our own feebleness and ignorance, anl with an unwonted glimpse into the meanings and possibilities of our fleeting days, we need, and ,we feel our need more vividly than ever, to put our poor trembling hand into the hand of one of the, world's strongest that we may be guided and held up. We cry in our help- lessness, "Lead me to the stout-hearted that I too may be brave; bring nse to the feet of the wisest that I may be his disciple; I am lost unless a saviour speedily appear." On reading this noble and in- spiring atteratee of St. Paul's we instinctively fleet that he possesses what we want. He may inspire us to obtain the strength we lack. His intense earnestness wins upon and fascinates us. Amid the passing sceneeof earth he has living truth th-at is to him exceeding precious and abiding. His feet are upon the rock; he is ant tossed by the seething and deetructive waves. The deepest cravings of his great soul are satisfied Worlds may fade, but his strength and joy alike remain. The excellency of the know- ledge of Christ Jesus is his all. That is the secret of his joy, and confidence, and devotion. Bat ;a it possible for this to be repeated, and by, us? "A chasm in which are sunk eighteen centuries septrates In..' That is true, but ' nothing essential is altered. The revelation of God's grace in Christ and the nature of man remain the same, even as sun and stars have abode in stately majesty. "The conditions of life have changed." That, too, is true. Paul's difficulties arose mairdy from the fact that Christianity even in its meet elementary form was a novelty. Judaic, Ritualistic, Greek and Roman philosophers, the idolatrous cities of Asia, and the devotees of pleasure united in opposing and hating it. Our difficul- ties often arise from the novelty of such mature devotion as St. Paul's. The philosonhiee, pleasures, and hindrances of Our day have nothing peculiar to themselves. The more intelligently we consider the conditions under which we Rye, the more deeply shall we lee convinced that we may reach a Christian manhood equal to the Apostles. He sur- rounded himself by the greatest of all truths-all that Christ was and is, all that He taught and imparted—and in that temple he lived and worshipped. So he became i rea- sonable enthusiast. The same temple we may enter. A like enthusiasm may be ours. The excellency of the know- ledge of Christ may solve our difficulties, it us for duty and make our life noble. With Paul see may know the in- comparable value of experimental Christianity, the joy and freedom, and stalwart strength of being new creatures in Christ. With him, for that "excellent knowledge," we may fling aside heartily habitually every, hindrance. With him we may only be content when successive disclosnresof the perfection of Christ are made to us; when we feel the impulses of vital union with the living Savicur, when we enter in the work of His kingdom, and for his sake into the fellowship of His sufferings. With Paul Vfe may per- petually aspire to the vast reward; we may holiefully, aye joyously, face the future, believing that through the happy toil and cross.bearing of those probationary years and triumph ever death, we may ultimately attain to the resur- rection nano life.-The Rev. J. Regimen, who at the conclusion of Mr. M'Turk's sermon addressed the congregation, said he should be very glad if he could carry them on with similar stirring remarks to which they had just listened. He should not, however, have many worth to say to them. We are, he continued, met together on the retreating edge of the old year and about to step on the margin of the new. The old year, laden with mercy and blessing, it may be with disobedience and sin, is gone, or nearly so. The new, with offers of grace and opportunities of good Is before, awaiting our high and -noble purposes and aspirations and our determined efforts to Serve and please Geri. So to us belong the pleasures of hope and the advantagee of reflection, and so while the days of our pilgrlinage are cheered with the pros.

pects of the fature,itindquirSd of us that we be instructed by the -lessons' of - the past. InstreCted by our own past we should also be improved by the past of others, especially the records of this book. The currents of the times in which we live, and which is eier bearing us on uninfluenced by Us, May frequently itnd variously affect no, especially in the removal or other. SVi9B of the mighty men who change the state of nations and ffect the well-being of multitudes. In this land and its ependencies we have bad many changes and losses since a last met—men in high plan s—members of both Houses of Parliament—lords and commoners—have been removed, men of letters and of law, of the army and civilians of high degrees; distinguished men of the Church in its various sections, and whose influence in life and perhaps in death we can neither grasp nor trace. It is too mighty in its range, too extensive in its sweep, but we know who bath said" all souli are Mine," and that the times of all are in His hand, and it should be ours to improve the events of His providence by seeking to perform or fulfil His will. . Mr. Eglinton then went on to say that some names would be mentioned in many assemblies that night. Notably appeared the names of Bishop Colenso and the ever-to-be-revered Dr. Moffatt. There were, however, events to which, perhaps, he should refer which I were to them of deeper, and it might be tenderer interest. Whilst there were some in that chapel who sat with them last year, the reaper had been amongst them, and some had bees cut down. The voice of the Master had been heard. 1 They thanked God b?cause they knew they were ready. From that gallery and from those pews some with whose form and voice they were perfectly familiar had passed away, but they rejoiced to know, as it bad been intimated, that they were now in the presence of the Lord. They had not only those with whom they had been assisted in church felowship and church worship, but some of them might have still tenderer memories. He had in his possession a picture presenting a most graceful form and lovely face—the form and face of a lady. At the base was inscribed, " Pensive memories." There were depicted two little shoes that once enclosed the two little feet now coffined. They thought of the vacant bed and cot, and some of them of the empty chair. When they looked at the old WWI ,v,-re the spectacles were wont to lie, they were reminded of those words exhorting them to go onward, and they should oopir the conduct of those dear friends, emulate their a ~l and catch their mantle, and, should be reminded that they should make their lives sublime. He had before him a scene which occurred several thousand years ago. There stood a vener• able man, his grey locks waving in the wind, his eye still piercing and his voice still firm, surrouiried by the elder *leaders and officers of his people, and also by their wives and little children, speaking to them of the memories of the past, and of God's goodness to their fathers and to them If he could call before them all His goodness to them, much more time than was available must be taken. "Choose you this day whom you will serve." So spoke J•shua, the distinguished successor of the illustrious Moses, the man who divided the inheritance of the tribes of Israel by lot. Danger stood thick around them, pushing them to the tomb. He trusted they would receive the exhortation which had been given—earnestly given, that they would in that service give their souls to God and seek the joy of salvation which flowed from His presence.—The service was brought to a conclusion by the pronouncing of the Benediction.
