div.head: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.
div.p: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.

A sermon appropriate to to the closing of the year was preached in Wycliffe Congregational Church, on Sunday evening, by the pastor (Rev. J. Yonge), who spoke on'. The opening of the Books of Judgment." The congregatton was very large, and the sermon most impressive. The following evening a watch-night service took place in the church, which was also conducted by Mr. Yonge,wben the attendance was again very large. The service opened with the singing of a hymn, followed by prayer and the reading of a portion of scripture. M. Tongs preached from Luke xli., 27, the words being "Blessed are those servants whom the Lord when He cometh shall find watching; verily I say unto you that He shall gird Himself and make them sit down to meat, and will come forth andrserve them." The preacher began by remarking that their very attitude at that service was that of watching. They were there for the purpose of watching the transition of their life from one of life's periods to another. They were met to watch in quietness, silence, and thought, tht! flight of time at a most impressive period; to witness one year depart and to welcome another as it came. And the season in which they were holding that service, and watching the interetsing and instructive transi- tion, was the night season. The duty of the day was done, the work of the world was hushed, the business of life was suspended, numbers of people were asleep ; and numbers of other people probably were holding their watch meeting in mirth, and possibly In revelry. They had found it to be a good think in times past, and he hoped they found it so now, to come into Ged's house at that hour that they' might help one another and have kindly thoughts and draw near to Him in whose hands their lives always were. While their particular meaning and intention in that service was not the watching for the coming of their Lord, they were reminded of the great end 1 when He would come, and they all of them understood, I he hoped, that Christ would come and see each personally 1 and actually. He supposed most of them believed in some way or measure that, according to the testimony of Scripture, Christ would come azain in this world for the purpose of judging it, and for the purpose of bringing in a new state of things. Let them remember that that coining of which the Scripture spoke was unmistakably IdraWieg nearer every year. They coold have very little doubt that a great number of people this year, in some parts Of the world particularly, Leed been led to imagine that the great day of the end was at hod—whin that terrible earthquake at Ischia'heppened. and the earth opened and hundreds of people were swal- lowed up. Surely some such thoughts had been present in their minds. ,And then, also, when that terrible eruption in the island of Java took place, some sort of feeling started in many mines, and some people whose wheels were easily moved might have been affected by the remarkable sunsets of only a few weeks ago. The preacher went nn to say that the Father kept all these things in His own keeping, and that we " know neither the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man cometbe" God, who bid from them individually the time when they had to die, kept in His own absolute keeping the greater • secret of the world's dissolution. .He thought there was considerable moral danger in indulging in these speculations, and spending their lives, in "'ague, indefinite looking for the second coming of Christ. By so doing they neglected the responsibilities and deities of life. Let none of them imagine that one of them was left out of that description of the ser- vants of the Lord, becense whether they knew it or not, whether any of them made any profession of it or not, it was still equally tree • that all of them, all who loved the, Lord, were intended to be servants of the Lord. It was a' great truth, and one which he felt none of them thoroughly realized, and which many of the altogether forgot, that every man's life was the vineyard of God. Every morning they rose from their bed God's call to them was e Go work' to-day in my. vineyard." A person might say that his life was his own, and he would do as he liked with it. A greater mistake mortal never made. He did not make his own life, and he did not himself maintain it. They might think because they worked hard and honestly that therefore they were upholding their life, forgetting the great truth that it was the strength of God which enabled then to work. Their lives were not their Own, awl however much they might wish it they could not lengthen them by a single hour. Teey were their Maker's property, and See life of each eine was the vineyard of God. It was their duty to do as. well as they could, and in every department of their life to be the servant of the living Gad. Some of them had gone further than that, and by their own free will taken up some special work. Some were Sunday school teachers, there were some amongst them who . preached, and some were engaged in other forms of service. Whit a fitting question it was to ask them- selves whether they had done their work as well as. they might have done it, and as well es they ought to have done it. The Father expected them to do it, for there was no place anywhere for slipshodness in God's service, and no place for negligence and indolence. IS, in their business, manly toil, home duties or other- wise they did not do as well as they could they were doing their work wrongly'; and if any of those engaged in religious work ever allowed themselves to get into habits of carelessness they were doing their Work wrongly. And since they did not know the hour when the ,Lord might come, how important it was for them always Le be living up to the standard as set forth in the passage of Scrip- ture which he had read, so- that when the Master came He might award them • the blessed- ness which was promised to His faithful servants. A short time was afterwards spent in silent prayer, and when 1883 had passed away an appropriate hymn was sung. Subsequently Mr. Tongs, in a few remarks urged those pre- sent to begin the New Year well as regarded their attend- ance at the house of God. At night they had a good at- tendance, but generally so good in the morning. It would cheer his heart and do them good to come on . a Sunday morning. Let them begin the New Year as-be thought they ought to do.—lt is needless to add that as. the congre- gation separated the usual New Year compliments were freely exchanged.

div.head: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.

A watch-night service was also held at this church. It was conducted by the Vicar, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, and there was a large Congregation. Hymns appropriate to the occasion were sung and the Vicar preached from Revela- tions xxii., 14, "Blessed are they that do His command- ments, that they may have a right to tree of life, and may enter in through the gates through the city.' In the con,rse of an excellent discourse. Mr. Wilkinson said that was the last day of the year 1883, end surely at that solemn time the thoughts uppermost in their minds might be defined under two heads—" How good and how kind has Almighty God been to us during the year which is passed, and how ungrateful we have been to Him for all His kindness to- wards us." He had no doubt many of them had read that day same of the leaders which had appeared in so many of their newspaPers commenting upon the year which was now so nearly at an end, and they would have gathered from them that as a nation they had very much to feel thankful for. They had had more than their usual prosperity, and they were* peace with the world. As membeis of the Church of England they had also very much to be thankful to God for, and he believed there never was a time when the Church was snore active, and certainly never when her members, both lay and. clericals had . a greater feeling of reeponsibility ; bud, as individuals, they hid to retnn thanks to God for many fa.

yours which they had received during the year. In •the few moments that remained of 1883 he would like to say a few works to them upon their personal blessings. Most present were in good health, and that had been the case with them during the past year; they had also strength, food, and raiment; they had been preserved from danger of body, and also from danger of soul. Again, how many spiritual blessings had they to be thankful for? They had to thank God for the means of grace, for the hope of glory, and that they had been kept from many sins. While reviewing the past year, they must acknowledge with shame and confusion of face that they had sinned against God, and they had not loved Him as intensely as they ought to have done. The last moments of the old, and the first of the new year were spent in silent prayer, after which a hymn was sung, and subiequently the Vicar intimated to the congregation that they would find his New Year's greeting in the 14th verse of the 13th chapter of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians--" The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost be with you all." The service was closed by the singing of a hymn. OLD FOLKS' TREAT AT STOCKTON HEATH. A very pleasant gathering took plan in Barn Chapel, Stockton Heath, when the second of a series of gatherings for aged people over 65 years and widows was held. There were between 60 and 70 present and their wants were attended to by Mesdames M. E. Edgeley, Pil- ling, Isherwood, Hamblett, Spencely, Worthington, Whitley, and Pearson.—After tea a meeting HAS held pre- sided over by the Rev. W. Billing, of Hill Cliff, who ad- dressed a few remarks to those present. He thought he could not do better than wish them all a happy new year. Many of them had known what want was, and known per- haps not a little suffering and trouble, but if they could put their trust in an over-ruling Providence and rest in His love, the new year would be a happy one. Might they not know want, but he abundantly satisfied so far as temporal things were concerned. Last year they had a similar gathering, and out of the number then invited ten hdd gone into eternity, four of whom were present last year. He hoped that would be a most pleasant and happy gathering, and the forerunner of many such —Mr. James Naylor then addressed the meeting, as also did Messrs. Thomas Goodier, John Spencelv, E. Johnson, and Whitley. Messrs. Pear- son' Jno. Grounds, J. Grounds, Miss Wilkinson and Mrs. J. Grounds rendered excellent selections of music, Mrs. Pearson presiding at the harmonium. Votes of thanks to the donors of this gathering, and to all who had assisted, and to the chairman were accorded, and the singing of the Doxolo,!y brought a very enjoyable evening to a close.

div.head: RUNCORN.
div.p: RUNCORN.

At Runcorn the New Year was lu-she:red in with the usual observances. Divine worship was held at the churches of the Establishment, and in most V the Nonconformist chapels; whilst the streets were paraded by bands of music, wait singers, and youths and men, who, animated by an exuberance of spirits, made night hideous by'a variety of noises. Most of the tradespeople closed their establish- ments, but the chemical works were open as usual. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL. On Sunday evening last the Rev. J. D. Thomas (pastor) preached an appropriate discourse founded on Hag. 1, 7. In the course of his remarks, the preacher said that these words, though spoken so many centuries ago, were not a defunct statute. They still conveyed a living message to the human heart. They suggested a need for reflection. There are times when it is very convenient to perform this duty. Both the character and circumstances of the times compel us to pause reflect, and examine ourselves. Such a time is the close of year. When it comes to the point of leaving one country for another, people are apt to think that they have complained too much of the old country— that it has not been such a bad place after all, and that the new may nt prove quite so good. So it is when we leave the old year to enter upon the new; we have complained much of the old one, but will the new prove better? Each year that comes to us is like one of the treasure cities of the Ancient Egyptians. Every month, week, minute, and second in the year is loaded with experiences which vary in their character. But these experiences do not vary in any arbitrary manner. 'Tie true that unforeseen events oc- casionally throw us into depths of grief; but as a rule the experiences which we require in the course of a year are pleasant or painful according to the relations in which we stand to each other, and to our Heavenly Father. Each year is also like a garden. Its minutes and secundssre as so many opening flowers, wherein we may rind much that will prove helpful to us in the future time. But while it is true that each year as it comes to us is like a treasure city, or a garden ; it is true, also, that each year as it departs from us is like a hive. The minutes and seconds of which it consists are as so many cells, and these cells are stored with something of our own production. What is the nature of the production the judgment day alone will reveal. In telling the story of the year he would not limit himself to the materials supplied by their experiences as private indi- viduals, but would take within the range of his review affairs both at home and abroad. The rev, gentleman then proceeded to review the year in its accidents, its extraor- dinary natural phenomena, and its obituary list, singling out for special mention the names of John Richard Green, Robert Moffat, and Thomas Holloway. The sermon was delivered to a good audience, and was listened to with evi- dent interest.--On Monday night, at 11-15, the annual watch-night service was held, The pastor preached again, taking as his text the words, "But the hour cometh." CHRISTMAS Tref..., AND 13AZAAR.—This was held on New Year' 11 .I.Jay, at the house of Mr. F. Fairhurst, Halton-road. ' One of the largest rooms in the house had been specially decorated and filled for the occasion. Two large holly trees were decked with toys antr sweetmeats of various descriptions. A large table in the C,,nt?C, ana smatter ones at the side, were fitted up with articles both useful and I ornamental. At five p.m . the room being filled with chil- dren and their friends, Mr. Fairhurst called upon the Rev. J. D. Thomas to open the proceedings. Mr. Thomas said he had attended many gatherings of a similar kind, but he did not remember that any one of them had afforded him so much pleasure as this, He would state briefly the reason why he felt so much pleasure on the pres4tot occasion. First, the work they saw before them had been accomplished by little children, the eldest not being more than eight or nine years of age. The idea had been started by little ones, and the woollen mats and dolls' clothes and other numerous articles were the work of little fingers. Second, the object of the Christmas tree was one of the most laudable. As a rule, Christmas tress were got up for the purpose of clearing off debts, but this one had an altogether different object in view. They had within the last week or two been enjoying them- selves very much. The little boys and girls, as well as their bigger friends, had been feasting themselves on such dainties as roast turkey and beef, mince pies and plum pud- ding, apples, oranges, grapes, and almonds. But, perhaps, all did not remember when they were enjoying so many good things, that in the same town were little boys and , girls who not only had not lasted such a thing as plum pudding, but were often without food of any description to satisfy their hunger. Some, however, did remember this long before Christmas came round, and they worked hard and long that their less fortunate brothers and sisters might be comforted. This Chr.s,mas tree is the result of their work, and the proceeds of the sale would be given to provide a free tea for some of the most destitute children in the mission district connected with St. Luke's Chapel, which is under Mr. Thomas's superintendence. Having invited the friends present to invest their money in the goods exhibited. Mr. Thomas declared the bazaar poen. In the course of an hour or two the whole of the articles had been purchased. Mr. James Craig contriiaated to the pleasure of the proceed- ings by giving a a recitation from the Merchant of Venice, and telling a few racy anecdotes.—A vote of thanks to miss Fairhurst, the prime mover in the work, wa, proposed by the Rev. J. D. Thomas, and seconded by Mr. Craig, and carried with acclamation. A sufficient sum was realsed to provide a free tea for about 100 children. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. The teachers of St. John's Presbyterian Sunday School had their annual meeting on Wednesday evening, when earnest ad- dresses on Sunday School work were delivered by the Rev. Evan Williams, Messrs. J. Kirkham, W. Leach, John Humphreys, F. Hewitt, and R. Baxter, Messrs. James Pritchard and James Kirkham were appointed superinten- dents; Mr. Thomas Dobson, secretary ; and Mr. J. H. Richardson, librarian. The school is in a most prosperous condition, having 202 members on the books with 16 teachers. The average attendance is 147. ST. JOHN THE EVANGELIST'S CHURCH.—The annual tea party took place at Weston on Wednesday night. The school had been beautifully decorated for the occasion by Mrs. T. Ford, assisted by Mrs. Claudet and Mr. and Mrs. Ellis. A large number partook of the tea provided, dona- tions of tables having been made by Mrs. Barclay, Miss Barclay, Mrs. Claudet, Mrs. Aaron, Mr. Ford, Mrs. Barrow, Mrs. Joseph Tudor, Mrs. Adcock, Mr. Armstrong, Mr. T. Bankes, Mr. Vause, Mrs. Moores, Mrs. Griffiths, Mrs. Light- foot, Mrs. Roberts, and Mrs. Percivals. The subsequent proceedings were presided over by the Rev. John Madden, curate in charge, who made an address. An interesting programme of songs, recitations, &c., was capitally gone through, Mrs. Claudet presiding at the piano.—On Thursday evening the scholars were provided with tea, and prizes were distributed to the successful children. MERSMY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN. —On New Year's Eve the annual tea meeting and entertainment, in connection with this mission, were held. About 100 persons sat down to tea, the tables being presided over by Miss Barclay, Mrs. Meadowcroft, Miss Mouritz, Mrs. Allen, Miss Garrett, Miss Owens, and Miss Allen. Subsequently the entertainment was held, the schoolroom being tastefully decorated with evergreens and mottoes, by Miss Garrett, Miss Owens, Miss Bowyer, Miss Davis, Messrs. Cu-eaves, Wakefield, and Lewis. There was a good audience, and Mr. J. Meadowcroft pre. sided. In opening the proceedings, the Chairman ' expressed his satisfaction that the entertainments ' provided year by year by Mr. Shaw, and those kind friends who were good enough to assist him were still regarded with that interest which first distinguished them, and that the meeting that night was quite as numer- ous and as enthusiastic as those held heretofore. It spoke very well for the work which was being done. He was highly gratified to learn from Mr. Shaw that the iyork of the mission was progressing, and that the room had become much too small for the purpose for which it was erected. On Sunday last there were 255 scholars in that Mena, and Mr. Shaw was unable to provide accommodation for all who wished to attend the evening service. Judging from the numbers that attended they might therefore conclude that the mission was doing a great work, and he was sure that if it was supported and encouraged as it deserved that it would continue to do good. Bat there was a difficulty to contend , with, as Mr. Shaw had pointed out, that if it continued to improve, how would he get the people within the four walls

of that building. (Applause.) It was a difficulty whigh he (the chairman) could not solve for him at the present time. (Applause.) The chairman then spoke in compli. mentary terms of the entertainment, which was proceeded with. On New Year's Day the annual Christmas tree and entertainment was given in connection with the Sunday school. A Christmas tree, tastefully decorated, was sus- pended from the roof, laden with a variety of articles, which were distributed to the children by Miss Garrett, Miss Davies, and Miss Owen. In the absence of Mr. Bridge- water, Mr. Shaw presided, and addresses were given by Mr. G. Howard and Mr. G. Mort. There was a musical enter- tainment.

HALTON PARISH CHURCH.-A vigil service was held in this church on New Year's Eve, at which there were sofas 120 persons present—a gratifying number for a country parish with a scattered population. Special lessons were read; special Psalms, too, the 39th and 90th, were sung, and the hymns "A few more years shall roll" and "Days and moments quickly flying, blend the living with the dead" were very effectively ren- dered by a full choir, after careful practice. The Vicar (Rev. J. Lockwood) gave an address based on the word, "The end," taken from Rev. 21, 6, in the course of which he touched upon the sad and lamented death, by accident, of his own cousin (by marriage), Mr. T. Wildman Barker, County Coroner of Lancashire, which took place on the previous Saturday. At the close of the rev, gentleman's ad' dress, three minutes were allowed for private prayer, at the expiration of which the church bell struck twelve, tolling out the old year 1883, and then the new Parish School bells, for the first time, for three minutes chimed in the new year 1884. The Vicar then gave those present, as well as all his parishioners, a hearty greeting for the New Year, and after- wards recited a short piece of poetry suitable to the occasion Tnere was a celebration of the Holy Communion after ser- vice, at which there were 23 communicants. At the close the Vicar resorted to the door, and shakinglaande with each one personally wished them heartily "A Happy New I Year."

WIDNES. _ The streets of Widnes presented an animated scene on New Year's Eve. The muddy thoroughfares were crowded with people, young and old, until an early hour on New Year's Day, youths marching about in organised bande singing familiar refrains or making discordant noises. ehe chemical works were conducting operations as usual, and from about five minutes to twelve until a few minutes, their whistles sent forth a united volume of sound, which must have penetrated the air for miles around. Watch-night services were held at most of the places of worship, and on the fol- lowing day several tea parties were held, while the Fara- worth Temperance Society held a demonstration. In the evening snow fell to some extent, imparting to the streets and buildings a Christmas-like appearance, the want of which has been generally lamented. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.—The annual tea party' was held on New Year's Day in the Hatchineon-street Chapel. The attendance was only moderate. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mrs Overton, Mrs H G Led- don, Mrs William Hill, Mrs Thomas Hill, Mrs T Marshall, Mrs Coxon, Mrs Halliday, Mrs E Seddon, and Miss Barker. After tea, a public meeting was held under the presidency of Mr J M Halliday. and addreses were delivered by Mr John Shuttleworth, the Rev J Morton (cir- cuit minister), and Mr J W Coxon. The choir, under the conductorship of Mr H J Seddon, assisted by the instru- mental band, readered several anthems during the evening, and Mr J Robinson contributed a solo oil the violin in neat style. • RAILWAY SERVANTS' SUPPER.—The men employed in the locomotive department of the London and North-Western Railway at Widnes had their minuet supper on the evening of Christmas Day, at Unsworth's Dining Rooms, Victoria. road. There were about fifty persons present, and a generous repast, consisting of various seasonable delicacies, was provided. Mr. Turnbull, locomative foreman, occupied the chair, and Mr. Smith, the station- master, the vice-chair. Amongst those present were Messrs. Robert Burton, T. Dainteth, C. Parry, P. Gill, A. Gibson, W. Parry, R. Briers, T. Webster, J. Wilson, and T. Fryer. Letters of apology for non-attendance were read from Mr. Carter, traffic inspector; Mr. Appleton, stationmaster, Run' corn; Mr. Smith, wagon inspector; and Mr. Bilsborongh, goods agent. The usual loyal toasts having been honoared, the Chairman observed that it gave him great pleasure to meet se many men that evening. Rtilway men had very' few opportunities of meeting together, and gatherings of that description served a very good purpose. Referring to the work of the past year. he said they could not comPle_i°, as it had been more successful than the previous year. hie knew that his department was in a very much better posi tion, and he concluded by wishing all present a happy and prosperous new year.—Mr. Smith, the vice-chairman, pro- posed the toast of the London and North-Western Railway Company in appropriate terms. He spoke of their enter- prise in seeking out and adopting the latest improvements in order to provide for the safety of life and limb. The company had a wide-world reputation. In connection with the toast he mentioned the names of Mr. Webb. Crewe, Mr. Newton, Peasley Cross, and the chairman.—The toast was "drunk with enthusiasm.—Mr. Wilson gave the kealth of Mr. Newton, which was cordially honoured.,—Other toasts followed.

Telegrams from Cairo state that the Mandi is gaining ground and that the insurrectionary movement is spreading northwards. It is also extending along the coast of the Red Sea. AN AnotrrrvE PROSECt TioN.—At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, on Monday, a man named Thomas Rogers was Charged with having driven a locomotive on the high. Way not having a person preceding it. An officer stated that on the Monday previous he saw the engine in Giller's- ' ,ans, Eccleston, without anyone in front of it. Re called noon the defendant to step, which he did, and witness then eiri the man who ought to have been in front walking be- ..ind the engine and smoking a pipe. On the summons being served upon him the defendant was said to have be- haved in a violent manner. After the case had been gone into the summons was withdrawn. ReILwAY COLLISION IN CANADA.—A collision occurred On Wednesday morning on the Grand Trunk Railway at a !port distance east of Toronto between a train which daily !eaves the city at 6.40 a.m. with a car attached to it for ;orkmen belongiag to the boltworks, and a goods train. !'enty-seven workmen were killed, and from 20 to 30 hurt. 1.. :us guard of the goods train is accused of being responsible tor the accident, and has been arrested. It is alleged that e,haki started his train without orders. Several of those who were injured are so seriously hurt that they are not e.!illepedcted to recover. The accident-lms cast a gloom over ;..e whole of the city. Many of the workmen who were leave families. According to later particulars of the ctollision 15 persons were killed outright while seven died ilbsequently in the hospital. The condition of several ripers of the injured passengers is regarded as hopeless. Subscriptions have been opened for the families of the vic- tims. _VEr. FOOTBALL. "o" Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Beweey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'alaek on Wednesday morning.

AllktikitoWg V. NEWTON NEATII.—The return match be- liWeen these two clubs was played at Newton Heath (Manches- ter) on Saturday afternoon last, in the presel.ce of a goodly number of spectators. The match was a "benefit" one, the proceeds being given to A. J. Dixon, one of the members of the Newton Heath Club, who recently had his leg broken. As the Manchester team was defeated by eight goals to nil at Earles- town, the latter found themselves opposed at Manchester by a very strong team. The Newton Heath captain won the toss. and for the first half played with the wind in theft favour. For about ten minutes the game was pretty even, 'Jut Ellison then scored a beautiful goal for the Visitors. Five, minutes later the same player again scored, and at half time, the score was Earies- town two goals, Newton Heath nor,e. On the change of ends the Earleston ans severely pleased their opponents, and after five minutes' play Ellison. again scored. Shortly offer an exciting scrimmage took Voice in front of Newton Heath goal, and the leather was kicked through by one of the home backs. As no other point was reglitered the match resulted in a win for Earlastown by four goals to nil. Teams: Earlestown J Appleton, goal; R Green and F Emmett, backs; 11 Bowker and J Green, half becks; J Duxbury and T Champion, right wing; J Eillson and J Mather, centre; J Bimm and J Cameron, left wing. Newton Heath: C Fulton, goal ; 3 Rigby and 0 Jones, backs; 0 Robinson H nowise, and J Crampton, half backs; A Shaw and J Morris, right wing; A Latham, centre; EDavies and Moffatt, left wing. CHESHIRE QUARTER SESSIONS. The winter quarter sessions for the county of Cheshire were opened at Chester Castle on Monday; Mr. Horatio Lloyd, the deputy-chairman, presiding. Mr. Ellis Davis, of Liscard, was foreman of the grand jury.—Mr. Lloyd, in delivering his charge to the grand jury, congratulated them on the smallness of the calendar, which only included seven cases. One of these, be pointed out, was a case of attempting to commit suicide, an • offence which had been rather frequent of late in this district. It was difficult to know how to deal with these cases effectually. It was a question whether they should not in future keep such per- sons in custody for a length of time, so that. they might effectually recover before being sent out again or whether they should not be sent to some place where they could be taken care of permanently. He congratulated the grand jury on the general decrease of crime in the county, and said that at Knutsford there were only twenty-three prisoners awaiting trial, as against fifty, the number awaiting trial there this time last year. CIVIL BUSINESS. Lord Egerton of Tatton presided over the civil business. A grant of £340 was made for additional cells at New Brighton Police Station, £3OO for repairs and additions at Birkenhead Police Station, and £l.lO for repairs at Egre- mont Police Station. A grant of £3OO was made for repairs of padded rooms at Parkside Asylum. Mr. Verdin called attention to the great difference between the cost of the maintenance of inmates at Parkside Asylum, which was 103 &I per week, and that at Upton Asylum, which was 7s 10d. That meant a difference of over £4,000 annually to the county,-The Chairman said the subject might be discussed at the April sessions, when the accounts came up. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. Mr. Stanhope Bull, the county surveyor, presented his report on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill for this session, in which there was some deviation from the original plan. In the proposed construction of docks for Warrington the dis- charge of flood water from Wilderspool-canseway would be effected, and he did not see any provision made for it.—lt was resolved that a committee be appointed to watch this and any other bills which may be introduced into Parliament during the ensuing session relating to the interests of this county, and to oppose or petition against any bill which may interfere with those interests. Mr. Wm. Laird addressed the court, pointing out how seriously the proposed canal and works in the Mersey might affect the channel and sandbanks opposite the port of Liverpool, and said that Birkenhead was opposing the bill strongly. The Chairman said that as far as the county was con- cerned they would not be able to offer any opposition to the bill. A committee was only appointed because special in- terests were affected. The following gentlemen were appointed the committee to watch any bills affecting the county :—Mr. Horatio Lloyd, Mr. Wood, Mr. OW. Latham, Mr. Tattoo, Mr. Thos. Ashton, Mr. Birley, Mr. Chadwick, Mr. Abel Brockley, Colonel France-Hayhurst, Mr. Peter Stubs, Mr. Edward Greenall, Mr. Trelawny, Mr. J. H. Leche, and the members of both houses of Parliament for the county. FOOT-AND-lICIUTU DISEASE. The Chief Constabfe eeported that 187 animals remained under treatment for foot-and-mouth disease at the last quarter sessions, since which the disease had appeared in twenty places; 321 animals had been attacked, of which three died, 418 recovered, and 89 remained under treat- ment.

RUNCORN LIBERALS AT HAWARDEN, A deputation from the Runcorn Liberal Association Waited upon Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., at Hawarden Castle, on Saturday, with the object of obtaining the assis- tance of the hon. gentleman at a political demonstration to be held early in the year. The deputation, which consisted of Messrs. R. Shaw, T. Hamiley, T. Norman, F. Fairhurst, and S. C. Beckett, drove from Chester to Hawarden in an open ca”riage with a pair of horses. They were fortunate enough to find both the Premier and his son in the pads, and ware very kindly received. They did not, however, reach Mr. Gladstone without considerable difficulty. They had hardly entered the precints of the castle grounds when a detective inquired the nature of their business. The pur- pose of their visit being explained the deputation was con- ducted to a portion of the park where Mr. Gladstone was aiming vigorous blows at a tree with a heavy axe. Mr. Herbert Gladstone was with his father, and the Runcorn Liberals quickly made known the object of their visit; but the hon. gentleman pointed out that in the present aspect of polit'cal affairs he could not accede to their request. As another reason why he could not take part in the proposed demonstration, he statcd that he felt he had as much time taken up by his own constituency, it being such a large one, as he could well devote to public oratory. Ha promised the deputation, however, that he would visit Runcorn upon a subsequent occasion, but when asked to fix the date said that was beyond his power. Meanwhile the Premier, with bare arms, uncovered head, and his braces tied round his waist, was industriously fell- ing the tree, and during a pause in the work the depata'tion congratulatti him upon the 74'h anniversary of his birth- day. He indulged in a friendly chat with the visitors, and thanked them very warmly for their greetings. Thfore they withdrew the deputation asked to be allowed to carry away a few ch;ps of the tree which lay scattered about. Mr. Glads'one, without hesitation, stooped down, and picking up several of the chips smilingly handed them to the party. After enjoyiny a few minutes further conversation, the de- putation withdrew and returned to Runcorn the same even- ing by train.
HALTON PARISH- CHURCH PARC.

CRIAL TEA. PARTY. The annual tea party in connection with the Halton Par- ish Church was held on Thursday night, when upwards of 200 persons sat down to an excellent tea. The following ladies presided over the tables :—Mrs and Miss Ackerley, Mrs Baguley, Mrs J W Baguley, Miss Chrim.s, Miss A Gordon, Mrs J W Haddock, Mrs Jeacock, Miss E Jones, Miss Kingston, Miss Kingston, Mrs Kinsey, Miss Ormsom Mrs J Stokes, Miss Short, Mrs Walton, Mrs Watkin, Mrs Weir, Mr s Walton, Mrs A Woodier, Mrs Wright, and Mrs Yapp. Subsequently, a meeting and entertainment, presided over by the Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar, was held. The Vicar, in an appropriate speech, reviewed the work of the parish for the past year, remarking that the attendance at church had increased very much during the year,while there had been a marked increase in the number of communicants. All worked well together, proof of which was found in the fact that they had a balance in hand at the last vestry meeting.—The entertainment was of a very interesting character. The choir, conducted by Mr Jeacock, rendered several glees, and the comic element was agreeably sustained by Mr William Porter, of Liverpool, and Mr J W Haddock; Mr John Ashton and Mr Rook also took part.

div.head: FREE BREAKFAST TO POOR CHIL-
div.p: FREE BREAKFAST TO POOR CHIL-
DREN AT RUNCORN.

Yesterday morning about 250 of the poor waifs of Run- corn were provided with a substantial breakfast in the Elles- mere-street Sunday School. The funds for this seasonable display of the Christmas charity had been partly obtained at the free .concerts organised by the Rev. W. Vause, and held each week for a considerable period past. The object of the concerts was known, and great interest was taken in the project by Mr. and Mrs. Vallee, and other ladies and gentlemen connected with the school. Money sufficient to provide breakfast for 150 children WAS raised, and tickets for that number only were distributed. Great care and discrimination were required in flailing the duty of distri h aim, and the hungry-looking faces and scanty clothing of many of C.. 170 youngsters who sat round the tables were evidences that tne d.eerving cases had been discovered. In satisfying the wants of the te.tre. Mr. and Mrs. Vanes were aided by Mrs. Gandy, Mrs. White, lies. Turnbull, Mrs. Scragg, Miss White, Mrs. Brindley, Mrs. Neil, Mrs. Miln- shay, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. Curzon, cud Messrs. Marlow, Stub, White, and Curzon. Each child was given two pieces of bread and butttr, of substantial tkickness, and a large cur- rant bun, and as much tea and coffee as they desired. Having received an nenapected donation of 100 buns, on Thursday evening, Mr. YAWS after the 170 had been fed was enabled to supply the wants of other 80 children who had collected round the school door. Mr. Vause contem- plates giving another treat, of a similar description before the end of the winter if he can obtain the necessary funds, and we hope that he will not be disappointed on this ground.

div.head: HALF-DAY HOLIDAY MOVEMENT IN WIDNES. –
div.p: HALF-DAY HOLIDAY MOVEMENT IN WIDNES. -

On Thursday evening a meeting of Widnes skopkeepers, convened by circular, was held in the Officers'-room, Volunteer Hall, with reference to the project, mooted a few weeks ago, of forming a Half-Day Holiday Association for the tradesmen of Widnes. There were about 25 persons present, and Mr. Briscoe was voted to the chair. He was supported by Messrs. Peat, E Wa ' rnham Bower, B. Booth, S. Guy, W. Palirt, T. Smith, McCollom, G. H. Wharton, F. Tebbutt, D. Brooks, Rted, Ellwood, Smith, Stead, and Hurst.—The CHAIRMAN said ha was sorry thEre was not a better attendance. Considering the size of the town, a larger audience might have been expected. tle was certain a half-day holiday each week would be a great boon to the tradesmen of Widnes if they could obtain it, and he thought the thanks of the meeting were due to who- I ever had originated the movement, which he should ; b 3 gad to support in everf way he could. (Hear, hear.) lie suggested that the town should be canvassed, and the opinion of the tradespeople thus obtained.— Mr. %VAUBAN observed that there was a general feeling in favour of the holiday, and Mr. STEAD said he should be glad to close ble establishment if his co-professionals would join the move- mint. He moved that the town be mapped into districts and canvasssers appointed.—Mr. Wannam seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—On the motion of Mr. McCora.om, seconded by Mr. BOOTH, Mr. Peat, who, we believe, is the originator of the movement, Was appointed secretary. A conversation ensued, and the town was di- vided into four districts, and a deputation of 16 persons was elected, four to work each district. The evident feeling of the meeting was in favour of a half-holidav, and it was stated that the only fear of the failure of the movement was the division of the tradesmen into two sections, one desiring the holiday on a Wednesday afternoon and the other on a Thursday. Another meeting will be held- in a week.

Tuesday last being New Year's Day, most of the shops and business places in Prescot were closed. The principal watch factories are closed all the week. Mr. Hewitt's men have New Year's week as a holi lay, and Mr. Berry's Christmas week. Caurtow TO Dive.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday last, John Perdue was summoned for obstructing the highway at Newton by allowing two horses and a wag- gannette to stand thereon, contrary to the by-laws —P.C. Spencer deposed that on the sth ult, he nw the defendant in charge of a waggonnette drama by two horses. They were standing in Mill-lane, Newt In. with a number of other vehicles plying for hire in connection with the Haydock Park Coursing Meeting. When a number of people left the station the defendant drew his horses and waggonette into the centre of the road and thereby obstructed it. He would not withdraw it when requested, and also refused to give his name or address. The defendant was fined lOs and costs.— John Griffiths was ordefed to pay the costs (6s 6d) for al- lowing his horse and ort to stind in Crow-lane without anyone in charge on the 14th December.—Ralph Whittle was summoned for a similar offence; committed in Queen- s'reet, Earlestown, on the 22nd ult.—P.C. WATEn CO3I2ANIES AND Tux Pmamc.—The committee of the Battersea Water Consumers' Defence Association have prepared and circulated a code of instructions to the con- sumers of the Southwark and Vauxhall Company's water which gives some useful information with reference to the rights and duties of either party. The committee pointed Out as an important factor that a water rate is in evcry 0a55 payable quarterly in advance, there being no exception whatever to this rule. It is not necessary for the company to make a demand, the duty of the consumers being to ten- der it on the first day of the quarter, or sooner if he likes. Neglect of this is the cause of nearly every success which the company have obtained in the law courts. The com- mittee point out that when the rateable value is not more than £2O the rate of six per cant. covers all charges, and they condemn the notices served by the company with refer- ence to two-gallon flushes, Sm., as so many attempts to make profit out of the ignorance of the consumer. The committee add that the only person liable for the rate is the person who uses the water, and a rate owing by one tenant cannot be recovered from another unless the latter Make a specific promise to pay. The recommendation of the committee is that each consumer should tender a quarter's rate in advance, based on the rateable value of his house as ascertained from the pariah books,

ANNOYING THE SALVATION ARMY AT WARRINGTON. A SERIOUS ATTACK. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Tuesday, Bodelie Knockton, fustian cutter, 6, Silver-street, Mary Baldwin, hawker, 30, Haydock-street, Margaret Callaghan, hawker, Friars' Green, Sarah Ann Taylor, hawker, 6, Haydock-street, Bodelia Loftus, fustian cutter, 14, Portland-street, and Margaret Baldwin, hawker, 30, Elaydock-et., were charged, toe first two named prisoners with unlawfully assaulting and beating one James Higham, on Sunday last, and all were charged with assaulting John Higham.—The Chief-Con- table (Mr. Hunt) said the complainants in this case were brothers and forge labourers, and lived in Stamford-street. They belonged to the Salvation Army, and on Sunday night they, with several associates, called in at the coffee- house near Mr. Jean's office, in Winwick-street, it being then about a quarter to 10, and on turning into the street, the evidence would show that the complainants were set upon by prisoners and a man named Baldwin, not in custody, in a moet disgraceful manner.—James Higham, who appeared In the witness box with his head bandaged, stated that as he and his brother were proceeding home shortly before 10 o'clock on tr unday night they were met near the Central station by prisoners. Knockton and Mary Baldwin first came and pulled his Army gaernsey backwards and for- wards, and then, with the others, followed them, throwing slush and atm es until they got to Town's End, when the girls called out "Johnny," and thereupon tho man not in custody cune up and "pitched" into complainant and his brother. Clogs were thrown at him. He went to the police station, and thence to the Infirmary. John Higham, the other com- plainant, said that last Sunday was his first appearance in the ranks of the Salvation Army. Knockton and the others threw stones, and it was a wonder that art infant which he was carrying was not killed. Callaghan threw a clog at them and a wound was inflicted on his head.—Joseph Board- man, a member of the Army, and other witnesses spoke of the clogs, mud, and stones being thrown by the prisoners, and the great disturbance thereby caused.— Inspector Sin- gleton produced the statements of prisoners which had been taken down in writing, and which formed their answers to the offence with which they were charged. Knockton said "All I have to say is that I was there. I did assault one but not the other; I don't know which." Mary Baldwin said "There was us Ire walking down near the Central Sta- tion, when one of the Highams turned round and knocked me down, saving There's one of the -- bitches that got us 14 days.' Margaret Callaghan admitted having as- saulted one of the complainants, whilst Sarah Ann Taylor had nothing to say. Loftus said "I saw the tallest of the Highams strike Mary Baldwin. I saw Margaret Callaghan down on the floor, and I pulled a man off her, and then he turned round and gave me a blow in the face and knocked me down."—The magistrates retired for coneideratioa, and on their return the Chairman (Major Cartwright) said it must be clearly understood that such conduct which prisoners were guilty of on Sunday night last must be stopped, and there was no way of doing that without inflicting a punishment. It was a disgraceful thing for the prisoners to assemble together as they did and make such an attack, because they must have known that complainants belonging to the Salvation Army were under a bond not to return blows, and they had sworn that they themselves never lifted a hand to the women. It was the wish of the magistrates to protect the Salvation Army people, and they must not be injured in the way they had. There was a long, black list against Knockton, who would now be sentenced to two months' imprisonment, and they directed Mary Baldwin and Callaghan to be im- prisoned for a like term. Taylor did not appear to have been so deep in the attack, and she would be sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.—Loftus was sentenced to a month's hard labour, and Margaret Baldwin was discharged, the magis- trates, however, cautioning her to keep better company and to avoid the Salvation Army if its appearance excited her to make a disturbance.—Counciller Monks observed that the Bench were determined to protect the Army in every- thing which was right and lawful, and they would be severe on people who assaulted its members simply on the feeling that the blows would not be returned. On Wednesday, John Baldwin, 30, Haydock-street, , brother of the two women, B atheist, who were be'ore the ' magistrates on Tuesday, was brought up charged with as- saulting James and John Higham, members of the Sal- vation Arrny.—The Chief Constable said prisoner sur- rendered about nine o'clock that morning on the charge as set forth. Ile then expressed his intention of pleading guilty. Prisoner was the original "Johnny" referred to in the evidence on the previous day, and took a very active part both.with his fists and clogs in the affray.—James Ifigham then stated that when the •" wenches' shouted "Johnny" prisoner came running from the direction of Town's Bid and pitched into witness, striking him with his fists repeatedly. He was also struck with clogs, but these were not thrown by prisoner. The latter struck his brother as well.—Alderman Burgess: Was the prisoner the ringleader, or did he originate the brawl ?—Witness: He did not start it,'but if he had come up quietly and asked what was the matter instead of pitching" into us as be did there would not have been so much bother.—John Hug- barn corroborated, and, in answer to Alderman Burgess, , gala 1,, Aid not strike or kick prisoner in any way.—Other' evidenna lla'° n given, prisoner said he was attracted to the distarteinCilbisseahoUtuflg out, ~ Oh, Johnny, they are killing rolly sister Mary the, Baldwin). He did not start the r0w,7.- plainants struck him first. He was knocked down by D.°, and struck by the other.—Alderman Burgess; But there is a witness who said it was your own friends who did it, and not complainant —Prisoner was sentenced to six weeks'. hard labour, the magistrates stating that such conduct must be put a stop to.

div.head: WARRINGTON ART GALLERY. EXPECTED LOAN FROM THE NATIONAL COLLECTOR.
div.p: WARRINGTON ART GALLERY. EXPECTED LOAN FROM THE NATIONAL COLLECTOR.
The following correspondence, which sufficiently explains itself, will be read with interest

T own Clerk's Office, Warrington 30th nay. 1883.—Dear Slr,—l am directed by the Council of this Borough to apply to , the Trustees of the National Gallery. for a loan of pictures or works of art for public exhibition in the Art Gallery of this towel, under and subject to to the National Gallery (Loan) Act, 1883. Will you be kind enough to inform me in what form the application must be made ?—Yours truly, W. EL BROOK —O. L. Eastlake, Esq., F.R.I 8.A.. Keeper and Secre- tary, National Gallery, Trafalgar Square, -London. London National Gallery. 28th June, 1883 •—Sirs—ln refry- ewe to your letter of the 30th ultimo, making an application for the loan of pictures under the National Gallery (Loan) Act of 1883, lam requested by the Trustees and Director t, make the following enquiries :-1 What amount of lineal wall space is available for permanently exhibiting the pictures in ques- tion? 2 What seniority des the building affird against fire and ether accidents? 3 To whose management is the gallery entrusted? 4 Under what conditions are the public admitted? 5 What is the present population of Warrington? 6 Are the authorities prepared to meet the cost of insurance, carriage, and pecking of any pictures which may be lent by the National Gall^ry ? On receiving answers to these ques • Lions, together with any fnrther particulars to which you may think it desirable to add, the Trustess and Director will give , the application favourable consideration.—l am, Sir, your obedient servant, CHARLES L. Eaartaaa, Keeper and Sc ore- tary —W. H. Monk, Erni Warrington. Town Clerk's Oflic,;, Warrington, 29th June, 18S3.—Sir,— am directed by tha_Museum Library. and Arts Committee to acknowledge the rrceipt of your letter of yesterday's date, and to inrorm you in reply thereto :-1. That there are 90 lineal feet in our Art Gallery for permanently exhibiting the pic- tures in question. 2. That the Art Gallery joins. the Museum, but is not attached to any other building. It is of modern construction. and was co-Wed for the purpose of exhibiting pictures. There are two hydrants of the largest size and a sufficient supply of water within the building, and there are other hydrant sin the street opposite the building.. There is always an attendant in the Art Gallery when it is open to the public. There are two means of exit from the Gallery. 37 The gallery is entrusted to the management of the Museum, Library and Arts Committee appAnted by the Town Council, to whom the property belongs. 4. The publicoare generally admitted free, but en .peeial occasions a small charge is made. If any charge is made to the e_hibition of pictures lent by the National Gallery, it is proposed to devote the proceeds to the completion of a new School of Art which is now in course of erection. 5. Pose population of the borough is about 42 000. 6. The committee are prepared to meet the cost of insurance. carriage and packing of any pictures which may be lent by the tgational GallerV.—l am. Sir, your obedie.A servant, W. It. BROOK, Town Clerk—Charles L. Eastlake, Esq., Keeper and Bseetary National Gallery, London. Town Clerk's 0111-e, Warrington, 11th December, 1883. Bir,-1 am directed by the Museum, Library, and Arts Com- mittee of this town to enquire whether the particulars fur- nished In my letter to you of the 29:h June last were satisfac- tory to the trustees and director of the National Gallery; if SO, the committee direct me again to urge your attention to their applicarion for a loan of pictures under the Ant of 1833. I am. sir, year obedient servant, WILLTAD2 EL BROOK.— Charles Ti. Eastlabe, Esq., keeper and secretary, National Gallery. London. National Gallery, London, 12th December, 1883.—Sir,—In reply to your letter of yesterday, I beg to inform you that ' your previous c immunieation, dated the 29t1i June last, was duly laid before the Trustees and Director of this Gellery and approved. ASSOOR an the various applications from provincial galleries under the National Gallery (Loan), act had been re- ceived tile Director proceeded to the allotment of certain pictures among,them,bnt circumstances intervened which pre- ven'ed him from completing this work before he left London for his oilldal journey on the Continent. The Director is ex— pected to return about the end of this month, when he will resume the allotment, and as soon as it is completed the pie- , tures proposed to be lent will be despatched to their destina- tion subject to the conditions already specifted.—lant Sir, your obedient servant, CHARLES L. EASTLAKV.—Wm. 11 Brook, Eeq., Town Clerk, Warriogton.

THE LAW OF RETALIATION.—Richard Brown WAX on Monday charged at the St. Helens Police Court with. har- ing assaulted Hugh Coyle. Mr. a 0. Swift appeared, for the defendant. Both men, it seemed, worked for Messrs. Pilkington, and in the course of some altercation which took place between them the complainant called the delendant "a liar," upon which the latter retaliated by giviag Coyle a blow on the eye, and knocking his head against a wall. The case was dismissed.

CRONLLY WORKING A, MR I AT NorrOw.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, William Renshaw was summoned for cruelly ill-treating and abusing a mare by working it in an unfit state, on the 6th December; and Wm. Wrigley was summone4 for allowing the mare to be worked in an unlit state.—lnspector Campbell, of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animal, proved that he saw the mare being worked in a very emaciated and weak state, while it had two large wounds on the legs Since then the horse had been destroyed.-.-The Bench fined Renshaw 10s. and cr.:149, and ordered Wrigley to Pay the casts.

The Prince of Wales will vieit Mr. Alfred de Rothschild, near Tring, on the 15th inst. ARREST OF AN ENGINE DErvalt.—An engine driver named Rowe has been arrested at Accrington charged with causing the death of a guard, who was killed in a recent col- lision at Rafford.

LONDONDERRY ELECTION.—The writ arrived yesterday The nomination will probably be on the 10th, and the poll- ing, if there should be a contest, on the 17th. The Irish Solicitor-General will probably be returned unopposed. GREAT FIRE IN DUNDEE.—Mesors. Lyell and Milroy's jute mills, near Dundee, were totally destroyed by fire yes- terday morning. The damage, which is estimated at £13,000, is covered by insurance. Four hundred workmen are thrown idle by the disaster. A committee of Brompton gentlemen have made an incur- sion into the more squalid districts of Southwark. Some of the most shocking "spots" in "horrible London" were found to be owned by the Corporation, the Board of Works, the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, and "a clergyman who holds a rich living in a south-west suburb in London." TERRIBLE STRUGGLE BETWEEN A POLICEMAN AND.A THlF2.—Early yesterday morning a suburb of Sheffield was the scene of a serious encounter between a policeman snd a man, who had been stealing potatoes from a garden. The thief was in the act of bringing away the potatoes when the officer suddenly made his appearance and fastened his hand- cuffs to one of his wrists. The man thereupon drew a snits with the other hand and stabbed the policeman in the cock, at the same time endeavouring to cut his throat. The con- stable made use of is staff -so effectually that both be and the prisoner had to be taken to the hospital where they now lie. TH YSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE AT WARRINGTON. BODY FOUND IN THE RIVER. ad), of John Mwrall, 38 years of age, who lodged mont-street, and who mysteriously disappeared from :dgings some few weeks ago,was found in the river near er's stage on Wednesday. Mr. Blunt, deputy coroner Cheshire held an inquest at the N„rton Arms on 1 • ursday.—George Morrell, brother to the deceased, gave , idence showing that the deceased bad suffered from in-i igestion and nervous debility for upwards of two years, nd that he had also ben, subject to fits of despondency. ' He had been attmded by Dr. Fox, and was last seen alive on the 28th of November. He had frequently said that he suffered more than a man could tell. The following letter, directed to witness, was found on a table at the deceased's [f lodgings on the morning ..of his disappearance :- 1 "My dear brother,—l cannot stay to bear it any longer; I have had as niuch as I can bear. Dear brother, I have ,XllO in the Building Society, so you must draw it, and'all my brothers and sisters share alike, with my father a share. I have some in the Stores also; you must draw that and share it among you all. And there is my watches and 'theme—yen mustdo the same with them', and all my clothes the s sine. I have £l2 in Buttermarket ; you must do the same with that. So good bye, dear brother, and God bless you. The boxes are all in the box. Don't let anyone see wltat is in the box." On the envelope were the words In the river." In consequenct) of this letter, and the disap- pearance of the deceased, the river was dragged, and a re- of £lO was offered for news of the deceased's where- abu- tg. JlZ:hincr. bowetZ, A'a., heard of him until his body was found in the riv a;cyc.—Stteant Spisks .er, a; Stated , stated that on Wednesday morning he rei.iveu ,;f"lllation of a body baying been seen in the river near Capner's stags. On going to ths place. he found the body floating in the water, the head being completely immersed, and the legs held oat of the water by an accumulation of mud and brambles. He at once got some canvass and a rope and hauled the body to the bank. It was greatly decom- posed, but he recognised it as that of the missing man Mor- rall. In the pockets he found 14s 9d, a tobacco pouch, and some papers. The papers were so rotten as to render the writing they bore undecipherable—Mr. Cook, with whom . the deceased lodge,l. said that about half-past four on the . . _ .
To in his Cf/

morning of the -28th November he heard the deceased leave the house, and on wing downstairs found the letter addressed to the deceased's brother. Deceased had been low-spirited for Bonne- time, and had eften said he would never get better. The deceased's bed had not been laid on during the night previous to his disappearance When the deceased was free•from the attacks referred to " he would sing like a nightingale."—Joseph Morrell, father to the deceased, said his son had been despondent for a long time. Some time since when deceased was passing the cemetery, where his mother was buried, be said" Oh, I wish I was lying by the side of my mother."-The jury returned a verdict of "Founi drowned.' —The foreman, Mr. Joseph Taylor, thought that it ought to be su4gested to the Chief Constable that the re- ward of £ll .be divided between the two officers (Sergeant Spinks and P.C. Holstead), who had the unpleasant duty of taking the body out of the water, and these who save the information of the body having been seen in the river.—The Coroner, who, however, said he had no control' over the reward, and the jury concurred in the foreman's remarks.

div.p: THE WARRINGTON THEATRE OF VARIETIES. ITS SAFETY FOR STAGE PLAYS. _

- At a meetitg of the Street Improvement and Lightint Committee of the Corporatlon, held on the 20th December last, a recommendation was adopted to the effect "Tint the Town Clerk give the necessary notice to the owner of the wood building in Sankey-street, known as the Theatre of Varieties, to remove the same, such notice to expire at the same time as the licence to perform stage plays in such betiding expires.—The Borough Surveyor submitted the following correspondence, which was ordered to be entered on the minutes:—

To the Street Improvement Committee.—Gentlemen —I am in receint of a letter from H. B. White, Fsq., clerk to the magistrates, of which the following is a copy :—" Dear beg to inform you that the magistrates at the Police Court on Monday last, on granting "Sr. Brinsley Sheridan a theitric al license for the Oben.. in Sankey-street, instructed me to with- hold, the same wont he produced to me a certificate-signed by you that Mr. Sheridan has done all in his power to prevent a fire occurring by having elated ail scenery, &e., with a sub- stance called 'cyaritte.' and by having provided 'eatincteurs,' and by having done all things that you think necessary for the safety of the public. On your giving the certificate, therefore, I will hand the license to Mr. Sheridsn.—Tours truly, (signed) if. B. WRITE, Clerk to the Borough ~lustices.' I consider it my duty to report to your committee in reference tothe building, seeing that you imposed certain conditions on Browd, the present owner and occupier, which have not been caned out. I have ascertained from ' Mr. Sheridan the position is which he proposes to put the scenery on the stage, and else the gas lights, required for the introduction ot stage plays. I consider the float or top lights, if carried oat as understood frmn. Mr. Sheridan's sketch and description, to be a great improvement‘upon the present lighting, and as far as possible a protection t the scenery. He also proposes to have : two' extincteurs," one on each sideof the stage, al ways charged with water, and Jones' fire extinguishing preparation, in the event of any fire emergency. The mode hi which he proposers to place wins and scenery is also an improvement upon what at present exists. This building when first constructed was not designed for a theatre, and would recommend to your committee that the following work and conditions should be carried out before any performance be allowed :.-Ist. That part of the south gable be covered with felting, to prevent the wind passing throughlhe open jalnts of bosrdings, and thus causing a current of air whfch would en- danoer the boarders from being set in motion and coming into o contact with any asts light. 2nd. That no side lights of any description be fixed. 3rd That the borders and all woodwork over the stage be coated with " Cyanite." 4th That no smoking be allowed on the premises.--TIIGX&S LONGDM, borough surveyor.—Dee. 20th, 1883.

The committee, while declining to take any responsibility with regard to the safety of the building, believe that the precautions recommended by the Borough Surveyor will diminish, but not do away wial the serious risk.

ITO THE FREEHOLDERS OF THE SOUTI-WEST DIVISION OF THE COUNTY OF LA.NCASTER. OFFICE OF CORONER. -- MY LORDS AND ORNTLEMEN,—The plat of °ironer for this Division of the County of Lancaster having become vacant in consequence of the dreadful accident in Pemberton, which caused the death of ths late T. W. Barker, Esq., I beg to an- nounce myself as a candidate for the office, and confidently to solicit your votes and support. I was admitted a solicitor in 1819, I have acted as Coroner for the Borough of Wigan for nearly ten years, and as the late Mr. Barker's deputy for this division of the oxinty since his appointments, during which I period 1 have had experience in inquiries resulting from all classes of accidents, and have held neatly I,ooi inquests. Raving always discharged these dela in a manner which I believe to have been satisfactory both to the county and borough authorities referred to, to yourselves and the public, I respect- fully submit my claims on the present occasion to your favour- able consideration. It will be impossible for me to have like pleasure of making a personal canvass of 91 large a conatita- ency, but my experience as Coroner and Deputy Coroner hats already made zee known to very many of the freelso'ders of the district. To thise gentlemen I refer, with every reliance for their opinion as to my ability and fitness for the appointment I now desire to have the honour of filling.-1 am, my Lords and Gentlemen, your obedient servant. LEVER R. ROWBOTTOM. Wigan, January 2nd. 1.13F4. COUNTY PALATINE OF LANCASTER.

COUNTY PALATINE okr LANCASTER. ELECTION OF COBONER. TO THE FREEHOLDERS OF THE WEST DERBY Mr LORDS AND GENTLEMAN, The melancholy death of Mr. Barker, Coroner for this Division or the Conre.y of Lan- caster (in whose favour I withdrew my candidature just a year ago) again puts the office in the gift of the Freeholders; and I beg thus formally to renew my application for the appoint- ment. Later print -of this address will be accompanied by a list of Noblemen and Gentlemen favourable to my present can- didature. Among these are numerous Magistrates of the St. Helens Prescot, and Widnes Divisions; several of the collea- gues with whom I have had the pleasure of acting in Ihe St. Helens Town Council; and others with whom I have had the honour from time to time of being associated, as to some in public movements, and as to others in a professional capacity. I have now practised as a Solicitor and Notary In my native Borough of St. Helens and its neighbourhood for between nine ,1 and ten years, and am, therefore, well known to a considerable. section of the voters in the forthcoming election. During that period I have, of course, from time to time appeared before the- successive County Coroners, their Deputies, and the Coroner for the City of Liverpool, and, still more frequently, in impor- tant cases before Magistrates and County Court , Jodges and Juries ; and have In these and other I ways, become sufficiently Seminar wlitta the law of evidence and the conduct of judicial investigations. I am decfdly of opinion that more wiling publicity should be given to the proceeding, of the Coroner's Court; that repre- sentatives or the Pr,es should be admitted as of right; and that , every facility should be afroftled to those attending its sittings. I either as friends of a deceased person or on behaif of other af- fected Interests, to extract the full circumstances of each fatal. , ity, and ascertain the attendant liabilities. My only difference , with the late Coroner, during his year of highly meritorious office, and that a perfectly friendly one, was on the question of addressing a Jury over whom he was presiding. Unless aocom- panted with this privilege of address, the right of ecoss-examin- , ing witnesses is often a feeble agency; and, in my view, tends to keep Coroner's Inquests out of en- I lightened harmony with modern legal institutions. i By far the larger numiaer of Inquests in this divisian take place in St. Helens and the neighbaurlng manufactsring towns of , Warrington, Widnes, and Earlestown. St. Helens is not -only a natural centre for the places just mention id. but is also within easy reach of every other district of the Division; if elected, I should continueto resida there; and, apart from all other con- siderations, it may be pointed out that an annual saving to the County in the matter of Coroner's mileage, to be measured by hundreds of pounds, would result from such an arrangement. I trust that the prospect of these possible reforms may secure me a large and intelligent poll. Every owner of a Freehold in any part of the County, no molter how small its value, provided such owner resides in the West Derby Division, is entitled to one of the votes which I am soliciting. • Permit me to subscribe myself, . My Lords arid Gentlemen, Your most obedient Servant, • HY. LINDON HILLY. 8, Hardshaw-street, Bt. Helens, 4th January, 1884,

TO THE FREEHOLDERS Olf. THE WEST DERBY . DIVISION OF THE. COUNTY OF LANCASTER. -- MY LORDS IND GERTLEMaX,—Owing to the lamented death ot my friend, Mr. T. W. Barker, the Coroner for this Division of the County, that office has become vacant. I beg most re- spectfully to offer myself as a candidate. I am a Barrister-at- Law of ten years' standing, and have beea one of the Deputy Coroners for this County for the past three years. I am a resident in this district, and having practised my profession, and also held many inquests within it for both Mr. Driffield and the late Coroner, I am personally }mown to many of 3-6 u. Should you do me the honour to elect me to the anc?ent and re sponsible office of Coroner for this division of the County, I will endeavour to merit your kindness by discharging my duty honestly, patiently, and courteously, and to the best of my ability. I have the honour to subscribe myself, • My Lords and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, WILLIAM HARDY. Pemberton, near Wigan, Jan, 3, 1834.
